It landed on Depression Cherry as one of the record's heavier, more shoegaze-leaning tracks. Releasing two albums out of one extended session was a first for the duo.

adrianne lenker|free treasure.fact: Adrianne Lenker has called "Free Treasure" one of her all-time favorite songs she's written, and its title came about by accident: she was singing it on a friend's stoop when Big Thief bandmate James Krivchenia chimed in with the words "free treasure" during the last chorus, and it stuck. The song landed on her 2024 album Bright Future, which earned a Grammy nomination for Best Folk Album, with singer Mat Davidson joining her on vocal and guitar harmonies.

vampire weekend|one (blake's got a new f.fact: Despite the odd parenthetical, there really is a Blake behind this Vampire Weekend deep cut: Ezra Koenig met a friend of his girlfriend's named Blake, and the name just stuck in his head. He had the melody worked out long before he had any lyrics, and he's said the song's loose energy actually traces back to a Metallica reference. It closes out side one of the band's self-titled 2008 debut.

this is lorelei feat. snail mail|two leg.fact: When Nate Amos, who records as This Is Lorelei, put together a deluxe reissue of Box for Buddy, Box for Star with guest reworkings, his very first thought was getting Snail Mail's Lindsey Jordan to sing "Two Legs." Jordan has called Amos one of the best songwriters of their generation and said recording vocals for it was a treat because it meant hearing his songwriting over and over. The redone version keeps the original's old-timey sampled texture but wraps it in Jordan's airy, doubled vocals.

squid|crispy skin.fact: "Crispy Skin" opens with a synth intro that nods to The Who's "Baba O'Riley" before Squid's jagged guitars take over. It's a single from their 2025 album Cowards, produced by longtime collaborator Dan Carey and featuring an unusually wide cast of guests, including Danish songwriter Clarissa Connelly, composer Tony Njoku, and the Ruisi Quartet on strings. The record was actually finished before the band's previous album, O Monolith, had even come out.

being dead|nightvision.fact: "Nightvision" was the third single from Being Dead's 2024 album EELS, produced by John Congleton. It's a quieter turn for the Texas trio, opening with a subdued, almost pop-leaning hook before an acoustic rhythm pulls it into folkier, nocturnal territory. The track runs under three minutes and sits as one of the album's moodiest detours.

hovvdy|bad news.fact: "Bad News" marked the first time since their 2016 debut Taster that both Hovvdy members, Charlie Martin and Will Taylor, traded off verses on the same song. It appears on their self-titled 2024 album, released to mark a full decade of the duo making music together. Martin has described it as "a whirlwind song about reckless behavior and the unlikely characters that weave in and out of your life."

sault|bitter streets.fact: "Bitter Streets" appears on Nine, one of several albums from SAULT, the deliberately mysterious UK collective led by producer Inflo and singer Cleo Sol. The group has built its reputation on surprise releases, dropping five full albums at once with almost no warning in 2022 alone. For years the band kept its lineup so secretive that fans and critics could only slowly piece together who was actually behind the music.

beach house|wild.fact: "Wild" was actually the earliest song Beach House wrote for their 2012 album Bloom, coming together while they were still mixing the previous record, Teen Dream. It was tracked during an intensive nine-week session at Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas. The song stands out in their catalog for its dramatic build and climax, capped by a shoegaze-leaning electric guitar bridge that's more amped-up than the duo's usual dream-pop sound.

chezile|beanie.fact: When "Beanie" dropped in late 2023, Chezile was essentially homeless and facing serious financial struggles; then the song took off on Spotify and TikTok's global viral charts and turned him into a name everyone suddenly knew. Despite the title, the word "beanie" never actually appears anywhere in the lyrics. Chezile wrote and produced the track himself, building it around a sampled loop under his own dreamy, bedroom-pop production.

feeble little horse|doorway.fact: "Doorway" opens feeble little horse's album bitknot, and it exists because of a happy accident: band members were driving when a scratched CD kept skipping between the same two seconds of audio, and they decided to build a song that sounded just like that glitch. It starts with a blast of feedback before settling into murmured vocals over drum machines and keyboards. One of the band's members has called making it one of his favorite memories from the record.

brent amaker and the rodeo|gut feeling.fact: Brent Amaker & The Rodeo's "Gut Feeling" is a spoken-word country cover of a deep cut from DEVO's debut album. The Seattle group, known for dressing entirely in black with cowboy hats, first made waves in cover circles with a country rendition of Kraftwerk's "Pocket Calculator" back in 2010. Amaker speaks the lyrics over a stripped-down arrangement, trading the original's tacked-on rave-up ending for a cleaner finish built around the guitar solo.

being dead|godzilla rises.fact: "Godzilla Rises" comes from Austin art-punk trio Being Dead's 2024 album EELS, produced by John Congleton. Despite the title, it's actually a tender love song addressed to the giant movie monster himself. The band's members -- Falcon Bitch, Shmoofy, and Nicole Roman-Johnston -- are known for swapping instruments and trading lead vocals throughout their live sets.

preoccupations|focus.fact: "Focus" is the lead single from Preoccupations' fifth album, Ill at Ease, out on Born Losers Records. The Calgary post-punk band's Matt Flegel co-produced the track with bandmate Scott "Monty" Munro, giving their usually shadowy sound an unexpected shimmer, with guitar work inspired by INXS. It's one of the shinier moments yet from a band built on darker post-punk.

sufjan stevens|the only thing.fact: "The Only Thing" is a hushed, finger-picked highlight from Sufjan Stevens' 2015 album Carrie & Lowell. For this record, Stevens did something he rarely does -- he handed over co-production duties to pianist and arranger Thomas Bartlett. The track also features guitar from Casey Foubert and Ben Lester, and was mixed by Stevens, Bartlett, and Patrick Dillett.

iron and wine|tree by the river.fact: "Tree by the River" appears on Iron & Wine's 2011 album Kiss Each Other Clean, the fourth record from Samuel Beam's long-running project. Beam built the album around recurring water and river imagery, using the river as a metaphor for both destruction and renewal. This particular song leans into pure nostalgia, painting a wistful snapshot of young love and adolescence.

cate le bon and bradford cox|secretary.fact: "Secretary" paired Welsh singer-songwriter Cate Le Bon with Deerhunter's Bradford Cox on their collaborative EP Myths 004. The two wrote and recorded the whole EP in just one week at a studio in Marfa, Texas, back in April 2018. The song itself is a cheeky tribute to bored office workers stuck eating "the same old plastic lunch."

wishy|fly.fact: Wishy is an Indianapolis indie-rock band built around Kevin Krauter, formerly of the band Hoops, and Nina Pitchkites, who actually met years earlier as students at Carmel High School. They didn't form Wishy together until 2021, after following separate musical paths. "Fly" opens their 2025 EP Planet Popstar.

beatrix|turn you down.fact: "Turn You Down" comes from Beatrix's sophomore album We Swallowed the Sky, the project of Los Angeles songwriter Arielle Kasnetz. Kasnetz grew up training in classical piano and vocal scales but didn't start writing her own songs until the pandemic, when she picked up an acoustic guitar she'd been given years earlier. For this album she worked as a trio with co-producers Philip Etherington and Ehren Ebbage.

mission of burma|that's when i reach for.fact: Mission of Burma bassist Clint Conley wrote and sang "That's When I Reach for My Revolver" for the band's 1981 EP Signals, Calls and Marches. It found a huge second audience in 1996 when electronic artist Moby covered it as the first single from his album Animal Rights. Moby even recorded an alternate, radio-friendly vocal take so MTV would air the video, retitling that version "That's When I Realize It's Over."

sasami|i'll be gone.fact: "I'll Be Gone" is a track from SASAMI's 2025 album Blood on the Silver Screen, written and composed by Sasami Ashworth. When the album got a deluxe "Director's Cut" reissue, the song came back in a whole new form: a remix by comedian and actress Patti Harrison.

mike d|switch up.fact: "Switch Up" is Beastie Boys member Mike D's debut solo single, and the first new music from anyone in that group since 2011. The track actually started as a home-studio experiment with his sons, Davis and Skyler Diamond, who record together as the duo Very Nice Person, with additional production from Carter Lang. Mike D even premiered the song live, dropping it online while he was still on stage at a sold-out LA show.

broken social scene|only the good i keep.fact: "Only the Good I Keep" is the second track on Broken Social Scene's 2026 album Remember the Humans, the Canadian collective's first new record in nearly a decade. For this song the band handed the mic to singer Hannah Georgas, who steps forward to lead it with striking clarity.

portishead|all mine.fact: "All Mine" was the lead single from Portishead's self-titled second album, released in 1997. Written by Geoff Barrow, Beth Gibbons, and Adrian Utley, and produced by the band with Dave McDonald, it became the Bristol trip-hop group's only song to crack the UK Top 10, peaking at number 8.

vampire weekend|campus.fact: "Campus" is built entirely around Columbia University, where Vampire Weekend's members met and formed the band. The lyrics reference real spots on campus -- Low Plaza and South Lawn get a shoutout, and the balcony in the bridge is Hamilton Hall. Former member Rostam wrote the music around a scenario from Ezra Koenig's short story "Cruel Professor," capturing the awkwardness of running into an old crush on campus every day.

lucy dacus|fool's gold.fact: Lucy Dacus wrote "Fool's Gold" right after hosting a New Year's Eve party, sitting alone in the quiet once every guest had gone home. Rather than being about a specific breakup, the song is more about the anxious overthinking that comes with a new year -- worrying you won't get where you hope to be, while still trying to trust that you will. It was released as a standalone single in 2019.

stereolab|aerial troubles.fact: "Aerial Troubles" marked Stereolab's return after a 15-year break, serving as the first single from their 2025 album Instant Holograms on Metal Film. The track rides a motorik beat from drummer Andy Ramsay, with a phaser-soaked guitar line from Tim Gane underneath Laetitia Sadier's harmonized vocals.

the beths|metal.fact: "Metal" is a single from The Beths' fourth album, Straight Line Was a Lie, released in 2025 on Anti- Records. The New Zealand band built the whole record around the idea that life doesn't improve in a straight line, but moves in cycles instead -- a theme "Metal" helped introduce before the album was even announced.

tiberius|painting of a tree.fact: Tiberius started as a solo project for songwriter Brendan Wright before growing into a four-piece out of Boston who call their sound "farm emo." The title "Painting of a Tree" comes from an offhand line Wright once heard from an eccentric older man: "an artist cannot paint a tree, unless they examine all aspects of it." The song appears on their 2025 album Troubadour.

turnstile|never enough.fact: "Never Enough" is the title track and lead single from Turnstile's fourth album, which came out in June 2025 on Roadrunner Records. The song gave the Baltimore hardcore band their first number one on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart, and the album went on to win Best Rock Album at the Grammys.

blu detiger|dangerous game.fact: "Dangerous Game" comes from bassist Blu DeTiger, who started playing bass at just seven years old. She wrote, produced, and played nearly every instrument on the track herself ahead of her 2024 debut studio album, All I Ever Want Is Everything.

victoryland|the ugliest girl on the beac.fact: Victoryland is a partnership between singer-songwriter Julian McCamman and producer Dan Howard, and "The Ugliest Girl on the Beach" marked a big milestone for the project -- it arrived alongside the announcement that the band had signed to the indie label Dead Oceans. The track is set to appear as a bonus song on the deluxe edition of their debut album, My Heart Is a Room with No Cameras in It.

american football|wake her up (feat. wis.fact: "Wake Her Up" teams Midwest emo pioneers American Football with shoegaze artist Wisp, appearing on American Football's fourth self-titled album from 2026. Frontman Mike Kinsella has called it the band's "best Smiths impression to date." The music video, co-directed by skate filmmaker Ty Evans and Oscar-winning director Cord Jefferson, follows Kinsella and Wisp on nighttime bike rides through Los Angeles while dreamlike images of Paris are projected around them.

arlo parks|heaven.fact: "Heaven" is a single from Arlo Parks' upcoming album Ambiguous Desire, a notable change of direction for the Mercury Prize-winning British singer. The song's driving bassline was inspired by an early-morning DJ set she caught from her friend, electronic artist Kelly Lee Owens, marking Parks' deepest dive yet into dance-music production.

lala lala|does this go faster?.fact: Lala Lala is the project of Chicago singer-songwriter Lillie West, and "Does This Go Faster?" arrived as her first song after signing to Sub Pop. It was co-produced by West and Melina Duterte of Jay Som, with Abby Black on drums and Sen Morimoto adding saxophone. West wrote the swirling, synth-driven track while traveling alone in Iceland, after putting her belongings in storage and stepping back from her old life to figure out what came next.

vampire weekend|pravda.fact: "Pravda," from Vampire Weekend's 2024 album Only God Was Above Us, takes its title from the Russian word for truth. Frontman Ezra Koenig has said the song was inspired partly by his own family history: his great-uncle Henry Shapiro was a longtime Moscow correspondent, and Koenig grew up hearing his grandmother's proud stories about her brother. The track even weaves in a balalaika as it muses on memory, time, and distance from home.

mac demarco|20191009 i like her.fact: "20191009 I Like Her" is one of 199 tracks on Mac DeMarco's 2023 surprise release One Wayne G, a nearly nine-hour compilation of demos recorded between 2018 and 2023. True to the album's concept, every song is titled with the date it was made, so this one was recorded on October 9, 2019. It's one of the more fleshed-out, lyric-driven demos on a tracklist that's mostly instrumental sketches.

spiritualized|here it comes.fact: The full title of this Spiritualized song is "Here It Comes (The Road) Let's Go," the lead single from 2018's And Nothing Hurt. Frontman Jason Pierce has described its lyrics as essentially "a list of instructions that, if followed, allows the listener to find my house," turning directions home into a sweeping, horn-and-harmony-soaked anthem. It's one of the more uplifting, cosmic-country moments in the band's catalog.

radiohead|feral.fact: "Feral" is one of the most abstract, largely instrumental tracks on Radiohead's 2011 album The King of Limbs, produced by longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich. Thom Yorke's voice is chopped into yelps and stutters that function more like another percussion part than a lead vocal, set against itchy, tribal drum patterns influenced by the dubstep and electronic scene surrounding artists like Burial and Four Tet. Fans and critics have often singled it out as the most compelling, fully-formed moment on an album that was initially underrated.

@|autosmile.fact: @ is the Philadelphia duo of Victoria Rose and Stone Filipczak, who built a cult following in the American underground with their acclaimed 2021 psych-folk debut Mind Palace Music. "Autosmile" is the title track of their first album for the label 4AD, a sprawling seven-minute ballad that leans into minimal acoustic guitar and the pair's intertwined vocal melodies rather than the electronic flourishes they're also known for.

red pk|brother.fact: Red PK is the project of Andy "Red" PK, a Chicago-based pedal steel and guitar player who spent years as a sideman for bands like Ratboys, Squirrel Flower, and Free Range before stepping out as a solo artist. "Brother" appears on Horse Like Me, his 2026 debut LP and the first time he'd recorded his own songs in a proper studio, working alongside friends Seth Engel and Nick Levine. Andy only picked up pedal steel a few years earlier, before quitting a day job in marketing in 2025 to pursue music full time.

black country, new road|happy birthday.fact: "Happy Birthday" is a baroque-pop single from Black Country, New Road's 2025 album Forever Howlong, the band's first studio release since 2022's Ants from Up There and since three members stepped up to share lead vocals. Critics compared its ornate arrangement to Joanna Newsom and The Beatles, and the band paired it with a stop-motion music video directed by Lesley-Anne Rose. Lyrically, it's a wry reminder that privilege doesn't guarantee happiness.

yeule|anthems for a seventeen year-old g.fact: yeule's cover of Broken Social Scene's "Anthems for a Seventeen Year-Old Girl" was recorded for the soundtrack to the 2024 film I Saw the TV Glow. Director Jane Schoenbrun had originally asked yeule to write an original song, but once the two started talking about this Broken Social Scene classic, they agreed a cover was the better fit. yeule's glitchy, digitally warped version speeds up the melody while keeping the emotional core of the original intact.

husker du|i apologize.fact: "I Apologize" appears on Hüsker Dü's sprawling 1984 concept album Zen Arcade, which the Minneapolis trio tracked and mixed in roughly two marathon days at a studio in Redondo Beach, California. Nearly the whole record, including this song, is first takes, a pace so punishing that singer Bob Mould's voice was reportedly shot by the end of the session. Despite the chaotic recording, "I Apologize" is often singled out as one of the album's most melodic, almost power-pop moments.

ken park|crawl.fact: Ken Park is the solo project of Liam Creamer, a San Diego native now based in New York who writes wistful, coming-of-age indie rock about the growing pains of chasing your dreams far from home. "Crawl" appears on his self-titled debut EP, released in February 2026 on TODO Records, built around an acoustic arrangement meant to evoke nostalgia mixed with optimism. Creamer has said it features some of the EP's most emotional vocal work.

neutral milk hotel|you've passed.fact: "You've Passed" is the second track on Neutral Milk Hotel's 1996 debut On Avery Island, produced by Robert Schneider of the Apples in Stereo as part of the lo-fi Elephant 6 recording collective. An alternate version, taped at frontman Jeff Mangum's father's house, later surfaced on a box set years afterward. Despite rarely being played live, it's frequently cited by critics as one of the best songs in the band's catalog.

l'rain|pet rock.fact: "Pet Rock" comes from L'Rain's 2023 album I Killed Your Dog, released through Mexican Summer. Brooklyn multi-instrumentalist Taja Cheek, who records as L'Rain, has described the hazy, guitar-driven track as "a morose ode to the white dad rock I never listened to." It's built on bright, twisting guitar lines under her serene, fuzzed-out vocals.

wallows|your apartment.fact: "Your Apartment" marked Wallows' first new music after their 2022 album Tell Me That It's Over, released as the lead single from 2024's Model. The song was co-written with Nate Mercereau, who has also worked with Andre 3000 and Shawn Mendes, and produced by John Congleton, known for his work with St. Vincent and Sharon Van Etten. It's a fast-paced, hook-driven track built around racing percussion and earworm guitar riffs.

wilco|we were lucky.fact: "We Were Lucky" comes from Wilco's 2019 album Ode to Joy, which frontman Jeff Tweedy built out from simple song sketches he first recorded with drummer Glenn Kotche before the rest of the band filled them in. That process gives the record, and this track, a stripped-down, minimalist feel, with Kotche's steady, understated drumming driving much of the album rather than his usual intricate percussion work. It's a quieter, more intimate turn for a band known for sprawling arrangements.

shelby natasha|it was mine.fact: Seattle songwriter and producer Shelby Natasha wrote "It Was Mine" for a project run by the Bushwick Bookclub, where musicians create songs inspired by whatever book the group is reading. At the time it was Isabel Allende's novel Violeta, narrated by an elderly woman looking back on her life, and Shelby has said the character reminded her of her own grandmother. The song, which blends Chinese folk influences with lo-fi R&B, appears on her debut EP released in 2026.

unknown mortal orchestra|heaven 7.fact: "Heaven 7" is one of eight tracks on Unknown Mortal Orchestra's instrumental album IC-02 Bogota, released in 2025 as the second entry in a series documenting the band improvising music in different cities around the world. The band traveled to Bogota, Colombia and recorded at Estudio Naranja partly to help break in their new keyboardist, Christian Li, jamming out hypnotic, largely wordless material. The series began with 2018's IC-01 Hanoi.

hatchie|lights on.fact: "Lights On" opens Hatchie's 2023 album Giving the World Away, the follow-up to her breakout debut Keepsake. The Australian dream-pop artist built the song around a drum beat inspired by Siouxsie and the Banshees' "Kiss Them for Me," and has said writing it pushed her to write more directly and personally than before. The accompanying video was directed by her longtime guitarist and collaborator Joe Agius.

weyes blood|grapevine.fact: "Grapevine" takes its title from the notorious stretch of Interstate 5 that climbs through Southern California's Tejon Pass, which Natalie Mering, who records as Weyes Blood, uses as a metaphor for old emotional entanglements that twist around us. She co-wrote and produced the track with Jonathan Rado for her 2022 album And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow. The song opens on acoustic guitar before eerie bells ring out over the chorus.

zzzahara|ghosts.fact: "Ghosts" is the lead single from zzzahara's 2025 album Spiral Your Way Out on Lex Records, blending influences from 2000s emo acts like Dashboard Confessional and Scene Aesthetic into a stripped-back, vocal-forward arrangement. The accompanying video, directed by Hannah Bon, renders zzzahara in 3D animation trapped in a surreal dream world, complete with singing cats and ghosts spilling out of lava lamps. It's a playful visual counterpoint to the song's moody tone.

father john misty|bored in the usa.fact: Father John Misty — real name Josh Tillman — built an actual canned laugh track right into the studio recording of 'Bored in the USA,' timing the laughs to land right after some of the song's bleakest lines, a trick he said was meant for 'neutralizing uncomfortable ideas.' When he performed it live on Late Show with David Letterman in 2014, his organ player cued the laughter in real time, leaving the TV audience unsure whether it was a real crowd laughing or part of the act. It remains one of the stranger production gags in modern singer-songwriter music.

american football|no feeling.fact: 'No Feeling' comes from American Football's fourth self-titled album, released in 2026, and features guest harmony vocals from Brendan Yates, frontman of the hardcore band Turnstile. Mike Kinsella told NME that Yates was originally supposed to be just one of several voices on a call-and-response chorus part, but after Yates asked to try a higher harmony of his own, his voice was so distinctive the part became his alone. It's a rare genre-crossing cameo between two very different corners of the rock world.

car seat headrest|overexsposed (enjoy).fact: 'Overexposed (Enjoy)' dates back to Car Seat Headrest's prolific Bandcamp years, appearing on the 2012 self-released album Monomania when Will Toledo was still a teenager recording dozens of albums alone in his bedroom. The track actually samples another one of his own songs, 'Sober to Death,' making it an early example of Toledo remixing himself years before he ever had a real audience. It's a neat piece of trivia for a songwriter who'd reach indie rock prominence a few years later with Teens of Denial.

beirut|a candle's fire.fact: 'A Candle's Fire' opens Beirut's 2011 album The Rip Tide with a single accordion that blooms into a full horn section, the signature sound bandleader Zach Condon built his career on. The track features Jon Natchez on baritone saxophone and background vocals from fellow singer-songwriter Sharon Van Etten. It's one of the brassiest, most orchestral moments on a record that otherwise leans into quieter, more intimate songwriting.

wild nothing|a dancing shell.fact: 'A Dancing Shell' comes from Wild Nothing's 2013 EP Empty Estate, recorded at Gary's Electric studio in Brooklyn in January of that year. The track opens with washy, wave-like percussion and a chirping synth arpeggio before building into a genuinely funky dance groove, with a burst of brass kicking in after the two-minute mark. It was a notable left turn for a band that made its name on dreamy, jangly guitar pop.

m83|lune de fiel.fact: 'Lune de Fiel' comes from M83 mastermind Anthony Gonzalez's 2019 album DSVII, which he recorded entirely on analog synthesizers as an homage to vintage video game soundtracks and '80s sci-fi film scores. The song's music video forms the second chapter of 'Extazus,' a three-part black-and-white short film directed by French filmmaker Bertrand Mandico. It's a good example of M83's ongoing side career of pairing its music with ambitious visual storytelling.

alabama shakes|sound & color.fact: The title track that opens Alabama Shakes' 2015 album Sound & Color begins not with guitars but with a vibraphone, an instrument nobody expected from the raw Alabama blues-rock band after their stripped-down debut. Brittany Howard and keyboardist Ben Tanner both played vibraphone on the track, which gradually builds into a lush string arrangement. The unexpected instrumentation set the tone for an album that pushed the band into much more experimental territory.

pup|olive garden.fact: 'Olive Garden' started life as a quiet acoustic guitar demo written by PUP singer Stefan Babcock, until drummer Zack Mykula heard it and pushed the band to make it as heavy as possible instead. The finished version, recorded with producer John Congleton in Los Angeles in 2024, buries that sweet vocal melody under a wall of detuned, grinding guitars on the band's 2025 album Who Will Look After the Dogs?. It's a good snapshot of PUP's habit of turning soft ideas into some of their loudest songs.

boygenius|me & my dog.fact: 'Me & My Dog' first appeared on boygenius' self-titled 2018 debut EP, one of several nearly finished songs each member brought into the studio for that project. The band loved the song's live ending so much — the house lights coming up at a sold-out Brooklyn Steel show that year — that they sampled the crowd's cheers from that exact moment and wove them into 'Letter to an Old Poet,' the closing track of their 2023 album the record. It's a rare case of a band sampling their own earlier concert to tie two albums together.

amyl and the sniffers|doing in me head.fact: Guitarist Dec Martens originally wrote 'Doing in Me Head' as a disco track inspired by the Gap Band, but once Amyl and the Sniffers got hold of it, it turned into a vocoder-laced punk song influenced by the Beastie Boys. It appears on the band's 2024 album Cartoon Darkness, which they recorded with producer Nick Launay at Dave Grohl's Studio 606 — on the very same mixing desk used for Nirvana's Nevermind and Fleetwood Mac's Rumours. Not bad company for an Australian punk band's growing catalog.

the smile|bodies laughing.fact: 'Bodies Laughing' appears on The Smile's 2024 album Cutouts, which was recorded during the very same sessions as its predecessor, Wall of Eyes. Thom Yorke and the band actually debuted the song live at a concert in Berlin back in 2022, two years before fans ever heard the studio version, which features Jonny Greenwood's ondes Martenot weaving through the mix. The Smile played that earlier live arrangement dozens of times before retooling it for the album.

cut worms|long weekend.fact: 'Long Weekend' comes from Cut Worms' 2026 album Transmitter, which bandleader Max Clarke recorded at Wilco's Loft studio in Chicago with Jeff Tweedy producing. Tweedy made the offer after Cut Worms opened for Wilco on tour, and the resulting track channels the melodic urgency of power-pop forebears like Big Star. It's a full-circle moment for a songwriter who grew up on exactly that kind of jangly guitar pop.

phoebe bridgers|lost boys.fact: 'Lost Boys' is the lead single from Phoebe Bridgers' 2026 album Lost Weekend, co-written with Christian Lee Hutson, Marshall Vore, Bo Burnham, and Alex G. Its music video reunites Bridgers with her boygenius bandmates Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus, alongside Alex G, for a medieval-themed visual. It's a nice reminder of how tightly connected this whole circle of indie songwriters really is.

cheekface|popular 2.fact: 'Popular 2' is a deadpan, upbeat single off Cheekface's 2024 album It's Sorted, built around the very modern itch to be noticed in a neighborhood full of doorbell cameras and porch security feeds. Frontman Greg Katz has described the album's running idea as the tug-of-war between wanting to belong to a community and wanting to stand out as an individual. It's classic Cheekface: a weird, hyper-specific observation turned into a genuinely catchy chorus.

been stellar|passing judgement.fact: 'Passing Judgement' is the lead single and second track off Been Stellar's 2024 debut album Scream From New York, NY, produced by Dan Carey. The band was still finishing the song's lyrics during their first-ever UK tour in the summer of 2022, which gives the final recording its loose, slightly chaotic live energy. Singer Sam Slocum has said the song is really about how judging others often comes from feeling unsure of yourself.

anna burch|not so bad.fact: Anna Burch wrote 'Not So Bad' just one day before heading into the studio to record her 2020 album If You're Dreaming, realizing the record needed one hopeful, escapist pop song to balance its more melancholy moments. Produced by Sam Evian, the track came together almost immediately, built around a light, jazzy chord progression and swirling saxophone. Burch has said her mom used to tease her for how sad her lyrics usually were — this one was the exception.

bjork and rosalina|oral.fact: Despite the title, 'Oral' is a 2023 charity duet between Björk and Rosalía written to protest industrial open-net salmon farming in Iceland. Björk actually wrote the song decades earlier, somewhere between her albums Homogenic and Vespertine, before rediscovering it in her archives while on tour in Australia. Both artists donated all proceeds from the song to AEGIS, a nonprofit formed to push back against the fish farms.

perfume genius|natural high.fact: 'Natural High' is Perfume Genius' first new song since his 2025 album Glory, co-produced with Pascal Stevenson of the band Fashion Club. The six-minute track was written for The Lesson, a music-and-dance stage collaboration with choreographer Kate Wallich, and gradually builds from moody keyboard figures into a full house-music rave-up by its end. It's a good showcase of how far Perfume Genius has pushed beyond traditional song structure in recent years.

vundabar|beta fish.fact: 'Beta Fish' is a single off Vundabar's 2025 album Surgery and Pleasure, the Boston trio's sixth record and first for the label Loma Vista. The hypnotic lyrics track the restless movement of a betta fish swimming in circles and biting at its own reflection, set to a repetitive, driving groove. Critics singled out the song's chanting final 90 seconds as some of the best songwriting on the whole record.

the stone souls|fuzz bass queen.fact: 'Fuzz Bass Queen' is a 2025 single from The Stone Souls, a desert-rock band out of Newcastle upon Tyne founded by Theodor Versteegen. Built around a heavily distorted, fuzzed-out bass line, the track mixes punk energy reminiscent of Green Day and Blink-182 with stoner-rock swagger, and its lyrics serve as a tribute to powerful women. One reviewer called it a contender for the best pop-punk anthem of the year.

red pk|get down.fact: 'Get Down' comes from Red PK's 2026 debut album Horse Like Me, recorded and mixed at Ohmstead studio in Chicago. The project is led by Andy 'Red' PK, a longtime touring guitarist and pedal steel player for Chicago bands like Squirrel Flower and Ratboys, who co-produced the record with drummer Seth Engel and close friend Nick Levine. It's his first time stepping out from behind other artists to front his own record.

genesis owusu|stampede.fact: 'STAMPEDE' is a standalone 2026 single from Ghanaian-Australian artist Genesis Owusu, released between his albums Struggler and Redstar Wu & the Worldwide Scourge. For the music video, Owusu returned to his home country of Ghana for the first time in eleven years, filming in the streets of Accra to spotlight local youth culture. He later performed the song as part of a cameo appearance on the TV series Heartbreak High.

beck|ride lonesome.fact: "Ride Lonesome" is the title track and opener of Beck's 15th studio album, released September 2026 — his first new album since 2019's Hyperspace, marking the longest gap of his career. He produced it himself and brought back longtime collaborator Nigel Godrich to mix, landing on the kind of intimate, cinematic sound that made his earlier records so beloved.

bonnie 'prince' billy|the world's greate.fact: Will Oldham, recording as Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, took R. Kelly's 2001 arena-sized anthem "The World's Greatest" and turned it into a hushed, mournful acoustic ballad for his 2007 covers EP Ask Forgiveness on Domino. It's a genre-hopping party trick he's pulled off more than once, finding the sad, quiet song hiding inside a big pop hit.

sufjan stevens|age of adz.fact: The title track of Sufjan Stevens' maximalist 2010 album The Age of Adz draws heavily on the prophetic, sci-fi-tinged visionary art of Royal Robertson, a self-taught Louisiana sign painter whose apocalyptic drawings Sufjan stumbled across and became fascinated with. That found artwork ended up shaping the record's whole cosmic, electronics-meets-orchestra sound.

bon iver|naeem.fact: This i,i (2019) track was originally titled "I Can Hear Crying," but Justin Vernon renamed it in honor of his friend and collaborator Naeem Juwan, the rapper/producer known as Spank Rock, who also co-wrote another song on the album. Vernon has called him "one of the most inspirational artists I know."

iron and wine|in your ocean.fact: Lead single from Iron & Wine's 2026 album Hen's Teeth, this one's a family affair — it marks the first time Sam Beam worked alongside his daughter Arden on a record, with the Grammy-winning Americana trio I'm With Her also guesting elsewhere on the LP.

show me the body|we came to play.fact: This ripper is the lead single off Show Me the Body's 2022 album Trouble the Water. True to the NYC band's signature, frontman Julian Cashwan Pratt still plays his trademark banjo on it — just run through a wall of effects and distortion, giving one of their most straightforwardly punky tracks an odd, twangy backbone.

stef chura|danny.fact: "Danny" is the lead single from Stef Chura's 2026 album Dancing Alone on the Concrete, her first LP in seven years. The horn-dusted, country-tinged track features a pretty unexpected guest pairing: R.E.M.'s Peter Buck and Mike Mills.

home is where|yes! yes! a thousands time.fact: Released in 2023 on Father/Daughter Records ahead of the album The Whaler, this is the Florida band's catchiest moment on record. Multi-instrumentalist Tilley Komorny said it has "the most pop elements" of anything they'd written, while still refusing to settle into a normal pop song structure — very on-brand for a band that treats midwest emo like a chemistry set.

beabadoobee|sun has set.fact: The first single from beabadoobee's 2026 album Pylon is a hard left turn into grunge and '90s alt-rock crunch, a heavier sound than anything she'd released before. She's said the lyrics came straight out of raw diary entries — words she once figured she'd never actually say out loud.

wilco|hearts hard to find.fact: This one's tucked into Wilco's sprawling 2022 double album Cruel Country, cut live at the band's own Chicago studio, The Loft. The sessions marked the first time all six members tracked together in one room since 2011's The Whole Love — Jeff Tweedy described that kind of live recording as "gathering around some wild collective instrument" that takes six sets of hands to play.

mitski|fireproof.fact: Mitski's "Fireproof" isn't actually a Mitski original — it's her cover of One Direction's song, recorded as a bonus track for the 2026 10th-anniversary deluxe reissue of Puberty 2. She swaps the boy-band original's soft acoustic strum for her own signature wall of fuzzed-out distortion.

alex cameron|strangers kiss with angel o.fact: This Springsteen-leaning duet with Angel Olsen comes from Alex Cameron's 2017 album Forced Witness, playing out as a couple trading barbed breakup advice. The music video, co-starring Girls' Jemima Kirke, follows two lonely strangers who find each other on a New York subway platform.

mac demarco|heart to heart.fact: From Mac DeMarco's 2019 album Here Comes the Cowboy, this breezy, laid-back track became his very first entry on the Billboard Hot 100, debuting at No. 98 — a quietly big milestone for an artist who built his following almost entirely outside the mainstream charts.

thao|sick of the times (ft. tune-yards,.fact: This is the lead single from Thao's upcoming 2026 album Show Me, her first in six years, co-produced by Tune-Yards' Merrill Garbus and Nate Brenner. It's a three-way team-up, stacking Thao's voice with Garbus and teenage punk outfit The Linda Lindas for one big, layered group vocal.

the national|your mind is not your frien.fact: Featuring Phoebe Bridgers, this track from The National's 2023 album First Two Pages of Frankenstein got its spark from an unlikely source: Matt Berninger grabbed Mary Shelley's novel off a shelf when he was stuck for inspiration, and the book's opening image of a ship adrift near the Arctic gave him the song's feeling of being unmoored. The video was directed by Bridgers' brother, Jackson.

cheekface|mft.fact: "MFT" is the third single from Cheekface's 2026 album Podium. True to the deadpan L.A. trio's style, the title is a dry acronym play on "MFT" — shorthand for Marriage and Family Therapist. Formed in 2017, the band pairs Greg Katz's talky lead vocals with Amanda Tannen on bass and Mark Edwards on drums.

goose|good times // end times.fact: Tucked away as track 13 on Goose's 2026 album BIG MODERN!, this shapeshifting, doomsday-clock-paced rocker had never been played live before the record came out. Its official video was directed by the band's longtime collaborator Will Thresher.

radiohead|subterranean homesick alien.fact: This OK Computer (1997) deep cut borrows its title from Bob Dylan's "Subterranean Homesick Blues," but the song itself traces back to a college essay Thom Yorke wrote imagining himself as an alien observing the people of Oxford. Radiohead layered in woozy electric piano chasing the vibe of Miles Davis' Bitches Brew.

the clash|straight to hell.fact: This 1982 Combat Rock track got a huge second life in 2007 when Diplo built the beat for M.I.A.'s 'Paper Planes' around its guitar riff, turning Joe Strummer, Mick Jones and the rest of The Clash into credited co-writers on one of the biggest crossover hits of the 2000s. The sample rippled even further when Jay-Z and T.I. sampled 'Paper Planes' itself for 'Swagga Like Us' — meaning a 25-year-old Clash riff ended up on a hip-hop chart hit too.

cake|the distance.fact: Released in 1996 as the first single off Fashion Nugget, 'The Distance' was actually written by CAKE's guitarist at the time, Greg Brown, who was surprised the band even picked it as a single. Frontman John McCrea has described it as a song about a race car driver straining toward a finish line he'll never reach — 'a song about success and failure, and failure of success.' It became CAKE's most enduring hit, climbing to No. 4 on the Alternative Airplay chart.

the magnetic fields|absolutely cuckoo.fact: This jaunty, ukulele-strummed opener was meant to kick off an even bigger project — Stephin Merritt first planned 69 Love Songs as a 100-song set before runtime reality set in. The whole album traces back to a songwriting dare Merritt set for himself, inspired by composer Charles Ives's 114 Songs, and 'Absolutely Cuckoo' still carries a trace of an even earlier plan to make the record alphabetical from A to Z.

tv on the radio|satellite.fact: 'Satellite' isn't just a deep cut — it's the very first TV on the Radio song ever officially released, opening the band's 2003 debut EP Young Liars. Built from Tunde Adebimpe's looped, near-barbershop vocal harmonies over David Sitek's fuzzed-out production, with a flute line courtesy of Antibalas's Martin Perna, it set the template for the band's genre-blending sound years before Dear Science made them indie-rock royalty.

alex cameron|red hook rain.fact: Alex Cameron has a side career you might not expect: he's co-written songs for the Killers, including tracks on Wonderful Wonderful and Imploding the Mirage. 'Red Hook Rain,' from his 2026 album Late to Set, was pitched by his own camp as 'Barry Gibb meets Martin Rev' — a heartbroken, hopeful detour written, fittingly, on the edge of an actual hurricane.

genesis owusu|runnin outta time.fact: By the time 'RUNNIN OUTTA TIME' came out, Genesis Owusu already had serious hardware on the shelf — his 2023 album Struggler won Album of the Year at the ARIA Awards. This track, from 2026's REDSTAR WU & THE WORLDWIDE SCOURGE, folds in New Order-style dance rhythms, turning one of the album's most exhausted stretches into one of its most danceable.

belle and sebastian|sleep the clock arou.fact: This nearly five-minute epic off 1998's The Boy with the Arab Strap features Isobel Campbell trading verses with Stuart Murdoch in one of the band's most richly arranged early duets. It's become a fan-favorite deep cut precisely because of that interplay — two voices circling each other over a patient, slow-build arrangement.

pulp|begging for change.fact: Pulp cut this one at the legendary Abbey Road Studios for War Child's HELP(2) charity album, with Damon Albarn, Grian Chatten, Kae Tempest and Carl Barat all pitching in on backing vocals alongside a children's choir. It's a full-circle moment for Jarvis Cocker: back in 1996, Pulp's Different Class lost the Mercury Prize to the original Help compilation, and Cocker still donated his band's own prize money to War Child.

the white stripes|hotel yorba.fact: The Hotel Yorba is a real, slightly run-down building in southwest Detroit that Jack White heard rumors about growing up, and the single version of this song was recorded live, on the sly, right inside room 206 of the actual hotel. The duo later shot the music video outside the building but were refused permission to film inside — legend has it they're banned from the place for life.

the white stripes|you're pretty good loo.fact: This one started life on 2000's De Stijl, but it got a second life two decades later: a live version recorded at a 2001 Louisville show was dug up for the 20th-anniversary White Blood Cells companion release. Fittingly, it's often singled out as maybe the gentlest, tamest song in the entire White Stripes catalog.

father john misty|the old law.fact: Before it had its final title, this song was known as 'God's Trash' when Josh Tillman started slipping it into his live sets back in late 2024. It finally got a proper studio release as a standalone Sub Pop single, produced by Tillman with Drew Erickson, bridging the gap between his albums Chloe and the Next 20th Century and Mahashmashana.

talking heads|(nothing but) flowers.fact: David Byrne wrote this one as a cheeky flip of Joni Mitchell's 'Big Yellow Taxi' — instead of paving paradise to put up a parking lot, he imagines all the strip malls reverting back to nature, with the narrator missing his Dairy Queen and Pizza Hut. The 1988 track, from the album Naked, features Johnny Marr of the Smiths on lead guitar and Kirsty MacColl on backing vocals.

dinosaur jr.|several got away.fact: This one marked Dinosaur Jr.'s return with their classic three-piece lineup — J Mascis, Lou Barlow and Murph — recording in short, intense bursts over about a year at a home studio in Amherst. It's the lead single off There Near, their first full album in five years.

the mountain goats|charlie sheen reaches.fact: This one kicks off Days, the Mountain Goats' 24th studio album, which John Darnielle wrote in a single two-week burst while his wife was away — a writing situation he's compared to how he banged out All Hail West Texas back in 2002. The record was cut at Sear Sound in Manhattan with producer John Congleton, with guests including harpist Mikaela Davis and backing vocals from Janis Siegel of the Manhattan Transfer.

l'rain|soulless cycle.fact: 'soulless cycle' served as the lead single for L'Rain's Fata Morgana, which she's described as the closing chapter of a four-album arc that started with her self-titled 2017 debut. The track was co-produced with Ben Chapoteau-Katz and leans into the record's blend of gospel, dancehall and tape-loop textures.

aldous harding|one stop.fact: Recorded at the storied Rockfield Studios in Wales with longtime producer John Parish, 'One Stop' is built around little more than a single piano motif and Harding's own multi-tracked voice. It even name-drops art-rock legend John Cale in the lyrics — 'I met the real John Cale, he had no words, but I don't mind' — and served as the first single off her 2026 album Train on the Island.

wild nothing|ocean repeating (big eye gi.fact: This one lands between Wild Nothing's two most acclaimed records, written and produced solo by Jack Tatum for the 2013 Empty Estate release, which bridged the gap between 2012's Nocturne and 2016's Life of Pause. It's a nice showcase of Tatum working entirely on his own rather than in the fuller studio setup he used on Nocturne.

francis of delirium|higher.fact: "Higher" comes from Francis of Delirium's 2026 album Run, Run Pure Beauty, and it has a real personal story behind it: singer Jana Bahrich wrote it while recovering from neck surgery. For the choir vocals on the track, she brought in her own speech therapist, who happens to sing in a choir herself.

sufjan stevens|futile devices.fact: "Futile Devices" opens Sufjan Stevens' 2010 album The Age of Adz with hushed piano and acoustic guitar, standing out as the gentle outlier on an otherwise glitchy, electronic record. The song had a second life too: Shigeto remixed it in 2012, and producer Doveman reworked it again in 2017 for the soundtrack of the film Call Me by Your Name.

sufjan stevens|lonely man of winter (dov.fact: This track has a delightfully odd backstory. In 2007, Sufjan ran a holiday "Xmas Song Xchange" contest and ended up trading away the rights to his original "Lonely Man of Winter" to the winner, theater artist Alec Duffy, in exchange for Duffy's own homemade Christmas song. Duffy held private listening parties with cookies and hot chocolate for over a decade before finally releasing it properly in 2018 as this Doveman-produced version with Melissa Mary Ahern, with proceeds benefiting his Brooklyn arts nonprofit JACK.

whitney|see you later, i'm gone.fact: Whitney formed in Chicago in 2015 out of the ashes of two other bands: guitarist Max Kakacek had just come off Smith Westerns, while drummer-turned-frontman Julien Ehrlich had been keeping time for Unknown Mortal Orchestra. "See You Later, I'm Gone" is a more recent single from the duo, continuing the warm, horn-dusted sound they've built since their 2016 debut Light Upon the Lake.

the beths|watching the credits.fact: Beths frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes has admitted she doesn't love actually watching movies, she just loves reading about them, often skipping straight to the Wikipedia plot synopsis. That habit of absorbing movies without watching them became the inspiration for "Watching the Credits," which was recorded during the Expert in a Dying Field sessions but held back to be its own standalone single, complete with violins and a key change.

band of horses|(biding time is a) boat t.fact: This fan favorite actually started out as a hard-to-find extra on Band of Horses' 2005 Tour EP before finally getting its due on the 20th-anniversary reissue of Everything All the Time. Its music video draws on the real story of the "52-hertz whale," whose calls are pitched differently from every other whale's, as a visual metaphor for the song.

soak|death valley fridge magnet.fact: "death valley fridge magnet" marked SOAK's (Bridie Monds-Watson) first solo single in more than four years, arriving on Rough Trade after a run that included a 2024 collaboration with Fred again.. Monds-Watson has said the song is really about leaning on friendship to find her way back to herself.

galaxie 500|isn't it a pity.fact: Galaxie 500 closed out their 1989 album On Fire with a hazy, reverb-soaked cover of George Harrison's "Isn't It a Pity," originally from his sprawling 1970 triple album All Things Must Pass. Producer Kramer gave it the same slow-motion, dream-pop treatment that defined the band's whole sound.

gilla band|alogia.fact: "Alogia" comes from Dublin noise-rock outfit Gilla Band's album Pugnello, a band that actually performed for years as Girl Band before all four members renamed themselves in 2021. They chose "Gilla," an old Irish given name, and apologized for not having thought through their original name sooner.

avalon emerson and priori|you're my worl.fact: "You're My World" paired Berlin-based producer Avalon Emerson with Quebec techno artist Priori as part of her ongoing collaborative series Perpetual Emotion Machine. It's dance music built on shared credit, splitting the difference between euphoric and trippy.

the cure|fascination street.fact: "Fascination Street" wasn't even supposed to be the lead single from Disintegration, that job was meant for "Lullaby," until The Cure's U.S. label pushed for this one instead. It paid off: the song became the first track ever to top Billboard's brand-new Modern Rock Tracks chart in 1989. One more quirk from those sessions: Robert Smith reportedly refused to speak out loud in the studio, passing notes to his bandmates instead.

lykke li|happy now.fact: "Happy Now" comes from The Afterparty, which Lykke Li has called her sixth and possibly final studio album. She's described the song's sound as what you'd get "if ABBA and the Prodigy had a baby and it wouldn't stop crying", a pretty perfect summary of its mix of pop sweetness and jittery energy.

unknown mortal orchestra|layla.fact: Don't let the title fool you, this "Layla" has nothing to do with the Eric Clapton classic. It's the lead single from Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2023 double album V, with bandleader Ruban Nielson drawing on Hawaiian hapa-haole music while recording much of the record in Hawaii.

the strokes|going shopping.fact: To tease "Going Shopping," The Strokes mailed out 100 numbered cassette tapes to fans on their text list the morning before the song's official release. The track, lead single from their 2026 album Reality Awaits, went on to spend two weeks at number one on Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart.

big thief|time escaping.fact: "Time Escaping" was tracked at a home studio in California's Topanga Canyon with engineer Shawn Everett, just one stop on a well-traveled recording trail. Big Thief cut the 20 songs on Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You across four separate sessions in four very different locations, from upstate New York to the Colorado Rockies.

modest mouse|life's a dream.fact: "Life's a Dream" is a standout from Modest Mouse's 2026 album An Eraser and a Maze, produced by Isaac Brock alongside Jacknife Lee and Suzy Shinn. Brock co-directed the song's trippy music video himself, shooting it around Portland as a kind of fever dream blurring sleep and waking life.

sharon van etten|our love.fact: "Our Love" comes from Sharon Van Etten's 2014 album Are We There, which she co-produced herself with Stewart Lerman. Part of it was tracked at Electric Lady Studios in New York, the storied room originally built for Jimi Hendrix.

chinese american bear|all the people.fact: "All The People" is the lead single off Chinese American Bear's album "Dim Sum & Then Some." The Seattle duo — real-life married couple Lingbo Anne Tong and Bryce Barsten — blend Mandarin and English lyrics over warbling guitars, synths, and disco strings, and Barsten directed the song's animated stop-motion video himself.

cornelius|sparks.fact: "Sparks" is a single off Cornelius mastermind Keigo Oyamada's 2024 album "Dream in Dream." The video, directed by longtime collaborator Koichiro Tsujikawa, follows a glowing burst of light shaped like a beating heart as it drifts across the American Southwest desert.

elliott smith|no name no. 5.fact: Tucked into Elliott Smith's 1997 breakthrough "Either/Or," "No Name No. 5" is a showcase for his one-man-band chops — Smith played the drums, acoustic guitar, and bass himself, with Rob Schnapf and Tom Rothrock producing alongside him.

mgmt|kids.fact: "Kids" started life years before "Oracular Spectacular" — Andrew VanWyngarden and Ben Goldwasser first played an early version back in 2003 as Wesleyan University students, cycling it through two self-released EPs before producer Dave Fridmann helped them re-record it (a semitone lower) for the 2007 album.

the lemon twigs|i just can't get over lo.fact: True to form for the D'Addario brothers, Brian and Michael wrote and produced "I Just Can't Get Over Losing You" themselves — it's the lead single off their 2026 album "Look for Your Mind!," fleshed out with touring members including Eva Chambers of Tchotchke.

brakence|cbd.fact: brakence (Randy Findell) was a self-taught teenage producer from Columbus, Ohio who wrote, recorded, and mixed basically all of "cbd" and the rest of his debut album "Hypochondriac" himself. NPR named the track one of its favorite songs of 2022.

nadia reid|oh canada.fact: For "Oh Canada," New Zealand songwriter Nadia Reid flew all the way to Virginia to record with producer Sam Taylor and the Spacebomb Records house band — the song doubles as a warm nod to the Canadian singer-songwriter lineage of Joni Mitchell and the Wainwrights that she admires.

beirut|elephant gun.fact: "Elephant Gun" got its start tucked onto the "Lon Gisland" EP before becoming the title track of Beirut's 2007 "Elephant Gun" EP — and it gave the band their first-ever music video, directed by Alma Har'el.

julia jacklin|the hardest thing.fact: "The Hardest Thing," the third single off Julia Jacklin's 2026 album "The Gem," comes with one of the year's most ambitious music videos — a single unbroken shot filmed entirely from a helicopter weaving through the Melbourne skyline, directed by Danny Cohen.

slint|breadcrumb trail.fact: The opening track on Slint's landmark "Spiderland" (1991), "Breadcrumb Trail" quietly shifts through unusual time signatures — 7/4, 12/8, 15/8 — while Brian McMahan half-sings, half-narrates a story about meeting a carnival fortune teller and riding a roller coaster. The math is nearly invisible under the song's hushed soft-loud-soft dynamics.

rostam feat. clairo|hardy.fact: "Hardy" reunites Rostam with Clairo, whose 2019 debut album "Immunity" he produced. The track's lush orchestral backbone actually began as an instrumental Rostam put together back in 2012, built around a sample of Georges Delerue's score for Truffaut's 1973 film "Day for Night."

mitski|remember my name.fact: "Remember My Name" is pure "Be the Cowboy" economy — Mitski and longtime producer Patrick Hyland pack the song's stadium-size drums and biting guitar hook into just two minutes and fifteen seconds, true to the album's philosophy of never overstaying a song's welcome.

fleet foxes|grown ocean.fact: Closing out "Helplessness Blues" (2011), "Grown Ocean" holds a neat bit of trivia: it's the only Fleet Foxes studio track to feature drummer Josh Tillman, who left the band the following year to launch his solo career as Father John Misty.

wipers|when it's over.fact: Clocking in past six minutes, "When It's Over" is one of the extended guitar "freakouts" that made 1981's "Youth of America" such a leap from the Wipers' earlier punk sound. Greg Sage's experimentation on that record is widely cited as a touchstone for the Pacific Northwest bands who came after, including Nirvana.

coco and clair clair|pop star.fact: "Pop Star" started as a standalone 2020 single before landing on Coco & Clair Clair's debut album "Sexy" (2022). It got a whole second life on the 2023 deluxe reissue, which included a "Pop Star" remix from Chaeyoung of K-pop group Twice.

geowulf|saltwater.fact: "Saltwater" was the song that introduced the world to Geowulf, the dream-pop duo of Star Kendrick and Toma Banjanin, who formed on Australia's Sunshine Coast in 2016 before relocating to London. The track blends Hawaiian slack-key guitar with woozy, '90s-slacker-pop production.

stephen malkmus|freeze the saints.fact: "Freeze the Saints" comes from Stephen Malkmus's 2005 solo album "Face the Truth," which he built largely on his own — playing and overdubbing most of the instruments himself, from banjo to sitar, around sessions with his band the Jicks. The ballad has stuck around as one of his most frequently played live staples ever since.

broken social scene|stars and sons.fact: "Stars and Sons" comes from Broken Social Scene's breakthrough "You Forgot It in People" (2002), the album that expanded the Toronto collective from a core quartet to eleven members, including Feist, and won a Juno Award for Best Alternative Album. More than two decades later, Toro y Moi covered the song for a 2025 tribute album celebrating the record.

sylvan esso|flood season.fact: Before Sylvan Esso ever hit a studio, Amelia Meath caught a chorus of North Carolina crickets on an iPhone voice memo while writing this song — and that field recording ended up woven right into the finished track. 'Flood Season' lands on the duo's 2026 album Ow infinity, written after Hurricane Helene pushed them out of their longtime home in Durham before a cross-country move landed them in the middle of LA's 2025 wildfires. Sometimes the best samples really are just the sound of your own backyard.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|the s.fact: King Gizzard ditched the guitars almost entirely for this one — the whole Silver Cord album grew out of drummer Michael Cavanagh buying an electronic Simmons drum kit and the band deciding to go full synth. It's actually two albums in one: a tight 28-minute 'Silver' edit and an 88-minute 'Gold' extended mix where every track stretches toward ten minutes. Released in October 2023, it's their 25th studio album, a staggering pace for a band that's barely been around a decade and a half.

wolf parade|you are a runner and i am my.fact: This one kicks off Wolf Parade's 2005 debut Apologies to the Queen Mary, which has a cool Modest Mouse connection: Isaac Brock heard the band, loved them, and personally helped record much of the album with engineer Chris Chandler at Audible Alchemy studio in Portland. A stripped-down version of the song had already circulated on the band's self-released 2005 EP before this fuller take became the album's opening statement.

rilo kiley|silver lining.fact: 'Silver Lining' comes off Rilo Kiley's fourth and final album, Under the Blacklight (2007), where the band deliberately chased a glossier, more radio-ready sound, dabbling in everything from yacht-rock grooves to disco sheen from track to track. The gamble paid off commercially, with the album becoming their highest-charting release, debuting at No. 22 on the Billboard 200.

the war on drugs|suffering.fact: 'Suffering' is a six-minute slow-burner off The War on Drugs' breakthrough Lost in the Dream (2014), an album that took eight months to make as the band bounced between a half-dozen studios, from the mountains of North Carolina all the way to the boroughs of New York City. That restless, drawn-out process became part of the record's legend, helping turn it into one of the most acclaimed rock albums of the 2010s.

sam fender|seventeen going under.fact: 'Seventeen Going Under' turned into a real trophy case for Sam Fender — it won the Ivor Novello Award for Best Song Musically and Lyrically in 2022, beating out heavyweight nominees like Adele, and helped him pick up Best British Alternative/Rock Act at the Brit Awards that same year. Not bad for the title track off just his second album.

vivian girls|can't get over you.fact: Vivian Girls set out to write a full-on, hooky '60s pop song with this one, and that's exactly what landed on their 2009 album Everything Goes Wrong. Fittingly lo-fi and fast, the whole record was tracked in just six days, with a lot of songs captured in single takes.

the avalanches feat. mgmt and johnny mar.fact: The Avalanches are famous for sample collages with barely any singing, which makes 'The Divine Chord' stand out — it's a rare full vocal number, with MGMT's Andrew VanWyngarden handling the verses over a bed of Johnny Marr's guitar. It's a highlight from 2020's We Will Always Love You, the star-studded follow-up to their long-awaited comeback album Wildflower, with guests ranging from Karen O to Leon Bridges.

st. vincent|the strangers.fact: 'The Strangers' opens St. Vincent's 2009 album Actor, which she wrote imagining it as a score for a movie that doesn't exist, drawing inspiration from Disney soundtracks and the opening-credits music of Woody Allen films. Pitchfork liked it enough to rank it among the best tracks of the entire 2000s decade.

starcrawler|roadkill.fact: 'Roadkill' marked Starcrawler's first release after signing to Big Machine Records in 2022, and it came with a fun crossover credit: it was produced by Tyler Bates, the film composer behind the scores for Guardians of the Galaxy and John Wick. The track also found the LA glam-rockers leaning harder into punk territory than their earlier, more theatrical material.

spoon|the way we get by.fact: Spoon's 'The Way We Get By,' off 2002's Kill the Moonlight, ended up everywhere in film and TV — it soundtracked scenes in Stranger Than Fiction and The O.C., and later turned up in Shameless. Britt Daniel built the song around that insistent piano riff and handclaps, turning a scrappy indie single into one of the band's most licensed tracks.

public image ltd.|this is not a love son.fact: John Lydon wrote 'This Is Not a Love Song' as a sly joke on himself — after his record label suggested he pen a nice, marketable love song, he responded with a tune where he plays an arrogant corporate sellout, tongue firmly in cheek. The gamble worked: it became PiL's biggest UK hit, climbing to No. 5 on the singles chart.

heavenward|wish.fact: Heavenward is the shoegaze-leaning side project of Kamtin Mohager, better known for fronting The Chain Gang of 1974, and 'Wish' comes off the project's debut EP, Staircase Music. Mohager has said the sound leans on '90s touchstones like Catherine Wheel and Swervedriver, calling the whole project a kind of personal therapy session.

guided by voices|my valuable hunting kni.fact: At a lean two minutes, 'My Valuable Hunting Knife' is classic peak-era Guided by Voices — a fragment of melody that barely has time to introduce itself before it's over. Robert Pollard liked it enough to re-record a fuller version for the Tigerbomb EP later that year, and the band even shot a brand-new music video for it to mark Alien Lanes' 25th anniversary reissue in 2020.

television|see no evil.fact: 'See No Evil' kicks off Television's landmark 1977 album Marquee Moon, built around Tom Verlaine playing a single, undoubled guitar line on his 1958 Fender Jazzmaster, no overdubs needed. The song's reputation has only grown since: R.E.M. loved it enough to cover it as one of their annual holiday fan-club singles.

iceage|shelter song.fact: 'Shelter Song' comes from Iceage's 2021 album Seek Shelter, the first time the Danish band brought in an outside producer — Sonic Boom, aka Pete Kember of Spacemen 3 — recording at Lisbon's Namouche studio. The track's big, reverb-drenched hooks get an extra lift from the Lisboa Gospel Collective on backing vocals, a world away from the band's early, more abrasive sound.

alvvays|not my baby.fact: 'Not My Baby' comes from Alvvays' 2017 album Antisocialites, co-written by Molly Rankin and Alec O'Hanley, who also co-produced the record alongside John Congleton. The band actually road-tested the song live for a couple of years before it ever made it onto tape.

modest mouse|doin' the cockroach.fact: 'Doin' the Cockroach' is one of the wilder detours on Modest Mouse's 1997 breakthrough The Lonesome Crowded West, with Tyler Reilly's fiddle sawing away alongside the band's usual guitar sprawl. Producer Phil Ek tracked it at Seattle's Avast and Jon & Stu's studios, helping turn the whole record into one of the defining underground rock albums of the '90s.

toro y moi|new beat.fact: "New Beat" was the lead single from Toro y Moi's 2011 album Underneath the Pine, a deliberate about-face from his sample-heavy debut Causers of This. Chaz Bear built the whole record on live instruments instead, drawing inspiration from horror-movie soundtracks and space-disco composers like Piero Umiliani.

sufjan stevens|mystery of love.fact: Director Luca Guadagnino originally asked Sufjan Stevens to narrate his 2017 film Call Me by Your Name, but Stevens offered to write an original song instead, drawing on the film's script and the source novel. The result, "Mystery of Love," earned Stevens an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song at the 2018 ceremony.

the afghan whigs|gentlemen.fact: The title track and album were recorded at the legendary Ardent Studios in Memphis in 1993, with the band deliberately aiming for a "cinematic" sound — they even worked in the rumble of a car crossing the John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge on the record's opening. Frontman Greg Dulli has said Gentlemen is the only album he can remember writing while out on tour.

sleater-kinney|anonymous.fact: "Anonymous" appears on Sleater-Kinney's 1996 album Call the Doctor, which the trio wrote in just three weeks and recorded in four days with producer John Goodmanson. The record is also notable for having no bass guitar at all — guitarists Corin Tucker and Carrie Brownstein built its entire sound from two interlocking guitar parts.

the clash|safe european home.fact: "Safe European Home" opens The Clash's 1978 album Give 'Em Enough Rope, the band's first record made with an outside producer: American hard-rock veteran Sandy Pearlman, best known for his work with Blue Oyster Cult. Pairing a scrappy UK punk band with a polished American studio pro was controversial among punk purists at the time, but the album gave The Clash their biggest audience yet.

the clash|gates of the west.fact: "Gates of the West" grew out of an early, pre-Clash Mick Jones song called "Ooh Baby Ooh," and the band spent well over a year reworking it, first attempting it during the Give 'Em Enough Rope sessions before finishing it in New York and London. Musically it nods to Booker T & the MGs' "Time Is Tight" and Mott the Hoople's "All the Way from Memphis" — fittingly, since the arrangement was apparently tricky enough that The Clash never once played it live.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|blame.fact: On this Omnium Gatherum track, guitarist Joey Walker recorded his slide-guitar solo using a 9-volt battery instead of a traditional slide, a moment captured in the band's behind-the-scenes documentary. The song also splits lead vocals between bandmates Ambrose Kenny-Smith and Stu Mackenzie, who trade verses and sing harmony throughout.

xtc|jason and the argonauts.fact: According to frontman Andy Partridge, the song came title-first-in-reverse — he was playing a guitar figure that evoked the feeling of sailing across open water, and "Jason and the Argonauts" was simply the image that fit the mood. The six-minute track, one of the longest on 1982's English Settlement, was recorded at the Manor Studios in Oxfordshire with producer Hugh Padgham.

the decemberists|the sporting life.fact: Colin Meloy has said "The Sporting Life" is semi-autobiographical, inspired by his own unglamorous youth-sports days growing up in Helena, Montana. Built on jaunty horns and a rhythm the band has likened to Iggy Pop's "Lust for Life," the song turns one embarrassing on-field stumble into a wry look at how seriously people take competitive sports.

m. ward|for beginners.fact: "For Beginners" is the hushed opening track on M. Ward's 2009 album Hold Time. That same record also features a guest appearance from country legend Lucinda Williams, who joins Ward on a cover of Don Gibson's "Oh Lonesome Me."

mac demarco|no other heart.fact: "No Other Heart" appears on Another One, a surprise eight-song mini-album Mac DeMarco wrote and recorded entirely on his own at his home studio in Far Rockaway, Queens, in just a few weeks in early 2015 — squeezed in between tour dates for his previous album, Salad Days.

the national|weird goodbyes (feat. bon i.fact: "Weird Goodbyes" grew out of National guitarist Aaron Dessner's ongoing side project Big Red Machine with Bon Iver's Justin Vernon, and that creative partnership is what brought Vernon onto the track. First released as a standalone single in 2022, the song later found a home on The National's surprise 2023 album Laugh Track.

the jam|the eton rifles.fact: Released in October 1979, "The Eton Rifles" became The Jam's first UK top-ten hit, climbing from a chart entry at No. 29 all the way to No. 3 within a month. Written by Paul Weller, it was the only single pulled from the band's album Setting Sons.

they might be giants|particle man.fact: "Particle Man" was never released as a single, yet it became one of They Might Be Giants' most recognized songs after Warner Bros. turned it into an animated music video for the 1991 series Tiny Toon Adventures. That TV exposure introduced a lot of young viewers to the band's 1990 album Flood for the first time.

faye webster|lego ring (feat. lil yachty.fact: Faye Webster enlisted Lil Yachty — a friend since middle school — for "Lego Ring," a standout from her 2024 album Underdressed at the Symphony. The track pairs Webster's airy delivery with Yachty's Auto-Tuned harmonies over distorted bass and piano.

swapmeet|i know!.fact: According to the Australian band, "I Know!" practically wrote itself, emerging almost by accident out of an in-between-songs practice jam, unlike anything else on the record. It now opens their debut album, Mount Zero, blending jangle-pop and shoegaze with echoes of '90s alt-rock acts like Pavement and Sonic Youth.

beach house|gila.fact: "Gila" is a highlight from Beach House's 2008 sophomore album Devotion, recorded at a space called Lord Baltimore over the summer of 2007. Devotion became the Baltimore duo's first album to chart on the Billboard 200.

beach house|apple orchard.fact: "Apple Orchard" is the third track on Beach House's self-titled 2006 debut, and its inclusion on Pitchfork's "Infinite Mixtape" series that August helped introduce the duo to a much wider audience. Years later, a stripped-down four-track demo of the song turned up as the B-side to the "Used to Be" single from their later album Teen Dream.

gglum|splat!.fact: "SPLAT!" marked London singer-songwriter Ella Smoker's first new release under her gglum moniker since her 2022 debut LP Weak Teeth, arriving alongside the announcement that she'd signed to the label Secretly Canadian. Her lo-fi, guitar-driven sound has drawn comparisons to Alex G, Phil Elverum, and Adrianne Lenker.

toro y moi|the loop.fact: "The Loop" is the third single from Toro Y Moi's (Chaz Bear) seventh album Mahal, released via Dead Oceans — the album title is Tagalog for "love." The track's slow-strolling bassline and velvety groove draw comparisons to acid-jazz legend Roy Ayers.

madi diaz|feel something.fact: "Feel Something" is the lead single from Madi Diaz's album Fatal Optimist, released on ANTI- and co-produced with Gabe Wax. Diaz has described the record as the closing chapter of a loose trilogy that began with 2021's History of a Feeling and continued on the Grammy-nominated Weird Faith.

kevin morby|100,000.fact: "100,000" appears on Kevin Morby's album Little Wide Open. Morby has said the song's guitar parts were inspired by Tom Verlaine's playing style, written together with frequent collaborator Meg Duffy, whom he describes as sharing a kind of "telepathic guitarmony shorthand."

wild nothing|to know you.fact: "To Know You" comes from Wild Nothing's third album, Life of Pause (2016), produced by Thom Monahan. It first appeared in late 2015 as one side of a double A-side single paired with "TV Queen," each track getting its own music video.

ginger root|no problems.fact: Ginger Root's Cameron Lew wrote "No Problems" without any particular plan for how it should sound, and the result ended up as one of his most quintessentially "Ginger Root" tracks, leaning hard into his city-pop influences with lush string arrangements. It's the second song on his 2024 concept album Shinbangumi.

the pretenders|message of love.fact: Written by Chrissie Hynde and produced by Chris Thomas, "Message of Love" was recorded at Pathé Marconi Studios in Paris in 1980. Drummer Martin Chambers recalled that the song came together quickly from a rough sketch — the band set up, rehearsed, and had it on tape in about two hours — and it went on to reach No. 11 on the UK singles chart.

crumb|the bug.fact: Crumb's "The Bug" traces back to the band's earliest tours, when singer Lila Ramani got the idea after waking up with bed bug bites at a motel in Nebraska and wandering the halls singing what became the song's outro. The band didn't actually finish recording it until years later, for their 2024 album AMAMA.

talking heads|girlfriend is better.fact: "Girlfriend Is Better," from Talking Heads' 1983 album Speaking in Tongues, contains the line "as we get older and stop making sense" — which gave the band's classic 1984 concert film, Stop Making Sense, its title. The song was credited collectively to all four band members: David Byrne, Chris Frantz, Jerry Harrison, and Tina Weymouth.

girl and girl|hello.fact: Girl and Girl formed in Queensland, Australia, after singer Kai James and guitarist Jayden Williams started jamming in Williams's mom's garage after school. James's aunt, nicknamed "Aunty Liss," stopped by one day after walking her dog, asked to sit in on drums, and stuck around for good; bassist Fraser Bell then rounded out the lineup. "Hello" comes from the band's 2024 Sub Pop debut album, Call a Doctor.

feist|i feel it all.fact: "I Feel It All" was the third single from Feist's 2007 album The Reminder, reaching No. 47 on the Canadian Hot 100. For a performance on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, Feist played the song acoustically aboard a moving tour bus, with a hand bell set standing in for the studio version's piano.

feist|so sorry.fact: "So Sorry" opens Feist's 2007 album The Reminder, recorded in a fast two-week session at La Frette Studios outside Paris in March 2006. It was produced by Feist, Gonzales, and Renaud Letang, with Gonzales himself playing piano, organ, vibraphone, and drums on the track.

glass beach|rare animal.fact: "rare animal" appears on glass beach's 2024 album plastic death, produced by Will Yip. The song's explosive gang-vocal section was recorded by every member of the band plus a friend they call their "secret fifth member," Daxe — frontperson J McClendon compared the effect to "a Greek chorus arguing with me."

radiohead|the numbers.fact: "The Numbers" is from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool. That October the band released an official video of Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood performing a stripped-down version of the song outdoors using a vintage Roland CR-78 drum machine, directed by filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson.

sharp pins|popafangout.fact: "Popafangout" is from Sharp Pins' 2025 album Balloon Balloon Balloon. Bandleader Kai Slater wrote and mixed the track himself, and its companion music video was shot on 16mm film.

beatrix|class reunion.fact: "Class Reunion" is by Beatrix, the Los Angeles-based chamber-pop project of singer-songwriter Arielle Kasnetz. It's a single from her sophomore album We Swallowed the Sky, and its music video leans into a quirky "Twin Peaks meets The Office" atmosphere set inside a sterile community center.

constant smiles|time measured in moonflo.fact: "Time Measured in Moonflowers," the lead single from Constant Smiles' 2025 album Moonflowers, features guest vocals from Cassandra Jenkins. Bandleader Ben Jones has said the song was inspired by Hayao Miyazaki's animated film The Wind Rises, built around the idea of riding inspiration the way a glider rides the wind.

sloan|so far down.fact: "So Far Down," written by guitarist Patrick Pentland, appears on Sloan's 2025 album Based on the Best Seller, the band's 14th studio record. The Halifax, Nova Scotia band is unusual in that all four members — Chris Murphy, Jay Ferguson, Patrick Pentland, and Andrew Scott — write songs and sing lead vocals, and the lineup has remained unchanged since forming in 1991.

heavenly|p.u.n.k. girl.fact: Heavenly formed in 1989 in Oxford, England, out of the ashes of the band Talulah Gosh, with Amelia Fletcher, Peter Momtchiloff, Rob Pursey, and Mathew Fletcher all carrying over from the earlier group. The band released "P.U.N.K. Girl" in 1993 on the indie label Sarah Records, and more than 30 years later the song found a whole new audience when it went viral on TikTok, helping spark a 2023-24 reunion tour.

glitterer|plastic.fact: Glitterer is the project of Ned Russin, also known as the bassist and vocalist of the band Title Fight. "Plastic" was the first song Glitterer ever wrote as a full band rather than a solo studio project, and it appears on the 2024 album Rationale, released via ANTI- Records.

nothing|a short history of decay.fact: Nothing recorded the album "a short history of decay" at Sonic Ranch studio in Texas, co-writing and producing it with Whirr guitarist Nicholas Bassett, with additional production and mixing from Sonny Diperri (known for his work with DIIV).
