The sessions also brought in outside contributors, including harpist Mary Lattimore on a couple of tracks and corridos musician Ricardo Ayub Chavira, who added brass.

dehd|dog days.fact: Dehd is a Chicago trio formed in 2015 by Jason Balla and Emily Kempf, who brought in friend Eric McGrady on drums; the band is known for its stripped-down, reverb-soaked pop sound. The one-take music video for "Dog Days," the opening track from their 2024 album Poetry, was filmed in a single unedited shot inside Bernice's Tavern in Chicago.

trembler|the gonzales shoulder.fact: Trembler is a four-piece band from Houston, Texas, made up of Luke Gonzales, CJ Anderson, Ceej Burton, and Martin Long. "The Gonzales Shoulder" appears on their 2026 EP Total Sorry, and reviewers noted the track's metallic tone and melodic guitar work drew comparisons to Death Cab for Cutie.

good looks|self-destructor.fact: "Self-destructor" is a Good Looks song about frontman Tyler Jordan parting ways with a former bandmate after they couldn't get past creative differences, despite still caring about each other personally. It appears on Lived Here for a While, the band's follow-up to their 2022 debut album Bummer Year.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|slow.fact: "Slow Jam 1" comes from King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2014 album I'm in Your Mind Fuzz and was recorded by engineer Paul Maybury at A Secret Location studio in Melbourne. It's one of the album's mellower, more analog-sounding psychedelic jams, with lyrics that are essentially a simple call to slow down and breathe.

good morning|ahhhh (this isn't ideal).fact: "Ahhhh (This Isn't Ideal)" appears on Good Morning Seven, the seventh record from Australian duo Liam Parsons and Stefan Blair, who built their own studio and spent about a year and a half writing and recording the album. The song was inspired by Nina Simone and MGMT, and lyrically grew out of Blair reflecting on his feelings about being in the band at that point in time.

the beths|knees deep.fact: "Knees Deep" was a last-minute addition to The Beths' 2022 album Expert in a Dying Field, built around one of guitarist Jonathan Pearce's standout guitar lines. Singer Elizabeth Stokes has said the song is a metaphor for her own habit of cautiously wading into things rather than diving in headfirst, an idea the music video plays with by showing the band bungee jumping.

devo|uncontrollable urge.fact: "Uncontrollable Urge," the opening track on DEVO's 1978 debut Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo!, was written and sung by keyboardist Mark Mothersbaugh and plays as a knowing homage to the Beatles, sharing a chord progression with "I Want to Hold Your Hand" and echoing the "yeah yeah yeah"s of "She Loves You." Mothersbaugh has also said John Lennon caught DEVO performing the song live at Max's Kansas City in New York in 1977, before it was officially released.

unknown mortal orchestra|everyone acts c.fact: "Everyone Acts Crazy Nowadays" is from Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2018 album Sex & Food, which the New Zealand band recorded piecemeal in six different cities around the world: Mexico City, Seoul, Hanoi, Reykjavik, Portland, and Auckland. The song was written by brothers Ruban and Kody Nielson, with Ruban also producing the record.

alex g|oranges.fact: "Oranges" appears on (Sandy) Alex G's eighth studio album, House of Sugar (2019), which the artist recorded across multiple cities including New York, Philadelphia, and St. Louis. The album's title comes from SugarHouse Casino in Philadelphia, now known as Rivers Casino.

future islands|vireo's eye.fact: "Vireo's Eye" comes from Future Islands' 2010 album In Evening Air, which the band recorded at a house in Baltimore's historic Marble Hill neighborhood between July 2009 and January 2010. The album's title was borrowed from a poem of the same name by American poet Theodore Roethke.

new order|sub-culture.fact: "Sub-culture" was the second single from New Order's 1985 album Low-Life, released on the Manchester label Factory Records. For the single, producer John Robie reworked the album track into a more club-oriented, electronic version, and a later batch of 1986 Razormaid remixes added extra vocals from Deborah Iyall of the band Romeo Void.

grandaddy|cabin in my mind.fact: "Cabin in My Mind" is from Grandaddy's 2024 album Blu Wav, the band's sixth record and first new album in nearly seven years, whose title is a portmanteau of bluegrass and new wave. Frontman Jason Lytle has said a friend coined the phrase "cabin in my mind" while they were traveling together on tour, and he liked the idea of it enough to build the song around it; the track also features pedal steel guitar, a first for the band.

arctic monkeys|cornerstone.fact: "Cornerstone" was the second single from Arctic Monkeys' 2009 album Humbug. Its music video was directed by Richard Ayoade, the actor/comedian known for The IT Crowd, who filmed frontman Alex Turner performing solo in a plain white room. Ayoade had already directed the band's "Crying Lightning" video from the same album, and the two later worked together again on Ayoade's 2010 film Submarine.

wishy|lovesick.fact: Wishy is an indie band built around Kevin Krauter (formerly of the band Hoops) and Nina Pitchkites, who first met in high school in Indianapolis but didn't start making music together until years later. "Lovesick," sung by Pitchkites, was released in 2026 as the lead single from the band's second album, Nature's Pill, on the Winspear label.

mitski|that's our lamp.fact: "That's Our Lamp" closes out Mitski's 2022 album Laurel Hell, written by Mitski and her longtime producer Patrick Hyland, who also produced the whole record. When asked to sum up the final track in three words, Mitski answered: "Carnival, happy, goodbye."

ducks ltd.|deleted scenes.fact: Toronto duo Tom McGreevy and Evan Lewis originally performed as "Ducks Unlimited," but shortened their name to Ducks Ltd. in 2021 to avoid any legal tangle with the real-life wetlands conservation group of the same name. "Deleted Scenes" comes from the duo's 2024 album Harm's Way, released on Carpark Records.

the mountain goats|this year.fact: "This Year" appears on the Mountain Goats' acclaimed 2005 album The Sunset Tree and has become the band's single most-performed song in concert. Setlist.fm logs it at more than 600 live performances, typically with the whole room singing the chorus back as one.

the antlers|carnage.fact: The Antlers began in 2006 as the solo home-recording project of Brooklyn singer Peter Silberman before growing into a full band for 2009's breakthrough Hospice; today it's back down to just Silberman and drummer Michael Lerner. "Carnage" is the lead single from 2025's Blight, the band's first new album in four years, which Silberman wrote after taking walks through the fields near his home studio.

upchuck|freaky.fact: Upchuck came together in 2018 out of Atlanta's skateboarding and DIY punk scene. "Freaky" is the lead single from their album Bite the Hand That Feeds, produced by Ty Segall and recorded at his home studio in Topanga Canyon, California, and its music video pays homage to actor Paul Reubens, best known for playing Pee-wee Herman.

daya|wildside.fact: Before launching her solo career, singer Daya (born Grace Tandon) sang the hook on the Chainsmokers' "Don't Let Me Down," which won the Grammy for Best Dance Recording in 2017 while Daya was still a teenager. "Wild Side" comes from her 2025 sophomore album, Til Every Petal Drops.

the jam|start!.fact: The Jam's 1980 UK number-one single "Start!" borrows its bouncing bassline from George Harrison's Beatles song "Taxman." Bassist Bruce Foxton said the band had been listening heavily to the Beatles' Revolver album at the time, and the riff crept into their new song without them fully intending it.

hand habits|way it goes.fact: "Way It Goes" is a track from Hand Habits' 2025 album Blue Reminder, the project of guitarist Meg Duffy, who wrote the song in a songwriting class. Duffy is also a sought-after touring and session guitarist who has played in the backing bands of Kevin Morby, Weyes Blood, and Sylvan Esso.

jose gonzalez|heartbeats.fact: Jose Gonzalez's hushed, acoustic-guitar version of "Heartbeats" is a cover of a 2002 song by Swedish electronic duo The Knife. His recording became a hit after it soundtracked Sony's famous 2005 "Bravia" TV commercial, in which 250,000 real bouncy balls cascade down a San Francisco street, pushing the song to No. 9 on the UK charts.

kate bush|deeper understanding.fact: Kate Bush originally released "Deeper Understanding" on her 1989 album The Sensual World, built around a lonely character's relationship with a computer, with the chorus voice created using an early vocoder. When she re-recorded the song for 2011's Director's Cut, Bush had her then-12-year-old son, Bertie, provide the spoken "computer" voice instead.

mac demarco|shining.fact: "Shining" opens Mac DeMarco's 2025 album Guitar, which he wrote and recorded entirely in his Los Angeles home studio over the course of just twelve days. The track introduces the high falsetto voice DeMarco leans on throughout the record, backed by light acoustic guitar and bass.

sharon van etten|consolation prize.fact: "Consolation Prize" is the second track on Sharon Van Etten's 2009 debut album, Because I Was in Love, making it one of the earliest songs she ever released. The record was later remixed and reissued in 2017 as "(it was) because i was in love," with two additional bonus tracks.

king tuff|twisted on a train.fact: "Twisted on a Train" is the lead single and opening track from King Tuff's 2026 album MOO, which Kyle Thomas recorded himself in Vermont on the same vintage Tascam 388 tape machine he used for his breakthrough album Was Dead. Every copy of MOO even comes packaged with a handmade mini-newspaper called The Daily Moo.

the flaming lips|waitin' for a superman.fact: "Waitin' for a Superman" was released as a single from the Flaming Lips' 1999 album The Soft Bulletin, the lushly orchestral record that transformed the Oklahoma band from noisy guitar-rock outsiders into one of the most acclaimed acts in American indie rock.

ginger root|loneliness.fact: "Loneliness" comes from Ginger Root's 2022 EP Nisemono (Japanese for "fake" or "fraud"), a project built around a fictional premise: mastermind Cameron Lew imagined being hired to secretly write songs for a fabricated up-and-coming Japanese idol from 1983, filtering 1980s city pop through his own lens.

vacations|next exit.fact: "Next Exit" was written by Vacations frontman Campbell Burns while the Australian band was on its first sold-out U.S. tour in early 2022, with the idea taking shape at a recording studio in Austin, Texas. It was co-produced by Burns and John Velasquez (known for his work with Zella Day and Gatlin) and marked the band's first new single since their 2020 album Forever in Bloom. The accompanying music video was shot on 16mm film to get a classic-cinema look.

sir chloe|forgiving.fact: "Forgiving" was produced by Steph Marziano, who Sir Chloe first worked with on a trial basis before deciding to record their entire sophomore album together. The pair ended up making the whole record over two months at Marziano's studio in London. The song appears on Sir Chloe's 2025 album Swallow the Knife.

talking heads|psycho killer.fact: The French-language bridge of "Psycho Killer" was written by bassist Tina Weymouth, who spoke French with her mother. David Byrne had originally wanted a Japanese-language verse, but when that didn't work out, drummer Chris Frantz suggested Weymouth translate it into French instead, which she finished in just over an hour. As a result, it's the only song on Talking Heads' 1977 debut album credited to all three of Byrne, Frantz, and Weymouth rather than Byrne alone.

tanukichan|thin air (feat. enumclaw).fact: "Thin Air" comes from Tanukichan's (Hannah Van Loon's) 2023 album GIZMO, which she wrote and recorded together with Chaz Bear of Toro y Moi. For this track the pair brought in Aramis Johnson of the Tacoma band Enumclaw as a featured vocalist.

last dinosaurs|collect call.fact: "Collect Call" was the lead single from Last Dinosaurs' 2022 album From Mexico With Love, a record guitarist Lachlan Caskey wrote entirely on his own while living in Mexico during the pandemic, separated from his Brisbane bandmates. The band chose "Collect Call" as the first single by group vote because it felt like the rockiest, most upbeat way to reintroduce themselves.

phoenix|if i ever feel better.fact: "If I Ever Feel Better" samples Japanese jazz musician Toshiyuki Honda's 1979 track "Lament." Released in 2000 from Phoenix's debut album United, it became the French band's highest-charting single internationally, reaching the top 10 in Belgium, Italy, and Spain.

fleet foxes|i'm not my season.fact: "I'm Not My Season" appears on Fleet Foxes' 2020 album Shore. Its music video was filmed inside St. Ann and the Holy Trinity Church in Brooklyn and directed by Sean Pecknold, the older brother of Fleet Foxes frontman Robin Pecknold, who has directed several of the band's videos.

xtc|dear god.fact: "Dear God" was originally tucked away as a B-side to the 1986 single "Grass," but American college radio DJs started flipping the record over and playing it instead, turning it into an unplanned hit that got it added to later pressings of the album Skylarking. The opening and closing vocal lines were actually performed by eight-year-old Jasmine Veillette, the daughter of a friend of producer Todd Rundgren, though in the music video her part is lip-synced by a boy.

bumper|black light.fact: "Black Light" comes from the 2020 EP pop songs 2020 by Bumper, a collaborative project between Ryan Galloway of the band Crying and Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast. It's one of several tracks the pair wrote together, blending synth-pop production with their indie-rock backgrounds.

gum|dud.fact: "Dud" opens Ill Times, a 2024 collaborative album by Jay Watson (of Tame Impala and Pond, recording as GUM) and Ambrose Kenny-Smith (of King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard and The Murlocs). The record was notably the first release on King Gizzard's own label imprint, p(doom) Records.

built to spill|i would hurt a fly.fact: "I Would Hurt a Fly" comes from Built to Spill's 1997 album Perfect From Now On, which the band had to record three separate times to get right. At one point producer Phil Ek was driving session tapes from Seattle to Boise for additional overdubs when the master reels were accidentally destroyed by heat, sending the band back into the studio once more before the album was finished.

habibi|on the road.fact: "On the Road" opens Habibi's 2024 album Dreamachine and was produced by Tyler Love and Jay Heiselmann, with contributions from James Richardson of MGMT. The Brooklyn band, co-founded by Detroit natives Rahill Jamalifard and Lenny Lynch, has been playing together since 2011.

ween|japanese cowboy.fact: "Japanese Cowboy," from Ween's 1996 album 12 Golden Country Greats, has a melody close enough to Vangelis' "Chariots of Fire" that the band has performed the two songs back-to-back as a medley in concert. The album later got a 30th-anniversary deluxe reissue featuring 26 previously unreleased demos and outtakes.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|intra.fact: "Intrasport" is a genre left-turn for King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard -- a synth-driven, disco-house-influenced track from their 2020 album K.G. The band leaned into the shift visually too, releasing a music video built around a surreal house party.

beck|teenage wastebasket.fact: "Teenage Wastebasket" appears on Beck's 1994 album One Foot in the Grave, which was recorded in the basement studio of Calvin Johnson, founder of K Records and the band Beat Happening. Johnson contributed production, co-writing, and backing vocals to the lo-fi, folk-leaning record, which went on to become one of K Records' most successful releases.

blood orange|mind loaded feat. caroline.fact: "Mind Loaded" appears on Blood Orange's (Devonte Hynes') 2025 album Essex Honey and is credited as a co-write between Hynes, Mustafa Ahmed, Caroline Polachek, and Lorde (Ella Yelich-O'Connor) — all four artists share songwriting credit alongside their guest vocals.

luisa wilson|small.fact: Luisa Wilson is a Memphis-born, New York City-based singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist who graduated from NYU's Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music, where she studied music production and songwriting. "Small," released in October 2024, was her debut single, blending her jazz-pop sound with R&B and Motown influences.

destroyer|times square.fact: "Times Square" comes from Dan Bejar's 2015 Destroyer album Poison Season, where the song is so central to the record's structure that it's split into three separate parts, with two versions bookending the album and a third placed at its center. It was released as the album's lead single in August 2015.

perfume genius|slip away.fact: The video for "Slip Away," the first single from Perfume Genius's 2017 album No Shape, was directed by Andrew Thomas Huang and features Mike Hadreas and dancer Teresa "Toogie" Barcelo moving through a lush, dreamlike landscape in towering high-heeled boots. Choreographer Sara Silkin built the routine around the challenge of dancing in those heels, giving the clip its theatrical, otherworldly feel.

andrew bird|fallorun.fact: Andrew Bird originally titled this My Finest Work Yet track "Fall of Throne," but when his wife misheard the phrase as "fall or run," he liked that better and renamed the song. Musically, Bird has said the track was inspired by New Order's "Ceremony," which he fell for after hearing it play in a public restroom.

amber arcades|goodnight europe.fact: "Goodnight Europe" was released as a single in April 2018 ahead of Amber Arcades' second album, European Heartbreak, and arrived with a short film that formed part of a loose trilogy of videos telling a modern love story. The project was released through the UK label Heavenly Recordings.

the cure|lullaby.fact: Robert Smith has said "Lullaby" grew out of a recurring childhood nightmare in which he was eaten by a giant spider, combined with memories of bedtime songs his father sang him that had oddly dark, cautionary endings. The Tim Pope-directed music video won Best British Video at the 1990 Brit Awards.

my morning jacket|just because i do.fact: This harmonica-driven track appears on My Morning Jacket's 2001 album At Dawn, recorded at a studio set up in a Kentucky barn where frontman Jim James famously tracked vocals inside an old grain silo. The natural echo from that unusual setup became a signature of the band's early sound.

the snails|big boy.fact: The Snails are a tongue-in-cheek side project born in Baltimore in 2008, featuring members of the band Future Islands performing under cartoonish snail aliases like Sandy Snailbelow and Snailliam. "Big Boy" appears on their 2013 release Worth the Wait.

mac demarco|the way you'd love her.fact: Released in 2015 as the first single from his mini-LP Another One, "The Way You'd Love Her" was written and recorded entirely by Mac DeMarco on his own at his home studio in Far Rockaway, Queens.

modest mouse|never ending math equation.fact: Originally demoed under the title "Infinite Math," this 1998 Sub Pop single is known for building to a climactic turntable-scratch solo, an unusual touch for the band at the time. It later became the opening track on Modest Mouse's 2000 rarities compilation, Building Nothing Out of Something.

the war on drugs|living proof.fact: This opening track from 2021's I Don't Live Here Anymore marked a change in process for frontman Adam Granduciel, who typically builds songs from layers of overdubs; instead, "Living Proof" was recorded live in real time with the full band at Electro-Vox Studios in Los Angeles. Its music video was shot on 16mm film by director Emmett Malloy at Panoramic Studio in Stinson Beach, California.

katy kirby|table.fact: Katy Kirby has said "Table" is a lighthearted outlier on her 2024 album Blue Raspberry, serving almost as an epilogue to the record, and that she simply finds it fun to sing. Like several songs on the album, it carries an official co-write credit for her backing band, since Kirby felt their playing shaped the songs enough to earn them songwriting credit alongside her lyrics.

the chemical brothers|the boxer.fact: "The Boxer," from 2005's Push the Button, features vocals and a co-write from Charlatans frontman Tim Burgess, marking his second collaboration with the Chemical Brothers after "Life Is Sweet" a decade earlier. The track builds on a sample of the duo's own earlier instrumental, "Orange Wedge."

black country, new road|strangers.fact: "Strangers" is a quieter, searching song about feeling slightly out of step with the world around you, where everyday objects and small signals start to feel like verdicts on whether you belong. Black Country, New Road released the track in March 2026 through War Child Records.

kevin morby|miles, miles, miles.fact: This track comes from Kevin Morby's 2013 debut solo album, Harlem River, which he assembled after leaving his earlier bands Woods and The Babies, sending home demos to collaborators Justin Sullivan and Rob Barbato to help flesh out.

the clash|pressure drop.fact: The Clash's version of this reggae standard, written by Toots Hibbert and first recorded by Toots & the Maytals in 1969, started life as a staple of their live sets on the 1977 White Riot tour before the band finally nailed a studio take at Marquee Studios in March 1978. It was released as the B-side to their 1979 single "English Civil War."

metric|victim of luck.fact: "Victim of Luck" opens Metric's tenth studio album and reflects frontwoman Emily Haines's idea that you can be just as destabilized by sudden good luck as by bad luck. The band recorded it at Electric Lady Studios with producer Gavin Brown.

galaxie 500|strange.fact: "Strange" appears on Galaxie 500's 1989 album On Fire, recorded at Noise New York and produced by Kramer, who became known for shaping the trio's hazy, reverb-heavy guitar sound. All three members, Dean Wareham, Damon Krukowski, and Naomi Yang, share the songwriting credit.

the national|tropic morning news.fact: The title phrase was coined by Matt Berninger's wife and longtime co-writer Carin Besser, who used "tropic morning news" as a name for the overwhelming daily flood of news people scroll through. As the lead single from 2023's First Two Pages of Frankenstein, the album version blends a live performance recorded in Hamburg with parts played by the London Symphony Orchestra.

mitski|why didn't you stop me?.fact: From 2018's Be the Cowboy, this song is about the regret of walking away from a relationship and then wishing your partner had fought to keep you there. It also plays with the unreliability of memory, as the narrator searches for an old photo where her ex looks the way she remembers him.

public image ltd.|flowers of romance.fact: After bassist Jah Wobble left the band, John Lydon and Keith Levene leaned into a nearly bass-less, percussion-heavy sound for this 1981 title track, built from tribal-style drumming, gamelan-inspired percussion, and oddball instruments like bowed bass and banjo run through heavy effects. Producer Nick Launay brought his love of big, gated drum sounds to the sessions.

iron and wine|me and lazarus.fact: "Me and Lazarus," from 2011's Kiss Each Other Clean, finds Sam Beam moving into a funkier, jazz-tinged sound built around electric piano and saxophone, a notable departure from Iron & Wine's earlier acoustic folk records. It pointed toward the horn-driven direction he'd expand on with the following year's Ghost on Ghost.

animal collective|did you see the words.fact: "Did You See the Words" opens Animal Collective's 2005 breakthrough album Feels. The band had their guitars retuned to match a friend's out-of-tune piano, giving the whole record its warped, shimmering sound, and this opener's cascading, falsetto-heavy harmonies help kick off what many critics consider the band's turning-point album.

fiona apple|hot knife.fact: "Hot Knife" closes Fiona Apple's 2012 album The Idler Wheel... as a joyful, round-like vocal duet, with Apple pounding out the rhythm on drums rather than a drum kit. The music video, directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, uses split-screen effects to pair Apple with her real-life sister, singer Maude Maggart.

spiritualized|always together with you.fact: "Always Together With You" opens Spiritualized's 2022 album Everything Was Beautiful with frontman Jason Pierce's young daughter Poppy announcing the record's title, followed by the same Apollo 11 radio-transmission sound effects that introduced the band's 1997 classic Ladies and Gentlemen We Are Floating in Space. It's a supercharged rework of a demo the band had floated around since 2014.

tame impala|solitude is bliss.fact: "Solitude Is Bliss" was the lead single from Tame Impala's 2010 debut album Innerspeaker, and Kevin Parker has called it "the most uplifting pop song" he could offer as a first introduction to the record. The single's artwork came from Australian artist Leif Podhajsky, who designed the visual look for the whole Innerspeaker era.

wednesday|handsome man.fact: "Handsome Man" comes from Wednesday's 2021 album Twin Plagues, written by frontwoman Karly Hartzman and produced by Adam McDaniel and Alex Farrar. The Asheville band, which features guitarist (and now solo star) MJ Lenderman, built the track around layers of fuzzy, feedback-heavy multi-guitar interplay, including steel guitar, alternating with quieter passages.

real estate|the main thing.fact: "The Main Thing" is the title track of Real Estate's 2020 album and was the last song written for the record. Frontman Martin Courtney wanted to write something like an inspirational anthem while weighing whether touring as a musician was compatible with being a parent of young kids, and the brief track builds to an energetic, psychedelic guitar solo.

beach house|lose your smile.fact: "Lose Your Smile" is a standalone Beach House single, paired with the B-side "Alien" and recorded at Palmetto Studio in Los Angeles following the release of their 2018 album 7. It was issued as a 7-inch rather than appearing on a full-length record.

wilco|spiders (kidsmoke).fact: "Spiders (Kidsmoke)" started out as a straightforward folk-rock tune Wilco played on the Yankee Hotel Foxtrot tour, but during the sessions for 2004's A Ghost Is Born the band transformed it into an 11-minute motorik workout built on Glenn Kotche's metronomic drumming and interlocking keyboards from Mikael Jorgenson and producer Jim O'Rourke. It became one of the band's first extended guitar epics, drawing comparisons to Krautrock acts like Can and Neu!.

r.e.m.|all the way to reno (you're gonna.fact: R.E.M.'s "All the Way to Reno (You're Gonna Be a Star)," from 2001's Reveal, was originally titled "Jimmy Webb on Mars" as what guitarist Peter Buck called a tribute to the songwriter the band admired. The title is intentionally ironic, since Reno, Nevada, is more of a modest Las Vegas stand-in than a place anyone actually becomes a star.

yo la tengo|is that enough.fact: "Is That Enough," from Yo La Tengo's 2013 album Fade, pairs the band's melodic songwriting with a full string quartet arranged by Tortoise guitarist Jeff Parker, giving it a lush, Burt Bacharach-style sweep. The accompanying video was directed by TV writer-producer Donick Cary and featured comic actor Fred Willard.

lia ices|earthy.fact: "Earthy" opens Lia Ices' 2021 album Family Album, starting with just Ices on solo piano before blooming into a psych-Americana jam midway through. The record was produced by JR White of the band Girls, and the "Earthy" video was shot entirely on Super 8 film by Conor Hagen.

radiohead|burn the witch.fact: Radiohead first attempted "Burn the Witch" during the Kid A sessions around 2000, finally releasing it 16 years later in 2016 with a striking stop-motion video. Director Chris Hopewell's claymation clip, built in just 14 days, deliberately apes the visual style of the classic British children's show Trumptonshire, giving the song a distinctive vintage-kids'-TV look.

cake|race car ya-yas.fact: "Race Car Ya-Yas" is a brisk, 81-second deep cut from CAKE's 1996 album Fashion Nugget, built around Vincent Difiore's signature trumpet alongside John McCrea's vocals. It's tucked among the album's bigger hits, "The Distance" and the band's cover of "I Will Survive," as one of the record's shortest, punchiest tracks.

panda bear and sonic boom|never givi'n i.fact: "Never Givin' In" opens Panda Bear and Sonic Boom's 2026 album A ? of WHEN with a delicate harp line sampled from an off-the-cuff recording. Sonic Boom had been so struck by harpist Mary Lattimore's playing that he recorded one of her soundchecks, and those loose, dreamy harp takes became the backbone of several songs on the record.

big thief|no reason.fact: Big Thief's "No Reason," from 2022's Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You, came together after the band heard someone playing flute from a nearby lookout tower while recording in the Colorado Rockies. That musician turned out to be Richard Hardy, a veteran session player who had worked with Carole King, and the band invited him to sit in, adding his flute to the finished track.

dinosaur jr.|blowin' up.fact: "Blowin' Up" comes from Dinosaur Jr.'s 2026 album There Near and is notably written and sung by bassist Lou Barlow rather than frontman J Mascis, a rarity for a Dinosaur Jr. single. The album was recorded almost entirely by the trio themselves at Amherst's Bisquiteen Studio, with local musician Ken Mauri contributing extra piano and organ.

m83|amnesia.fact: "Amnesia" comes from M83's 2023 album Fantasy, which Anthony Gonzalez made as a deliberate return to the guitar-and-synth energy of the band's 2005 breakout Before the Dawn Heals Us. Rather than building to one big explosion, the song is constructed as a patient slow-burn, blending M83's trademark cinematic scale with more spacious arrangements.

weyes blood|twin flame.fact: "Twin Flame," from Weyes Blood's 2022 album And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow, playfully pokes fun at the New Age idea of a "twin flame" soulmate. Natalie Mering has described the twin-flame concept as the destructive kind of soulmate, where the highs and lows are so extreme the relationship can't last, set here to downtempo, '80s-tinged electronic production.

dogwood|prairie ships.fact: "Prairie Ships" is a 2026 archival release from Dogwood, a country-rock band formed in 1971 in Montevallo, Alabama, that recorded at Muscle Shoals' East Avalon studio with producer Paul Hornsby but never landed a record deal. Decades later, their unreleased original recordings are finally surfacing through a series of archival single releases.

softcult|pill to swallow.fact: "Pill to Swallow" was the first single teasing Softcult's self-produced 2026 debut album, When a Flower Doesn't Grow. The Ontario sibling duo handle nearly everything themselves: Phoenix Arn-Horn produces and engineers while Mercedes Arn-Horn writes the songs and directs the band's music videos.

cherry glazerr|told you i'd be with the.fact: "Told You I'd Be With The Guys" opens Cherry Glazerr's 2017 album Apocalipstick, the band's major-label debut, and was written by frontwoman Clementine Creevy. The album was produced by Joe Chiccarelli and Carlos de la Garza, who polished up the band's garage-rock sound, with keyboardist Sasami Ashworth (later known as solo artist SASAMI) and drummer Tabor Allen rounding out the lineup.

death cab for cutie|stone over water.fact: "Stone Over Water" is a 2026 single from Death Cab for Cutie's album I Built You a Tower, written by frontman Ben Gibbard. The record was produced by John Congleton and pieced together partly at Animal Rites studio in Los Angeles, with additional sessions recorded at band members' own homes in Seattle, Bellingham, Los Angeles, and Portland.

dazy|i get lost.fact: Dazy is the recording project of Richmond, Virginia musician James Goodson, who mixes fuzzed-out '90s alt-rock guitar crunch with hip-hop-inspired production touches. "I Get Lost" appears on his short EP I GET LOST (when i try to get found), released in December 2024 via Lame-O Records.

alabama shakes|future people.fact: "Future People" comes from Alabama Shakes' 2015 album Sound & Color and was co-written by the whole band - Brittany Howard, Heath Fogg, Zac Cockrell, and Steve Johnson - together with producer Blake Mills. The blues-rock track is built around a tricksy, fuzz-bass guitar part that climaxes in a wall of distorted, reverb-heavy sound.

belle and sebastian|young and stupid.fact: Belle and Sebastian released "Young and Stupid" in 2022 as a single from their album A Bit of Previous. Frontman Stuart Murdoch sings it from the perspective of his whole generation looking back fondly on youthful recklessness, and the lyric video was built entirely from childhood and teenage photos of the band members themselves.

black belt eagle scout|at the party.fact: "At the Party" is the opening track and lead single from Black Belt Eagle Scout's 2019 album At the Party With My Brown Friends on Saddle Creek Records. Written by Katherine Paul in her bedroom, the song reflects on finding the inner strength to support the people close to you, built around the comfort of a tight-knit friend group.

phoebe bridgers|that funny feeling.fact: Phoebe Bridgers released her studio cover of Bo Burnham's "That Funny Feeling" in October 2021. She and Burnham had already debuted it live together as a surprise duet at Largo at the Coronet in Los Angeles that August - the song's first-ever live performance - before she put out her own version.

ramones|pinhead.fact: The Ramones' "Pinhead," from 1977's Leave Home, ends with the band's famous rallying cry "Gabba gabba hey." That chant traces back to the 1932 Tod Browning film Freaks, which the band caught at an art-house cinema after an outdoor gig got rained out, and a line from the movie became the inspiration for the song's "we accept you, one of us" refrain.

anna burch|party's over.fact: Anna Burch wrote "Party's Over" after a night out that didn't go the way she'd hoped, and it became one of the first songs written for her album If You're Dreaming. The self-directed music video leans into dark comedy, casting Burch as a bride left at the altar when her groom goes on the run - from a sea monster.

bat for lashes|laura.fact: "Laura" is the only co-written song on Bat for Lashes' 2012 album The Haunted Man, penned with Justin Parker after Natasha Khan's label pushed her to write something with single potential. She worked out the piano chords with Parker, then recorded her vocal take - the one that made the final record - the very first time she sang it.

hatchie|obsessed.fact: Hatchie's "Obsessed," the third single from her 2019 debut album Keepsake, was inspired by Harriette Pilbeam's teenage habit of latching onto a new best friend for support. She's described it as ultimately a celebration of a formative friendship that pushed her to become a more adventurous person.

phantogram|all a mystery.fact: "All A Mystery" marked Phantogram's 2024 signing to Neon Gold Records and takes its title from a line Josh Carter and Sarah Barthel used to sing together back when they first started writing songs in a barn-turned-recording-studio. Produced by John Hill, the single later appeared on their fifth studio album, Memory of a Day.

vampire weekend|everlasting arms.fact: "Everlasting Arms" appears on Vampire Weekend's 2013 album Modern Vampires of the City, written by Ezra Koenig and produced by Ariel Rechtshaid and Rostam Batmanglij. It's one of several tracks on the record built around the band's classically trained, baroque-pop arrangements.

arctic monkeys|old yellow bricks.fact: "Old Yellow Bricks," from Arctic Monkeys' 2007 album Favourite Worst Nightmare, was co-written by Alex Turner and Jon McClure of Reverend and the Makers - old flatmates from their Sheffield days. Its title nods to The Wizard of Oz's yellow brick road, and the song closes with the winking line "Dorothy was right though."

julia jacklin|get away from me (i think.fact: Julia Jacklin's "Get Away From Me (I Think I'll Love You Soon)" is a breezy slice of '80s-inflected jangle pop that introduced her 2026 album The Gem. The record takes its name from a small Melbourne bar Jacklin frequented after moving there from Sydney, and it was recorded at Rat Shack studio with Jacklin co-producing alongside Robert Muinos.

portishead|wandering star.fact: "Wandering Star," from Portishead's landmark 1994 debut Dummy, was written by Beth Gibbons and Geoff Barrow and produced by Adrian Utley alongside the band. Its eerie atmosphere is built partly around a sample of Eric Burdon and War's "Magic Mountain," woven into the trip-hop sound that helped define the genre.

the beths|your side.fact: "Your Side" is a bonus track on the 2023 deluxe reissue of The Beths' album Expert in a Dying Field. The New Zealand band wraps the warm, sincere love song in a breezy touch of '70s-style sway, full of devotion and promises to travel through the night just to be there for someone.

unknown mortal orchestra|like acid rain.fact: "Like Acid Rain," a short interlude from Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2015 album Multi-Love, was written by brothers Ruban and Kody Nielson. Ruban produced, mixed, and engineered the entire record himself, while Kody flew out to Portland for five weeks to play drums and keyboards on most of the sessions.

ty segall|black paint.fact: "Black Paint" is the gritty first single from Ty Segall's 2026 album Chrome, his 18th studio record. It was recorded at Sonic Ranch in Texas with his full band - Ben Boye, Evan Burrows, Mikal Cronin, and Emmett Kelly - with Cooper Crain of Bitchin Bajas and Stereolab producing.

the clash|clash citry rockers.fact: "Clash City Rockers," written by Joe Strummer and Mick Jones, was released as a standalone single in February 1978 between The Clash's first two albums. Its middle musical section is built on the old English nursery rhyme "Oranges and Lemons," giving the band's self-mythologizing anthem an unexpectedly playful foundation.

scott mcmicken and the ever-expanding|re.fact: "Reconcile" comes from Scott McMicken's 2023 solo debut album Shabang, his first release after stepping away from his longtime band Dr. Dog. Rather than recording with old friends, McMicken worked with a cast of musicians hand-picked by producer Nick Kinsey, deliberately encouraging improvisation in the studio to capture a loose, free-spirited energy. McMicken has described the song as a way of staying close to "the open spirit of letting go."

pom poko|cheater.fact: "Cheater" is the title track of Norwegian art-punk band Pom Poko's 2021 second album, released on the UK label Bella Union. The band formed in Trondheim after three music-conservatory students recruited singer Ragnhild Fangel Jamtveit for a one-off literary festival gig and just kept going. Musically, the track swings from whisper-quiet verses into a loud, stuttering punk instrumental breakdown by its end.

tom waits|way down in the hole.fact: Tom Waits wrote "Way Down in the Hole" for the 1987 Steppenwolf Theatre stage production Frank's Wild Years before it appeared on his album of the same name. It became famous years later as the theme song for HBO's The Wire, which used a different recorded version each season, including renditions by the Blind Boys of Alabama, the Neville Brothers, Steve Earle, and Waits's own original.

the big pink|no angels.fact: "No Angels" marked The Big Pink's return in 2022 after a decade away, and frontman Robbie Furze built the track around a sample of "Light On" by the little-known band Bad Cop, which he'd stumbled on by chance while listening to the radio during a drive to visit a friend in Los Angeles. The shoegaze-leaning single was produced by Tony Hoffer, known for his work with Beck, Air, and Phoenix.

pavement|stereo.fact: Pavement's 1997 single "Stereo," from the album Brighten the Corners, opens with Stephen Malkmus wondering aloud about Rush singer Geddy Lee's famously high voice: "How did it get so high? I wonder if he speaks like an ordinary guy?" A bandmate chimes back, "I know him, and he does" — one of indie rock's more memorable random celebrity shout-outs.

low|no comprende.fact: "No Comprende" comes from Low's 2015 album Ones and Sixes, recorded with producer BJ Burton at Justin Vernon's (Bon Iver) April Base Studios, not far from the Duluth, Minnesota duo's home. The track pairs Alan Sparhawk's heavily distorted guitar with a slow build into a cavernous, atmospheric finale.

they might be giants|they'll need a cran.fact: "They'll Need a Crane," from 1988's Lincoln, was the first song They Might Be Giants ever performed on network television, appearing on Late Night with David Letterman in 1989. Songwriter John Linnell said the tune started, as many TMBG songs do, from an old Gerry & the Pacemakers guitar riff paired with a title the band liked, with the song built around it afterward.

japanese breakfast|everybody wants to lo.fact: "Everybody Wants to Love You" appears on Japanese Breakfast's 2016 debut album Psychopomp. The recording features bassist Peter Bradley playing alongside bandleader Michelle Zauner's own guitar and keyboard parts — Bradley later married Zauner and went on to become the band's touring guitarist.

sparks|girl from germany.fact: "Girl From Germany" appears on Sparks' 1974 breakthrough album Kimono My House, recorded in London after Ron and Russell Mael relocated from Los Angeles and assembled an entirely new British backing band. Produced by Muff Winwood, the album shot to No. 4 on the UK charts and earned the Mael brothers their first gold disc.

whitney|no matter where we go.fact: "No Matter Where We Go" comes from Whitney's 2016 debut Light Upon the Lake, written by Chicago duo Max Kakacek and Julien Ehrlich (previously of Smith Westerns and Unknown Mortal Orchestra, respectively). The song rides a chugging, Creedence Clearwater Revival-style groove topped with vocal harmonies reminiscent of Crosby, Stills & Nash.

rostam|back of a truck.fact: On "Back of a Truck," from his 2026 album American Stories, Rostam swaps in a different classic song lyric each time the chorus repeats, including lines borrowed from Bob Dylan's "Don't Think Twice, It's Alright" and the Supremes' "You Keep Me Hangin' On." Musically it blends twangy pedal steel with Middle Eastern microtonal electric saz, aiming for the feeling of driving across America with the windows down.

the chemical brothers|let forever be.fact: "Let Forever Be" was co-written with, and features vocals from, Oasis's Noel Gallagher. Its 1999 music video was directed by Michel Gondry, who reimagined kaleidoscope visuals practically — instead of a digital effect, he filmed real dancers multiplying into repeated, perfectly synchronized formations. The video went on to win a string of major awards.

alt j|left hand free.fact: Alt-J has called "Left Hand Free" the "least alt-J song ever" — a Southern rock-flavored jam the trio wrote almost as a tongue-in-cheek joke around a guitar riff, after their label pushed them for a more radio-friendly single. It ended up becoming one of the biggest hits from their 2014 album This Is All Yours anyway.

the xx|i dare you.fact: "I Dare You" is widely considered the most upbeat, hopeful song on the xx's 2017 album I See You, with Romy Madley Croft and Oliver Sim trading vulnerable lines about taking a chance on new love. Its music video was shot as a tribute to Los Angeles, where the band wrote and recorded much of the record.

stereolab|percolator.fact: "Percolator," from Stereolab's 1996 album Emperor Tomato Ketchup, rides an unusual 5/4 rhythm topped with vibraphone, angular strings, and a cartoonish analog synth, reflecting the band's love of 1950s/60s space-age "bachelor pad" pop. The album itself takes its title from a 1971 experimental film by Japanese director Shuji Terayama.

the antlers|palace.fact: "Palace," from the Antlers' 2014 album Familiars, draws on the extended architectural imagery that runs through the whole record — songwriter Peter Silberman uses palaces, fortresses, and mausoleums as metaphors for the elaborate mental structures people build around memory and identity. It's one of the few songs on the album addressed directly to its subject.

kate bush|wuthering heights.fact: Kate Bush wrote "Wuthering Heights" in a single night after catching just the final ten minutes of a 1967 BBC adaptation of the Emily Bronte novel, before she'd even read the book. She insisted on it as her debut single over her label's preferred choice, and when it hit No. 1 in the UK in 1978, she became the first female artist to top the British chart with a self-written song.

big thief|spud infinity.fact: "Spud Infinity," from Big Thief's 2022 album Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You, gets its distinctive twang from a jaw harp played by Noah Lenker, the younger brother of singer Adrianne Lenker. The playful, folk-flavored track quickly became a fan favorite for its loose, celebratory energy.

king tuff|sun medallion.fact: King Tuff (Kyle Thomas) has said "Sun Medallion" grew out of a dream and centers on a small charm he once bought at a hospice thrift store that he felt carried real power. The psychedelic pop song is loosely set in his hometown of Brattleboro, Vermont.

westside cowboy|the wahs.fact: Manchester band Westside Cowboy — Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell, and Paddy Murphy — has said "The Wahs" started out almost as a joke before they realized the riff was too good to leave behind. The foot-on-the-accelerator track channels a 1990s American indie-rock sound.

king krule|seaforth.fact: King Krule's saxophonist Ignacio Salvadores joined the band after Archy Marshall spotted him playing sax under a bridge in East London, and the Argentine multi-instrumentalist became a key collaborator on 'Seaforth.' The song was the atmospheric lead single from 2023's Space Heavy, produced by Dilip Harris with King Krule's longtime touring band of Salvadores, George Bass, James Wilson and Jack Towell.

sonic youth|what we know.fact: This driving rocker from 2009's The Eternal is one of only two Sonic Youth songs with guitarist Lee Ranaldo on lead vocals, the other being 'Walkin Blue.' Its guitar riff was written as a nod to Sonic's Rendezvous Band, the short-lived Detroit rock group formed by former MC5 guitarist Fred 'Sonic' Smith.

sylvan esso|kick jump twist.fact: Originally released as a 2016 B-side to 'Radio,' this bubbly synth-pop track later found a home on Sylvan Esso's 2017 album What Now. Singer Amelia Meath has said the song is about the performances we all put on for other people - practicing a look in the mirror, rehearsing how we present ourselves - set to a frenetic, retro-futuristic beat.

sharon van etten|let go.fact: Sharon Van Etten wrote 'Let Go' in 2020 with producer Giorgio Angelini and composer Mike Semple. When she released it as a single, she paired it on the B-side with a cover of 'Some Things Last a Long Time' by Texas singer-songwriter Daniel Johnston.

guv|let your hands go.fact: GUV is the solo project of Toronto musician Ben Cook, who rebranded from his earlier name Young Guv. 'Let Your Hands Go,' the lead single from the 2026 album Warmer Than Gold, leans hard into early-'90s UK sounds - part Madchester rave, part shoegaze, part Britpop - and features guest vocals from Hatchie and Turnstile's Meg Mills.

joy division|atmosphere.fact: Joy Division first worked up this song under the working title 'Chance' for a 1979 Manchester radio session before recording the version we know that October with producer Martin Hannett at Cargo Studios in Rochdale. As with much of the band's writing process, Peter Hook's layered bassline came together first, with Bernard Sumner's synths and Stephen Morris's drums building the song's hazy, atmospheric wall of sound around it.

beck|wow.fact: Beck has said 'Wow' came together almost by accident - he stumbled onto a flute-like synth riff while working on a different song, picked up a mic, and freestyled the vocals on the spot. He nearly left it off 2017's Colors entirely, doubting anyone would like it, until his label pushed to release it as a single.

strand of oaks|radio kids.fact: 'Radio Kids,' the first single from Strand of Oaks' 2017 album Hard Love, is Tim Showalter's tribute to growing up in the '80s and '90s with a blank cassette loaded in the tape deck, waiting to record a favorite song off the radio. It captures that solitary ritual of music fandom while hinting at the wider community of fans doing the same thing all over the world.

operation ivy|knowledge.fact: At Operation Ivy's final show at Berkeley's Gilman Street, singer Jesse Michaels introduced this song simply by saying it's 'about growing up.' Green Day later covered 'Knowledge' on their debut album, and it remains the only song from that record they still play live.

mgmt|flash delirium.fact: 'Flash Delirium' was recorded for 2010's Congratulations with producer Pete Kember (aka Sonic Boom, formerly of Spacemen 3) and mixed by David Fridmann. MGMT had initially planned to release no singles at all from the album to keep it a unified listening experience, but ended up putting this track out as a free download before its single release.

my morning jacket|lowdown.fact: 'Lowdown' comes from My Morning Jacket's 2001 sophomore album At Dawn and later turned up on the band's live album Okonokos. It's become a genuine setlist workhorse for the band, performed in concert well over 250 times.

caribou|odessa.fact: Dan Snaith's wife gave him swimming lessons as a Christmas gift a few years before making 2010's Swim, and that new hobby directly shaped the album's sound - he wanted the music to feel like water, full of waves flowing through the mix. 'Odessa,' the album's opener and first single, emerged from roughly 600 ideas Snaith worked through before settling on the final nine tracks.

bon iver|woods.fact: 'Woods,' from Justin Vernon's heavily Auto-Tuned 2009 Blood Bank EP, caught Kanye West's ear, who sampled it for 'Lost in the World' on 2010's My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy. West's call about the sample led to an invitation for Vernon to fly out and work directly in West's Hawaii studio sessions.

this is lorelei|oh no now my.fact: 'Oh No Now My,' from Nate Amos's 2026 album The Singer in My Band, went through three entirely different versions before landing on its final form. The finished track stacks vocal harmonies up to Beach Boys-level heights over heavier, low-tuned guitars than much of the rest of the record.

wolf parade|you're dreaming.fact: 'You're Dreaming' is a staccato-organ-driven rocker from Cry Cry Cry, Wolf Parade's 2017 comeback album made after the band's hiatus following 2010's Expo 86. It served as the record's second single.

the jam|beat surrender.fact: Paul Weller wrote 'Beat Surrender' to mark the end of The Jam, and the band went out on top - it became their fourth and final UK number-one single in December 1982. The title plays on the 1979 disco hit 'Sweet Surrender' and the military term 'beating retreat,' and the band's other contender for the single, 'Solid Bond in Your Heart,' later became a hit for Weller's next band, the Style Council.

soccer mommy|out worn.fact: 'Out Worn' was one of the new songs Sophie Allison added to Collection, her 2017 breakout mini-album of reworked bedroom-pop recordings. She's said the song is about feeling a need for validation in a relationship, and NPR's Songs We Love singled it out as an early sign of her growth as a songwriter.

young fathers|i saw.fact: 'I Saw' appears on Young Fathers' 2023 album Heavy Heavy. Built around the insistent refrain 'I saw what I saw, I keep on walking the line,' the track channels the Scottish trio's themes of resolve and self-belief.

belle and sebastian|expectations.fact: 'Expectations' appears on Belle and Sebastian's 1996 debut Tigermilk, which began as a class project - Stuart Murdoch's demos were picked for a recording session run by students in a music-business course at Glasgow's Stow College. That college assignment ended up launching both the album and the band itself.

caroline polachek|welcome to my island.fact: Caroline Polachek originally wrote 'Welcome to My Island' during sessions for her 2019 album Pang but shelved it, feeling it was 'too bratty.' She revisited and finished it for 2023's Desire, I Want to Turn Into You, opening the song with an operatically trained scream and calling it the 'brattiest song' she's ever made.

big red machine|phoenix (feat. fleet fox.fact: Fleet Foxes' Robin Pecknold wrote his verses on 'Phoenix' as a kind of dialogue with Justin Vernon, recalling a real conversation the two once had backstage in Phoenix, Arizona. Anaïs Mitchell contributed the chorus lyrics, and the track - from 2021's How Long Do You Think It's Gonna Last? - features a brass arrangement by The Westerlies.

magazine|a song from under the floorboar.fact: Magazine's 1980 single was inspired by Fyodor Dostoevsky's novella 'Notes from Underground,' with the title drawing on a more literal translation of the book. It was produced by famed Manchester producer Martin Hannett and released on Virgin Records ahead of the album The Correct Use of Soap. Simple Minds (who toured with Magazine in 1979) later covered the song, and Morrissey recorded his own version as a B-side in 2006.

r.e.m.|radio free europe.fact: R.E.M. recorded their debut single in April 1981 in producer Mitch Easter's converted-garage studio in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. It came out that July on the tiny independent label Hib-Tone, making it the band's first-ever release, before they re-recorded it for 1983's Murmur. In 2009 the Library of Congress added the song to the National Recording Registry for helping set the template for college-radio indie rock.

fleet foxes|i am all that i need / arroy.fact: This nine-minute medley opens 2017's Crack-Up and picks up musically right where Helplessness Blues left off six years earlier -- that album's closer ends in the key of F without resolving, and this one begins exactly there. Its title references Arroyo Seco, a dry-stream tributary of California's Salinas River, and the track closes with a swirl of field recordings: ocean waves, a passing train, the band's own lawyer's voice, and a Brooklyn high school choir's cover of 'White Winter Hymnal.'

tame impala|end of summer.fact: Kevin Parker quietly previewed 'End of Summer' during a surprise DJ set at Barcelona's Nitsa Club in June 2025, months before releasing it as his first new Tame Impala material since revisiting Lonerism for its tenth anniversary. As usual, Parker wrote, performed, produced, recorded, and mixed the track entirely himself, this time from his home studio in Fremantle, Western Australia.

slowdive|machine gun.fact: 'Machine Gun' is the second track on Slowdive's 1993 album Souvlaki, built from the same hazy, reverb-soaked guitar layers that define the record's shoegaze sound. Songwriter Neil Halstead wrote much of Souvlaki while processing the end of his real-life relationship with bandmate Rachel Goswell, who still shares co-lead vocals with him on the track.

st. vincent|the melting of the sun.fact: 'The Melting of the Sun' appears on St. Vincent's 2021 album Daddy's Home, a record built around a warm, vintage '70s New York sound. The track features backing vocals from Kenya Hathaway, daughter of soul legend Donny Hathaway, alongside singer Lynne Fiddmont, and the band performed it on Saturday Night Live shortly after its release.

turnstile|underwater boi.fact: This Glow On track was recorded with producer Mike Elizondo, whose studio pedigree includes close work with Dr. Dre, according to Turnstile bassist Franz Lyons. For the music video, the band's own drummer, Daniel Fang, directed and built the entire animated world inside the classic MMORPG 'Second Life.'

sleater-kinney|modern girl.fact: Released on 2005's The Woods, 'Modern Girl' is structured in three distinct musical sections mapping onto the emotions 'happy,' 'hungry,' and 'angry,' as Carrie Brownstein sings in character as someone whose comfortable, consumer-driven life unravels. The song's key lyric later gave Brownstein the title for her 2015 memoir, Hunger Makes Me a Modern Girl.

woods|be all be easy.fact: Woods originally released 'Be All Be Easy' on their 2011 album Sun and Shade, then re-recorded it for a 2013 7-inch single to capture the more muscular arrangement it had grown into on tour. That single, backed with a cover of the Kinks' 'God's Children,' marked the studio debut of new drummer Aaron Neveu and served as a farewell recording at Rear House, the home studio the Brooklyn band had used for a decade.

yeah yeah yeahs|slave.fact: 'Slave' is track five on Yeah Yeah Yeahs' 2013 album Mosquito, co-produced by Dave Sitek of TV on the Radio and Nick Launay. It's one of several songs on the record built around dub-reggae-influenced rhythm and production techniques, a notable departure from the trio's earlier, more stripped-down punk sound.

konk|elephant.fact: Konk were a New York dance band active from 1980 to 1988, blending disco, funk, Afrobeat, and post-punk alongside downtown-scene peers like ESG and Liquid Liquid. 'Elephant' was a highlight of their club sets at legendary venues like Paradise Garage and Danceteria, and it later resurfaced on the 2004 retrospective compilation The Sound of Konk.

shannon and the clams|it's too late.fact: On this track from 2015's Gone by the Dawn, Clams guitarist Cody Blanchard takes over lead vocals from usual frontwoman Shannon Shaw, giving the song a raw, pleading edge. Blanchard wrote and is credited as the sole composer of the track.

pavement|the hexx.fact: Pavement first played a faster, louder version of 'The Hexx' live on their Brighten the Corners tour; that recording was later edited and retitled '...And Then' for release as a vinyl B-side to 'Spit on a Stranger.' For Terror Twilight, the band re-recorded it with producer Nigel Godrich into the slow-building, atmospheric closer that many critics called the closest Pavement ever got to sounding like a Radiohead record.

yo la tengo|periodically double or tripl.fact: This 2009 track from Popular Songs was one of the first Yo La Tengo songs that could fairly be called 'boogie,' built on a bluesy rhythm and Green Onions-style organ that critics compared to Booker T. & the M.G.'s and Sun Ra. Ira Kaplan's lyrics name-drop both Marcel Proust and Judge Judy, and the song's music video is shot entirely in stop-motion using pieces of fruit.

broken social scene|halfway home.fact: 'Halfway Home' was Broken Social Scene's first new song in seven years when it arrived in 2017 as the lead single from Hug of Thunder. The band debuted it live on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert around the same time.

angelo de augustine|toil and trouble.fact: The title track from Angelo De Augustine's 2023 album nods to the witches' chant in Shakespeare's Macbeth ('double, double, toil and trouble'), reimagined as a meditation on who's really steering a curated, filtered version of reality. De Augustine wrote, arranged, performed, and produced the entire album himself across 27 different instruments, and the song's stop-motion video centers on an animated singing cauldron.

wilco|ashes of american flags.fact: This Yankee Hotel Foxtrot track was recorded at Wilco's own Chicago studio, The Loft, during sessions that ran from late 2000 into the summer of 2001. Keyboardist and engineer Jay Bennett spent painstaking effort crafting the song's ten-second crossfade into the following track, 'Heavy Metal Drummer,' aiming for a seamless transition between the two very different songs.

hamilton leithauser|knockin' heart.fact: Leithauser wrote and recorded 'Knockin' Heart' in a single evening, then shelved it for over a year before releasing it as the lead single from 2025's This Side of the Island. He built the track around a power-trio concept inspired by Nirvana, layering together three separate bass parts -- one of his own plus two recorded by The National's Aaron Dessner.

deep sea diver|billboard heart.fact: Jessica Dobson wrote the title track of 2024's Billboard Heart after a songwriting session with bandmate (and husband) Peter Mansen hit a wall and the two started bickering; once he stepped out, she kept playing and the song took shape. Dobson has cited the simplicity of Tom Petty's songwriting and the mood of Wim Wenders' film Paris, Texas as inspirations for the track.

ramones|i wanna be your boyfriend.fact: Drummer Tommy Ramone wrote this track partly as a counterpoint to the band's run of 'I Don't Wanna' songs, like 'I Don't Wanna Walk Around with You.' It's the slowest song on the Ramones' 1976 debut album and the most unusually arranged, featuring a twelve-string guitar, glockenspiel, and tubular bells played by outside studio musicians, with engineer Rob Freeman even joining in on the closing backing vocals.

adrianne lenker|blue and red horses.fact: "Blue and Red Horses" is a highlight from Adrianne Lenker's third solo album, abysskiss (2018), released on Saddle Creek Records. The ten songs were written while Lenker was touring with Big Thief, and the album was recorded at Panoramic House overlooking the Pacific in West Marin, California, with producer Luke Temple and engineer Gabe Wax. Most tracks, including this one, were captured in just one or two takes.

alex g|change.fact: "Change" appears on Alex G's fourth album, Trick, which he self-released on Bandcamp in November 2012 while still a student at Temple University in Philadelphia. The lo-fi record was written, performed, and recorded entirely on his own, and it was later reissued with a professional remaster through Lucky Number in 2015. Early albums like Trick spread by word of mouth and built his cult following before he signed to a bigger label.

amber arcades|right now.fact: "Right Now" comes from Fading Lines (2016), the debut full-length by Amber Arcades, the recording project of Dutch singer-songwriter Annelotte de Graaf. She made the album in New York with producer Ben Greenberg of the band The Men, with musicians from Quilt and Real Estate filling out her backing band.

andrew bird|when that helicopter comes.fact: Andrew Bird's version of "When That Helicopter Comes" is a cover of a song written and originally performed by the Handsome Family's Brett and Rennie Sparks. Bird recorded it for Hands of Glory (2012), a companion album to his record Break It Yourself built around classic country and folk covers plus one new original. The backing group on the sessions took its name, Hands of Glory, directly from the record.

andy shauf|the magician.fact: "The Magician" opens Andy Shauf's 2016 concept album The Party, which plays out as a series of vignettes set over the course of one house party. Shauf wrote, performed, engineered, and produced almost the entire record himself, with the sole exception of the string arrangements, which were composed and played by Colin Nealis.

babehoven|blue around you.fact: "Blue Around You" is a single from Babehoven's album I See Them, I See Me, the Hudson, New York-based project of Maya Bon and Ryan Albert. The track leans into fiddle-heavy, country-tinged instrumentation and was produced by Phil Weinrobe, an engineer also known for his work with Big Thief, and released through Double Double Whammy Records.

beach fossils|daydream.fact: "Daydream" is a highlight from Beach Fossils' self-titled 2010 debut album, released on Captured Tracks. Frontman Dustin Payseur wrote, recorded, and produced the entire record himself, blending jangly post-punk guitar lines with a hazy, lo-fi sheen that helped define the early-2010s Brooklyn indie scene.

beach house|used to be.fact: "Used to Be" began life as Beach House's debut single, released on Carpark Records in October 2008 and written and produced by Victoria Legrand and Alex Scally with Chris Coady. The duo re-recorded the song for their 2010 album Teen Dream, and the original 2008 version later resurfaced on their 2017 compilation B-Sides and Rarities.

beirut|vagabond.fact: "Vagabond" appears on Beirut's third studio album, The Rip Tide (2011). Critics singled it out as the record's turn toward orchestrated, '70s-style AM pop, a notable stylistic shift from the Balkan-brass sound bandleader Zach Condon had built his earlier releases around.

big thief|not.fact: "Not" was the lead single from Big Thief's fourth album, Two Hands (2019). The band first recorded it live at Sonic Ranch studio in Tornillo, Texas, during the album's main sessions, but felt the take needed more room to breathe, so they scrapped it and re-recorded the song months later at Sound City Studios. Producer Andrew Sarlo, who has worked on every Big Thief album, oversaw both versions.

big thief|orange.fact: "Orange" is the sixth track on Big Thief's third album, U.F.O.F. (2019), produced by longtime collaborator Andrew Sarlo. Its gentle, softly strummed arrangement has drawn comparisons to folk singer-songwriter Joan Shelley, giving the song a melody that feels centuries old within the album's more atmospheric material.

bon iver|00000 million.fact: "00000 Million" closes Bon Iver's 2016 album, 22, A Million, a piano-driven track that ties together the record's roughly thirty minutes of experimental production. Every song title on the album begins with a number holding personal significance to bandleader Justin Vernon, who described the "22" as representing himself and the closing "million" as something vast and elusive.

bright eyes|four winds.fact: "Four Winds" is the second track on Bright Eyes' 2007 album Cassadaga, named for the small Florida town where part of the record was made. The song was released as the album's first single in March 2007, first appearing as the title track of the standalone Four Winds EP before the full album followed the next month.

built to spill|in the morning.fact: "In the Morning" appears on Built to Spill's 1994 album There's Nothing Wrong With Love, recorded at John & Stu's studio in Seattle and produced by Phil Ek. The album became a touchstone of 1990s indie rock, loosely centered on songwriter Doug Martsch's reflections on growing up, and it later received a 30th-anniversary vinyl reissue from Sub Pop.

bully|stuck in your head.fact: "Stuck in Your Head" is a track from Bully's 2020 album SUGAREGG, the first Bully record made as a true solo vehicle for frontwoman Alicia Bognanno. Bognanno, who studied audio engineering before starting the band, co-produced the album with John Congleton and Graham Walsh and released it through Sub Pop.

camera obscura|honey in the sun.fact: "Honey in the Sun" appears on Camera Obscura's 2009 album My Maudlin Career, written by frontwoman Tracyanne Campbell. The Glasgow band reunited with producer Jari Haapalainen, who had also helmed their earlier album Let's Get Out of This Country, recording in Stockholm with string and horn arrangements by Björn Yttling of Peter Bjorn and John.

car seat headrest|cute thing.fact: "Cute Thing" was first released on Car Seat Headrest's 2011 Bandcamp album Twin Fantasy, written and recorded entirely by Will Toledo on his own as a teenager. Seven years later, Toledo re-recorded the whole album with a full band for Twin Fantasy (Face to Face), giving "Cute Thing" a fuller, more polished studio treatment.

caroline|dark blue.fact: "Dark Blue" opens the self-titled 2022 debut album by the London band caroline and was actually the very first song the group wrote together after forming in 2017. Built around one hypnotic, repeating guitar figure played by the eight-piece band, the track was first released as a single in 2020 before being reworked into the album version.

cat power|metal heart.fact: "Metal Heart" is a standout track from Cat Power's fourth album, Moon Pix (1998). Chan Marshall wrote much of the record in a short burst after a strange, unsettling night at a rural South Carolina farmhouse, then traveled to Melbourne, Australia, to record it with Mick Turner and Jim White of the band Dirty Three.

courtney barnett|anonymous club.fact: "Anonymous Club" began as a hushed, confessional song on Courtney Barnett's 2013 EP A Sea of Split Peas, built around the idea of unplugging from your phone to be fully present with friends. The title was later reused for Anonymous Club, a 2021 documentary about Barnett, and for that film's instrumental score she teamed up with drummer Stella Mozgawa (Warpaint, Kurt Vile), the two improvising music together in the studio while watching the finished cut.

destroyer|tinseltown swimming in blood.fact: Despite its dark-sounding title, "Tinseltown Swimming in Blood" is Dan Bejar's gauzy, synth-driven satire of Hollywood's manufactured glamour, built on the dreamy, '80s-influenced production that defines Destroyer's 2017 album ken. The track closes with Bejar repeating the line "I was a dreamer, watch me leave," a wink at making it as a musician on his own terms. Destroyer performed the song live in the studio for NPR shortly after the album came out.

father john misty|ballad of the dying ma.fact: "Ballad of the Dying Man" was the second single from Father John Misty's 2017 album Pure Comedy. Josh Tillman tracked the album's lead vocals and basic instrumentation live, often in just one or two takes, at United Recording Studios in Los Angeles, then brought in composer Gavin Bryars to write orchestral string, horn, and choral arrangements, with additional contributions from Nico Muhly and Thomas Bartlett.

fiona apple|fetch the bolt cutters.fact: The title track that opens Fiona Apple's 2020 album Fetch the Bolt Cutters ends with the sound of her own dogs barking into the microphone, and several of her pets are individually credited by name in the album's liner notes. Apple recorded much of the record by jamming around her Venice, California home with her band, turning household objects into makeshift percussion instruments.

fleet foxes|sunblind.fact: "Sunblind" opens Fleet Foxes' 2020 album Shore and works as a thank-you note from frontman Robin Pecknold to the musicians who shaped his songwriting. He told Apple Music he wanted the track to feel like "a mission statement for the record -- kind of cite-your-sources energy," weaving in nods to artists like Richard Swift, Judee Sill, and Jimi Hendrix. Shore itself was announced only a day before its surprise release, timed to land on the 2020 autumnal equinox.

fontaines d.c.|tongue.fact: "Tongue" is a single from Fontaines D.C., showing the Irish band pushing into more experimental production. Bassist Conor Deegan manipulated tape speed using a technique associated with Prince, while guitarist Carlos O'Connell ran Grian Chatten's vocals through a sampler to warp them into an unsettling, pitch-shifted register.

frankie cosmos|one year stand.fact: "One Year Stand" appears on Frankie Cosmos' 2022 album Inner World Peace, released via Sub Pop. Greta Kline's band recorded it with producers Nate Mendelsohn and Katie Von Schleicher at Figure 8 Recording in Brooklyn, trimming the tracklist down from more than 100 songs Kline had written during the pandemic; bandmate Lauren Martin's Hammond organ and synth drones give the song its intimate glow.

guided by voices|to remake the young fly.fact: "To Remake the Young Flyer" is a Tobin Sprout-written, Sprout-sung track from Guided by Voices' 1996 album Under the Bushes Under the Stars, the last record for over a decade to feature the classic mid-90s lineup of Sprout, Kevin Fennell, and Mitch Mitchell. The brief, under-two-minute song was engineered by John Shough and later resurfaced on the compilation The Best of Guided by Voices: Human Amusements at Hourly Rates.

hiatus kaiyote|red room.fact: "Red Room" came together in a single overnight studio session in Brazil, in the studio of famed composer Arthur Verocai, during sessions for Hiatus Kaiyote's 2021 album Mood Valiant. Drummer Perrin Moss said it came together faster than anything the band had written before, while singer Nai Palm traced the song's title and warmth to a red light in her vocal booth that reminded her of red-tinted windows from a childhood home.

innovations|seabird.fact: "Seabird" was written by Billy and Bobby Alessi and first released by the soft-rock duo Alessi Brothers in 1976. The little-known group Innovations put out its own dreamy, synth-tinged cover a year later on one of only two singles it ever released. The song has since become a cult yacht-rock favorite, covered by acts like Metronomy and featured on the soundtrack to Taika Waititi's Hunt for the Wilderpeople.

interpol|stella was a diver and she was.fact: Interpol frontman Paul Banks has never explained exactly who "Stella" is, keeping the lyrics deliberately open to interpretation -- a hallmark of the band's early songwriting style. Musically, the track's droning guitars and reverb-soaked atmosphere are often singled out as one of the clearest nods to Joy Division on Interpol's acclaimed 2002 debut, Turn on the Bright Lights.

iron & wine|about a bruise.fact: "About a Bruise" comes from Iron & Wine's 2017 album Beast Epic, where Sam Beam pairs plucky piano, harp, and rhythm against heavier lyrical content. The song leans on vivid Southern imagery -- skies full of prayers, duck hunting, mall cops in Mobile -- building to a choir chanting "This is Alabama."

jack white feat. q-tip|hi-de-ho.fact: Jack White built "Hi-De-Ho" around a sample of Cab Calloway's 1943 tune "Hi-De-Ho Man" after hearing it on the radio and wanting its scatting to ride over a drumbeat; White had been a Calloway fan since childhood, when his father showed him old footage of the bandleader. White sent the track to Q-Tip, who reportedly sent back his own scatting vocal just five minutes later, and the song appears on White's 2022 album Fear of the Dawn.

japanese breakfast|paprika.fact: "Paprika" opens Japanese Breakfast's 2021 album Jubilee with a burst of horns and strings inspired by the "Parade" theme from Satoshi Kon's 2006 anime film of the same name. Michelle Zauner, who had spent the prior years taking music theory and piano lessons to sharpen her composing, worked with bandmate Craig Hendrix and a small ensemble of string and horn players to build the song's marching-band-style crescendo.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|paper m.fact: King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard recorded almost all of their 2015 album Paper Mache Dream Balloon inside an empty shipping container on a family farm in country Victoria, Australia, trading their usual heavy psych-rock gear for nylon-string guitars, clarinet, double bass, cello, and hand drums. The title track is about turning troubles into something else entirely -- frontman Stu Mackenzie has described it as daydreaming your worries onto an imaginary balloon and letting them float away.

kurt vile|mount airy hill (way gone).fact: Kurt Vile named "Mount Airy Hill (Way Gone)" after the quiet, tree-lined Philadelphia neighborhood where he lives, which he's described as the place that makes him feel "completely calm." He recorded the song, from his 2022 album (Watch My Moves), in OKV Central, the home basement studio he finished building just before the pandemic began.

lyres|i want to help you ann.fact: Boston garage-rock institution the Lyres recorded "I Want to Help You Ann" on December 21, 1981, releasing it in 1983 on the local Ace of Hearts label. The pulsing, tremolo-driven single helped revive vintage 1960s garage-rock sounds with a new punk-era energy, landed at number 24 on The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop critics' poll of that year's best singles, and was later covered on a 1998 single by the Chesterfield Kings.

madi diaz|worst case scenario.fact: "Worst Case Scenario" was released in October 2024 as a new track on the deluxe edition of Madi Diaz's album Weird Faith. Diaz described the song as coming from a habit of coping with anxiety by mentally rehearsing the worst possible outcome in advance, as a way to feel prepared for whatever might happen. The track is a gritty indie-folk song built around her conversational, diary-like lyrics.

mission of burma|trem two.fact: "Trem Two" appeared on Mission of Burma's 1982 debut album Vs., released on the Boston indie label Ace of Hearts Records, and was also issued as its own single. The album captured the chaotic energy of the band's live shows, leaning on tape-manipulation effects from member Martin Swope. Ahead of release, The Boston Phoenix praised the track, writing that it "sounds like the creation, destruction, and rebirth of the universe in four minutes."

mitski|star.fact: "Star" was co-written by Mitski and her longtime producer Patrick Hyland for her 2023 album The Land Is Inhospitable and So Are We, released as one of two singles on August 23, 2023. Its grand, twinkling arrangement was partly built from layers of organ parts painstakingly programmed into MIDI, with Mitski citing minimalist composer Terry Riley's repetitive style as an inspiration. She has said the song served as the album's guiding "North Star" while writing the rest of the record.

mj lenderman|you don't know the shape i'.fact: "You Don't Know the Shape I'm In" appears on MJ Lenderman's 2024 album Manning Fireworks, which topped several year-end best-of lists. Its title nods to The Band's classic "The Shape I'm In," and the finished track features clarinet from Shane McCord after going through several reworked versions in the studio. Lenderman walked through the song's evolution from demo to final recording in an episode of the podcast Song Exploder.

mount kimbie|shipwreck.fact: "Shipwreck" started as one of the earliest instrumental demos Mount Kimbie wrote for their 2024 album The Sunset Violent, and it became a core thread running through the record. The album arrived seven years after the duo's previous full-length, 2017's Love What Survives, and "Shipwreck" was released as a single ahead of it.

nation of language|weak in your light.fact: "Weak in Your Light" opens Nation of Language's 2023 album Strange Disciple and was recorded in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn, with producer Nick Millhiser, also known for his work in Holy Ghost!. Frontman Ian Devaney wrote and sang lead on the track, pairing yearning vocals with the band's signature bouncy, minimalist synth-pop sound.

ora the molecule|nobody cares.fact: "Nobody Cares" is a single by Norwegian artist Ora the Molecule (Nora Schjelderup), taken from her sophomore album Dance Therapy, released March 21, 2025. The track pairs deadpan vocals with breezy, disco-tinged production and playful "la-la-la" hooks throughout.

parannoul|we shine at night.fact: "We Shine at Night" was released by South Korean musician Parannoul on January 28, 2023, as the fourth track on the album After the Magic. The six-and-a-half-minute fuzz-pop track features guest vocals from Seoul singer Della Zyr, a string arrangement by Rei Miyamoto of the Osaka band Vampillia, and trumpet from Fin Fior.

parquet courts|total football.fact: "Total Football" opens Parquet Courts' 2018 album Wide Awake! and takes its title from a tactical system popularized by the Dutch national soccer team at the 1974 World Cup, in which any player could fill any position on the field. Singer Andrew Savage said the soccer concept gave him a starting point for lyrics about the balance between collectivity and individuality.
