pavement|harness your hopes.fact: Pavement recorded "Harness Your Hopes" during sessions for 1997's Brighten the Corners, but it was left off the album and tucked away as a B-side on the 1999 Spit on a Stranger EP. Decades later, streaming-algorithm discovery turned the once-overlooked B-side into Pavement's most-streamed song, and it became the only Pavement track ever certified gold.

peach pit|alrighty aphrodite.fact: "Alrighty Aphrodite" was an early single from Vancouver band Peach Pit's 2018 debut album, Being So Normal. Its lyrics borrow imagery from classical art, opening with a nod to Botticelli's The Birth of Venus, where the goddess stands in a giant clamshell, and later referencing the sculpture known as the Crouching Venus.

phosphorescent|impossible house.fact: "Impossible House" comes from Phosphorescent's 2024 album Revelator, which songwriter Matthew Houck produced and recorded in his own Nashville studio over about six months. The lyrics include a playful pop-culture reference, likening a character to "that McCallister kid" left home alone, a nod to the Home Alone movies.

pixies|dig for fire.fact: "Dig for Fire" appeared on Pixies' 1990 album Bossanova and marked the first time the band used a drum machine, with Dave Lovering playing live drums on top of it. Frontman Black Francis has described the song as a deliberate homage to Talking Heads, joking he was "not even trying to hide" the David Byrne influence. An earlier, very different version of the song had actually been recorded with Steve Albini back in 1987 during the Surfer Rosa sessions.

pj harvey|missed.fact: "Missed" is the second track on PJ Harvey's 1993 album Rid of Me, produced by Steve Albini, with Rob Ellis on drums and Stephen Vaughan on bass. A demo version of the song later surfaced on her 2022 compilation B-Sides, Demos & Rarities.

pj harvey|you said something.fact: "You Said Something" appears on PJ Harvey's 2000 album Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea, which won the Mercury Prize in 2001. The song is set on a rooftop in Brooklyn at one in the morning, and it was later paired with "This Is Love" for a 2001 single release.

pom pom squad|doll song.fact: "Doll Song" is the ninth track on Pom Pom Squad's second album, Mirror Starts Moving Without Me, released October 25, 2024. Its music video leans into the song's doll imagery, with frontwoman Mia Berrin appearing as a porcelain-style figurine.

portishead|roads.fact: "Roads" is the eighth track on Portishead's 1994 debut album Dummy and is notable for containing no samples, unlike most of the record, instead built around Beth Gibbons' vocals and a Fender Rhodes-style keyboard theme. Despite becoming one of the album's most beloved songs, it was never released as a single, though it later turned up on the soundtracks for the films Nadja and Tank Girl.

quarters of change|heaven bound.fact: Quarters of Change formed in New York City in 2017 when Ben Acker and Jasper Harris, who met in elementary school, joined with Ben Roter and Attila Anrather. "Heaven Bound" is a single from the band's sophomore album Portraits, blending late-2000s rock and dream-pop influences.

quivers|apparition.fact: Quivers are an alt-rock quartet from Melbourne, Australia, made up of Sam Nicholson, Bella Quinlan, Michael Panton, and Holly Thomas. "Apparition" arrived in 2024 when the band signed to Merge Records, and it appears on their album Oyster Cuts, with a sound the band has said borrows a bit from the Rolling Stones and Pavement.

r.e.m.|aftermath.fact: "Aftermath" was released as the second single from R.E.M.'s 13th studio album, Around the Sun, in November 2004. Written by Peter Buck, Mike Mills, and Michael Stipe and produced by Pat McCarthy with the band, the song reached number 41 on the UK Singles Chart.

radiohead|bloom.fact: "Bloom" opens Radiohead's 2011 album The King of Limbs. Thom Yorke has said the song was inspired by the original BBC Blue Planet documentary series, calling the idea of discovering unknown forms of life one of the most profound concepts he'd encountered. Years later the band reworked the track with composer Hans Zimmer as "(ocean) Bloom" for a Blue Planet II trailer.

radiohead|decks dark.fact: "Decks Dark" is the third track on Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool. Its string and choir arrangements were written by Jonny Greenwood and performed by the London Contemporary Orchestra under conductor Hugh Brunt, giving the track its distinctive female-chorus backdrop.

radiohead|fake plastic trees.fact: Thom Yorke wrote "Fake Plastic Trees" after being struck by the artificial plants and manufactured feel of London's then-newly redeveloped Canary Wharf docklands. During recording for The Bends, producer John Leckie sent the rest of the band out of the room so Yorke could cut a quiet guide vocal alone, and Jonny Greenwood recalled Yorke nailing it in three takes.

real estate|water underground.fact: "Water Underground" is the lead single from Real Estate's 2024 album Daniel, co-written with Sammi Niss and produced by Daniel Tashian. Its music video pays tribute to the 1990s Nickelodeon sitcom The Adventures of Pete & Pete.

ride|peace sign.fact: "Peace Sign" began as a jam at guitarist Andy Bell's OX4 studio in 2021 and was originally titled "Berlin." It became a single from Ride's 2024 album Interplay, with Bell saying the lyrics were inspired by the documentary The Alpinist, about free climber Marc-Andre Leclerc.

samia|lizard.fact: "Lizard" appears on Samia's 2025 album Bloodless, which was recorded at Sylvan Esso's Betty's studio in Durham, North Carolina, and at collaborator Jake Luppen's Minneapolis studio. The album was produced by longtime Samia collaborator Caleb Wright alongside Luppen.

sigur ros|blooberg.fact: "Blodberg" (Icelandic for thyme) marked Sigur Ros's first new music in seven years when it was released in 2023. The roughly seven-minute track features orchestral contributions from the London Contemporary Orchestra, conducted by Robert Ames, with Jonsi singing partly in Icelandic and partly in the band's invented language, Hopelandic.

silver jews|people.fact: "People" appears on Silver Jews' 1998 album American Water, the record that reunited David Berman with Pavement's Stephen Malkmus, who trades vocal lines with Berman throughout the song. The track rides 1970s-style wah-wah guitar and is often cited by fans as a prime example of Berman's witty, detail-packed songwriting.

siouxsie and the banshees|monitor.fact: "Monitor" appears on Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1981 album Juju, featuring guitarist John McGeoch's hypnotic, distorted playing and production by Nigel Gray. The lyrics imagine a world watched over by surveillance screens, giving the song an Orwellian, CCTV-style atmosphere years before such themes became common in pop music.

sleater-kinney|get up.fact: "Get Up" was released as a single from Sleater-Kinney's 1999 album The Hot Rock and marked a deliberate shift toward a more melodic, danceable sound compared to the band's earlier, rawer records. Its music video was directed by filmmaker Miranda July.

slowdive|alison.fact: "Alison" opens Slowdive's 1993 album Souvlaki. Early versions of the Souvlaki material were initially rejected by Creation Records boss Alan McGee, who then gave the band full creative control; around the same time Slowdive reached out to Brian Eno, who admired their music and ended up contributing to two other tracks on the record.

sonic youth|bull in the heather.fact: "Bull in the Heather" is the lead single from Sonic Youth's 1994 album Experimental Jet Set, Trash and No Star. Kim Gordon said the song is about "using passiveness as a form of rebellion," and its title borrows the name of a racehorse that won the 1993 Florida Derby. The Tamra Davis-directed video features a visibly pregnant Gordon dancing alongside Bikini Kill's Kathleen Hanna.

spellling|portrait of my heart.fact: "Portrait of My Heart" is the title track and opener of SPELLLING's 2025 album of the same name, her follow-up to 2021's The Turning Wheel. Singer Chrystia Cabral said she used the song's propulsive drum groove and anthemic "I don't belong here" chorus to work through performance anxiety, opting for a tighter, more rock-oriented sound than her earlier material.

spoon|don't you evah.fact: "Don't You Evah" is a cover of "Don't You Ever" by The Natural History, a New York indie band fronted by Max Tepper, a friend of Spoon's Britt Daniel. Because The Natural History's own album was delayed for contractual reasons, Spoon's version on Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga (2007) actually came out before the original recording.

st. vincent|northern lights.fact: For the frenzied guitar solo on "Northern Lights," from 2011's Strange Mercy, Annie Clark (St. Vincent) used an unusual delay pedal called the Sitori Sonics Tapeworm, which has two built-in synth oscillators. It's considered one of the more inventive pedal choices on the record, which Clark recorded with longtime producer John Congleton in her hometown of Dallas.

sylvan esso|rooftop dancing.fact: "Rooftop Dancing" was the second single from Sylvan Esso's 2020 album Free Love. Its music video, directed by Cheryl Dunn, follows a roller skater gliding joyfully around New York City and was conceived as a tribute to the resilience of New Yorkers during a difficult year.

sylvan esso|train.fact: "Train," from Sylvan Esso's 2020 album Free Love, grew out of singer Amelia Meath's goal of writing a song that was, in her words, "almost disgustingly" catchy. The duo later reworked the track for their WITH LOVE EP, released that December.

talking heads|love -> building on fire.fact: "Love -> Building on Fire" was Talking Heads' debut single, released in February 1977, seven months ahead of their first album. It was recorded at Sundragon Recording Studios in New York while the band was still a trio, before keyboardist Jerry Harrison joined, and was produced by Tony Bongiovi and Tom Erdelyi (better known as Tommy Ramone).

talking heads|love for sale.fact: Despite sharing its title with the Cole Porter standard, Talking Heads' "Love for Sale" is an original David Byrne composition written for the 1986 film True Stories, which Byrne also directed. Byrne wrote the lyric in the style of a TV commercial pitch, borrowing real ad slogans like Greyhound's "Leave the driving to us" and Coke's "It's the real thing."

tame impala|expectation.fact: "Expectation" was recorded by Kevin Parker in mid-2009 at Wave House in Injidup, Western Australia, during the sessions for Tame Impala's debut album Innerspeaker. Released as the album's third single in December 2010, the six-minute track was mixed by Dave Fridmann and features cover art by Australian artist Leif Podhajsky.

the apples in stereo|energy.fact: "Energy," from The Apples in Stereo's 2007 album New Magnetic Wonder, got a music video directed by actor Elijah Wood, marking his directorial debut. Wood was a longtime fan of the band and had signed them as the first act on his independent label, Simian Records, after meeting frontman Robert Schneider at SXSW in 2003.

the black keys|all hands against his own.fact: "All Hands Against His Own" appears on The Black Keys' 2004 album Rubber Factory, which was recorded in an abandoned General Tire factory in the band's hometown of Akron, Ohio. The duo tracked the album on a reel-to-reel recorder using tape recycled from old fried-chicken radio commercials that never aired.

the black keys|just got to be.fact: "Just Got to Be," released in 2007 from The Black Keys' album Magic Potion, was recorded by Dan Auerbach and Patrick Carney in Akron, Ohio. The song later turned up on the soundtrack of the video game NHL 08 and in an AT&T commercial, and its music video shows the duo performing on stage at Akron's Italian Center with no audience present.

the cure|high.fact: "High" was released in March 1992 as the lead single from The Cure's album Wish, reaching number one on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart and number eight on the UK Singles Chart. It's credited to all five members of the band at the time (Robert Smith, Simon Gallup, Porl Thompson, Boris Williams, and Perry Bamonte) and was produced by Smith with David Allen.

the damned|neat neat neat.fact: "Neat Neat Neat," the Damned's second single, was released on Stiff Records in February 1977 alongside their debut album Damned Damned Damned. Written by guitarist Brian James and produced by Nick Lowe at Pathway Studios in London, its driving bassline was later ranked among Stylus Magazine's Top 50 basslines of all time.

the dismemberment plan|what do you want.fact: An early version of "What Do You Want Me to Say?" was first released as a 7-inch single in November 1997, before the song was re-recorded for the Dismemberment Plan's 1999 album Emergency & I. That album was produced by J. Robbins and Chad Clark, primarily at Water Music Studios with additional sessions at Inner Ear Studios.

the flaming lips|do you realize??.fact: "Do You Realize??," from The Flaming Lips' 2002 album Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots, was named Oklahoma's official state rock song in 2009 by executive order of Governor Brad Henry. The honor followed an online poll in which the Oklahoma City band's song beat out nine other finalists, including "Heartbreak Hotel," co-written by Oklahoman Mae Boren Axton.

the flaming lips|ego tripping at the gat.fact: "Ego Tripping at the Gates of Hell" first appeared on The Flaming Lips' 2002 album Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots, then lent its title to a 2003 EP featuring club remixes of the song plus new original tracks. Several of those extra recordings were later gathered into the band's 2022 20th-anniversary Yoshimi box set.

the mountain goats|mobile.fact: "Mobile," from The Mountain Goats' 2021 album Dark in Here, recasts the Biblical story of Jonah with a Southern setting on the Gulf Coast in Mobile, Alabama. The track features veteran Muscle Shoals session players Spooner Oldham on electric piano and Will McFarlane on lead guitar.

the olivia tremor control|define a trans.fact: "Define a Transparent Dream" comes from The Olivia Tremor Control's 1996 album Music from the Unrealized Film Script: Dusk at Cubist Castle, a concept record built around an unproduced film script co-written by band member Will Cullen Hart. The sprawling, genre-blending album featured contributions from fellow Elephant 6 collective members Jeff Mangum (Neutral Milk Hotel) and Robert Schneider (The Apples in Stereo).

the raincoats|fairytale in the supermark.fact: "Fairytale in the Supermarket" was the debut single by London post-punk band The Raincoats, recorded in March 1979 and released that April on Rough Trade. The all-female group performed it along with two other songs for BBC Radio 1 DJ John Peel around the same time. The song found a second life decades later after Kurt Cobain publicly praised the band, and it was later featured on the soundtrack to Mike Mills' 2016 film "20th Century Women."

the strokes|take it or leave it.fact: "Take It or Leave It" closes The Strokes' 2001 debut album "Is This It," written by Julian Casablancas and produced by Gordon Raphael. The entire album was tracked in only about six weeks at Raphael's small Transporterraum studio in New York City, with Casablancas pushing the band to keep performances raw, often recording songs in just a take or two.

the strokes|the adults are talking.fact: "The Adults Are Talking" opens The Strokes' 2020 album "The New Abnormal," their first LP produced by Rick Rubin, recorded at his Shangri-La studio in Malibu. The band actually debuted the song live at the Wiltern Theatre in Los Angeles in May 2019, almost a full year before its studio version was released. Its music video, directed by Roman Coppola, imagines a future where the band competes against android ballplayers.

the sundays|here's where the story ends.fact: "Here's Where the Story Ends" was written by Sundays members David Gavurin and Harriet Wheeler for the band's 1990 debut album "Reading, Writing and Arithmetic," produced by the band with Ray Shulman. It became the group's biggest international hit, topping the US Modern Rock Tracks chart even though it was never issued as a UK single. In 1998, dance duo Tin Tin Out reworked the song into a UK top-10 hit that went on to win the 1999 Ivor Novello Award for Best Contemporary Song.

the vaselines|molly's lips.fact: "Molly's Lips" was written and first recorded by Scottish duo Eugene Kelly and Frances McKee of The Vaselines, appearing on their 1988 "Dying for It" EP. Kurt Cobain was a huge fan and had Nirvana cover the song for a 1990 BBC Radio 1 John Peel session (drummer Dave Grohl's first with the band), later included on 1992's "Incesticide." Cobain's championing of the duo helped reunite The Vaselines, and Kelly even joined Nirvana on stage to perform the song at the 1991 Reading Festival.

the war on drugs|harmonia's dream.fact: "Harmonia's Dream," from The War on Drugs' 2021 album "I Don't Live Here Anymore," takes its title from the German krautrock supergroup Harmonia, formed by Cluster's Hans-Joachim Roedelius and Dieter Moebius with Neu! guitarist Michael Rother. Frontman Adam Granduciel has described being a longtime devotee of that scene's records. The track, co-produced by Shawn Everett and co-written with keyboardist Robbie Bennett, earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rock Song.

this is lorelei|where's your love now.fact: "Where's Your Love Now" is a 2024 single by This Is Lorelei, the solo project of Water From Your Eyes' Nate Amos, from his album "Box for Buddy, Box for Star." The song drew wider attention after Waxahatchee's Katie Crutchfield covered it with Brad Cook at a Newport Folk Festival afterparty, calling it one of the best songs she'd ever heard, and later performed it in-studio for KEXP.

tom waits|goin' out west.fact: "Goin' Out West" appears on Tom Waits' 1992 album "Bone Machine," which won the Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album. Waits co-wrote the song with his wife, Kathleen Brennan, and recorded it in a stark cellar room at Prairie Sun Recording with just a cement floor and a water heater for ambience, featuring Larry Taylor on electric upright bass and Joe Gore on guitar.

trace mountains|in a dream.fact: "In A Dream" is the opening track and lead single from Trace Mountains' 2024 album "Into the Burning Blue," produced by Craig Hendrix (known for his work with Japanese Breakfast). Songwriter Dave Benton has said the track began as a prompt from a songwriting workshop he teaches, and that he was picturing Bruce Springsteen's "Tunnel of Love" and David Lynch's "Blue Velvet" while writing it.

ugly casanova|parasites.fact: "Parasites" appears on "Sharpen Your Teeth," the 2002 album by Ugly Casanova, a side project of Modest Mouse frontman Isaac Brock. The song started life as an unreleased Modest Mouse demo from the band's 1993 "Parasite Sessions." Brock originally tried to keep the Ugly Casanova project separate from his main band by crediting songwriting to a fictional collaborator named Edgar Graham.

vampire weekend|hannah hunt.fact: Ezra Koenig began writing "Hannah Hunt" years before its release, starting the lyric while he was still a student at Columbia University. Vampire Weekend couldn't find the right musical arrangement for it in time for their first two albums, finally completing it for 2013's "Modern Vampires of the City" with producer Ariel Rechtshaid and bandmate Rostam Batmanglij.

waxahatchee|right back to it (feat. mj l.fact: "Right Back to It" is the lead single from Waxahatchee's 2024 album "Tigers Blood," recorded at Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas with producer Brad Cook. Katie Crutchfield wrote it backstage at Virginia's Wolf Trap while opening for Sheryl Crow and Jason Isbell, and the duet with MJ Lenderman marked his first appearance on the Billboard charts.

wilco|cousin.fact: The title track of Wilco's 2023 album "Cousin" marked the first time in over a decade that the band brought in an outside producer, Welsh musician Cate Le Bon. Tweedy and Le Bon first met when her band played Wilco's own Solid Sound Festival in 2019, leading to an invitation to produce the record at the band's Chicago studio, The Loft.

woods|bleeding blue.fact: "Bleeding Blue" is the third track on "Love Is Love," the 2017 album by Brooklyn folk-rock band Woods, who formed in 2005. The song stands out for its horn-gilded arrangement, with Alec Spiegelman on sax and flute and Cole Kamen-Green on trumpet giving it a funkier sound than much of the band's earlier catalog.

yo la tengo|rickety.fact: "Rickety" is one of only two brand-new originals on Yo La Tengo's 2015 album "Stuff Like That There," a record that revisited the stripped-down, acoustic covers-album concept of their 1990 release "Fakebook." It's been described as a gentle indie-pop song about the ups and downs of a long relationship.

alex g|harvey.fact: Harvey appeared on Alex G's 2014 album DSU and is often cited as a fan-favorite entry point into his catalog. The song is sung from the perspective of what sounds like a child or an imaginary friend, repeating the mantra 'success for my buddy, success for my friend,' giving it a disarmingly simple but emotionally layered feel. Critics have praised it as a perfect, airy-yet-angular pop song that still sounds sleepy and wide awake at once.

cut copy|belong to you (feat. kate bolli.fact: Cut Copy's 'Belong to You' came together after a friend introduced the band to singer Kate Bollinger while they were finishing the track, and they asked her to try a vocal part that ended up shaping the whole song into a duet. The band also brought in pedal-steel player 'Evil' Graham Lee of the legendary Australian band The Triffids to add a sci-fi country twist to the disco-leaning pop arrangement. It's one of the rare times Cut Copy has built a song around collaborators outside their core lineup.

radiohead|ill wind.fact: 'Ill Wind' was a bonus track tucked into the deluxe box set of Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool, released alongside the band's unused James Bond theme 'Spectre.' Built on a bossa nova rhythm with Thom Yorke singing in falsetto over icy layered synths, it stayed a rarity until the band finally put it on streaming services in 2019. Once released, it quietly climbed to No. 8 on Billboard's Alternative Digital Songs chart.

cate le bon feat. john cale|ride.fact: 'Ride' appears on Cate Le Bon's 2025 album Michelangelo Dying and features a guest vocal turn from John Cale, the Welsh musician and founding member of The Velvet Underground. The hypnotic, interlocking vocal performance between the two is considered one of the album's most striking moments, a notable pairing of two generations of Welsh experimental songwriting.

vampire weekend|big blue.fact: On 'Big Blue,' from 2019's Father of the Bride, Ezra Koenig addresses the Earth itself with the affectionate nickname that gives the song its title, treating the planet almost like an old friend. Despite the playful title, the song has the quiet, hymn-like earnestness of a devotional, with Koenig repeating the same humble verse over and over like a mantra. Koenig has cited Kacey Musgraves' Golden Hour as an influence on the album's warm, countryish psychedelia heard here.

the decemberists|calamity song.fact: Colin Meloy wrote 'Calamity Song' shortly after finishing David Foster Wallace's novel Infinite Jest, and even pitched a music video built around a recreation of the book's apocalyptic tennis-court war game 'Eschaton.' Meloy has also said the song grew out of binge-listening to R.E.M.'s second album Reckoning, and the opening guitar riff bears a close resemblance to that record's 'Talk About the Passion.'

angel olsen|enemy.fact: 'Enemy' is track ten on Angel Olsen's 2014 breakthrough album Burn Your Fire for No Witness, which the singer recorded in an abandoned chapel. Described by critics as understated yet cathartic, the song includes one of the record's most direct lyrical moments, with Olsen singing plainly, 'You could be the only one who knows the truth of me.'

nation of language|across that fine line.fact: 'Across That Fine Line' was released in June 2021 as the lead single from Nation of Language's second album, A Way Forward, written by frontman Ian Richard Devaney with music co-composed by Aidan Noell and Michael Sue-Poi. The synth-pop trio performed the song as musical guests on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, filmed in an empty room at the Brooklyn venue Baby's All Right while waitstaff wandered through the shot.

royel otis|car.fact: 'car' was released as a single ahead of Royel Otis's sophomore album Hickey, co-written with producers Blake Slatkin and Omer Fedi, who've also worked with artists like Gracie Abrams and The Kid Laroi. The song was named BBC Radio 1's 'Hottest Record' on release, and its road-trip theme later inspired the duo's 'Meet Me in the Car' tour name.

fontaines d.c.|starbuster.fact: 'Starburster' was the lead single from Fontaines D.C.'s 2024 album Romance, with frontman Grian Chatten writing it after an anxious moment he experienced at London's St Pancras train station. He's said he initially wrote the rapid-fire, hip-hop-and-electronica-tinged verses almost as a joke, but when the band heard it they took it seriously, and it became the band's first entry on the UK Singles Chart.

modest mouse|heart cooks brain.fact: 'Heart Cooks Brain' is the second track on Modest Mouse's 1997 album The Lonesome Crowded West, built around drummer Jeremiah Green's stuttering, hip-hop-influenced breakbeat under Isaac Brock's spiraling, cyclical guitar lines. The track also layers in turntable scratching deep in the mix, an unusual touch for the band's raw, lo-fi indie rock sound at the time.

lucy dacus|nonbeliever.fact: 'Nonbeliever,' from Lucy Dacus's 2018 album Historian, is actually a splice of three separate songs she'd written at very different points starting in 2011. None of the individual versions felt complete on their own, so in 2016 Dacus realized what they had in common, cut them apart, and reassembled the best pieces into one finished song.

car seat headrest|not just what i needed.fact: This Car Seat Headrest track began life as 'Just What I Needed/Not Just What I Needed,' built around an interpolation of The Cars' 1978 hit, for the 2016 album Teens of Denial. After the record's release, The Cars' Ric Ocasek withdrew permission for the sample, forcing Matador Records to pull and destroy existing vinyl copies; Will Toledo then wrote an extended, fully original replacement version of the song for the revised pressing.

beck|que' onde guero.fact: Beck has said 'Que Onda Guero,' from his 2005 album Guero, is 'about growing up' in the Chicano neighborhood of Los Angeles where he spent part of his childhood, built like a 'watercolor, pen-and-ink' sketch of the area. To capture that atmosphere, he recorded ambient street sounds like pushcart vendors, a popsicle cart, and kids playing soccer and wove them into the track. The title itself is slang Beck says he regularly heard shouted at him growing up in the neighborhood.

the mountain goats|sicilian crest.fact: 'Sicilian Crest,' from The Mountain Goats' 2019 album In League with Dragons, reportedly started as just a strange phrase John Darnielle had jotted in a notebook before he built the song around it while messing around at the piano with his son. Musically, it's one of the album's grandest, lushest moments, driven by florid piano and explosive drumming from Jon Wurster, with a dance-rock feel critics compared to New Order.

elliott smith|son of sam.fact: Despite its ominous title, Elliott Smith was explicit that 'Son of Sam,' from his 2000 album Figure 8, is not about the real-life serial killer of that nickname. The title instead plays on a kind of internal duality, with the song riding a sunny, Beach Boys-meets-Beatles arrangement that contrasts with its wordplay. Its music video, directed by Autumn de Wilde, followed Smith chasing a self-moving red balloon through black-and-white freeze frames inspired by the 1962 French film La Jetee.

siouxsie and the banshees|peek-a-boo.fact: 'Peek-a-Boo' was built by taking a reversed loop of a brass-and-drum part the Banshees had originally arranged a year earlier for a cover of John Cale's 'Gun,' then layering in a new melody, a one-note bass line, and a distinctive accordion part. The unusual combination, which NME once called 'Oriental marching band hip hop,' gave Siouxsie and the Banshees their first-ever entry on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 1988.

spoon|rent i pay.fact: 'Rent I Pay' was the lead single from Spoon's 2014 album They Want My Soul, and frontman Britt Daniel has said the title phrase, 'that's the rent I pay,' was an expression his brother used to say. Daniel knew the song was special the moment the band first played back the basic recorded track in their rental van after a day in the studio, recalling that it gave him chills.

andy shauf|call.fact: 'Call' appears on Andy Shauf's 2021 album Wilds, one of nine songs culled from roughly fifty tracks he recorded during the sessions for his 2020 concept album The Neon Skyline. Wilds functions as a companion piece to that record, revisiting the same pair of characters and their relationship from different angles and points in time.

stereolab|three-dee melodie.fact: 'Three-Dee Melodie' opens Stereolab's 1994 album Mars Audiac Quintet, a record widely seen as the moment the band fully fused their love of lounge and exotica with their krautrock-indebted grooves and analog synthesizers. The album marked a turning point toward a more accessible, melodic sound while keeping the band's experimental edge intact.

tom waits|all the world is green.fact: 'All the World Is Green' comes from Tom Waits' 2002 album Blood Money, a collaboration with playwright Robert Wilson and co-writer Kathleen Brennan built around Georg Buchner's play Woyzeck. Within that story the song functions as a tender love song, essentially a soldier's paean to his wife. It later turned up on the soundtracks to the films The Secret Life of Words and The Diving Bell and the Butterfly.

yeah yeah yeahs|hysteric.fact: 'Hysteric,' from Yeah Yeah Yeahs' 2009 album It's Blitz!, is built on a looping guitar riff that owes a clear debt to Blondie's 'Atomic.' Karen O sings the unguarded line 'you suddenly complete me' without a trace of her usual irony, a notably vulnerable turn for a singer known for ferocity. The track closes on a drifting, whistled outro that became one of the album's most distinctive moments.

the strokes|oblivius.fact: 'Oblivius' was one of three songs on The Strokes' 2016 EP Future Present Past, alongside 'Drag Queen' and 'Threat of Joy,' each meant to represent a different timeframe for the band; 'Oblivius' stood in for the present. It was recorded with producer Gus Oberg in sessions split between New York City and Austin, Texas, blending the lo-fi feel of Room on Fire with the moodier touches of First Impressions of Earth.

the magnetic fields|i don't believe you.fact: 'I Don't Believe You' appears on The Magnetic Fields' 2004 album i, a concept record where all 14 songs - sung entirely by Stephin Merritt and sequenced alphabetically - begin with the letter 'I.' Unlike much of Merritt's other work, i was recorded using only hand-played instruments, with no synthesizers at all.

bully|all i do.fact: 'All I Do' opens Bully's 2023 album Lucky for You, building from a shimmering, reverb-laden guitar line into the record's trademark huge riffs. Frontwoman Alicia Bognanno made the album with producer JT Daly at his Nashville studio, and it took roughly seven months to finish - the longest gestation period of any Bully record up to that point.

adrianne lenker|sadness as a gift.fact: 'Sadness as a Gift' is a single from Adrianne Lenker's 2024 solo album Bright Future, recorded in fall 2022 at the rural analog studio Double Infinity and co-produced with Philip Weinrobe. The warm, strummed arrangement is colored by Josefin Runsteen's violin, and Lenker has described the song as being about the end of a relationship.

tunde adebimpe|magnetic.fact: 'Magnetic' comes from Thee Black Boltz, TV on the Radio frontman Tunde Adebimpe's debut solo album, released on Sub Pop in April 2025. At just two and a half minutes, its minimalist electro-punk pulse recalls his old band's early-2000s Brooklyn DIY days, with lyrics musing on 'the human race in the age of tenderness and rage.'

the cramps|garbageman.fact: 'Garbageman' helped launch The Cramps' 1980 debut LP, Songs the Lord Taught Us, which the band recorded in Memphis with Big Star's Alex Chilton producing at the old post-Sun Sam Phillips Recording studio. Rolling Stone later named the album one of its 80 greatest records of 1980, cementing its reputation as a founding psychobilly landmark.

thundercat|children of the baked potato.fact: Thundercat released 'Children of the Baked Potato,' featuring Remi Wolf, as a single on September 15, 2025, ahead of his album Distracted. The title nods to The Baked Potato, the longtime hole-in-the-wall jazz club in LA's San Fernando Valley that has showcased fusion players for decades and shaped both musicians' backgrounds, with Thundercat calling Wolf 'a child of the Baked Potato like me.'

perfume genius|normal song.fact: 'Normal Song' first appeared on Perfume Genius's 2012 album Put Your Back N 2 It. Years later, its use in film and television earned it a nomination for 'Best Sync Usage' at the 2017 Libera Awards, which honor independent labels and artists.

japanese breakfast|posing in bondage.fact: 'Posing in Bondage' sits on Japanese Breakfast's 2021 album Jubilee, the first record where Michelle Zauner co-wrote full orchestral string and horn arrangements herself rather than leaving those decisions to the studio. She credited the confidence to arrange more ambitiously to having dipped into strings and horns in smaller doses on her previous album, Soft Sounds from Another Planet.

big thief|no fear.fact: 'No Fear' appears on Big Thief's 2025 album Double Infinity. It's a hypnotic, mantra-like piece built from looping bass and guitar, with Adrianne Lenker repeating spare, meditative lines like 'there is no fear, mind so clear, mind so free.'

cafune|the moment.fact: 'The Moment' opens Cafune's 2025 album Bite Reality, released September 12, 2025. Sedona Schat sings lead with Noah Yoo on guitar and Connor Parks on drums, self-produced by the duo and mixed by Noah Glassman.

the antlers|something in the air.fact: 'Something in the Air' is a 2025 single from The Antlers' album Blight, inspired by singer Peter Silberman's walks near his home recording studio. He's described the song as being about 'a looming threat that can take many forms,' part of an album that grapples broadly with climate anxiety and humanity's quiet, cumulative impact on the natural world.

the beths|great no one.fact: 'Great No One' is the opening track and lead single (released October 2017) from The Beths' 2018 debut album Future Me Hates Me. Frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes has described the record's songs broadly as being about infatuation and self-directed telling-offs, delivered through the band's signature hyper-melodic power-pop.

sharon van etten|i'll try.fact: 'I'll Try' is a track from Sharon Van Etten's 2022 album We've Been Going About This All Wrong, repeating its simple title phrase over icy synths and big drums. The song finds Van Etten pushing back against public judgment and sticking to what she believes, set to an upbeat arrangement of distorted guitars and layered instrumentation that contrasts with the album's more somber moments.

beach house|real love.fact: 'Real Love' is the ninth track on Beach House's 2010 breakthrough album Teen Dream, recorded not in their native Baltimore but at Dreamland, a converted church studio in upstate New York. The album was produced by Chris Coady, who also worked with TV on the Radio, Yeah Yeah Yeahs, and Blonde Redhead, and 'Real Love' is often singled out as one of the record's rare moments of hope amid its wintry, lovelorn tone.

tune-yards|limelight.fact: 'Limelight' is the lead single from Tune-Yards' 2025 album Better Dreaming. Merrill Garbus and Nate Brenner wrote it after a night of dancing to George Clinton with their young child, who ended up singing on the finished track; the song almost got left off the record before fan and family response convinced them to keep it.

the national|i need my girl.fact: 'I Need My Girl' is a single from The National's 2013 album Trouble Will Find Me. It's one of the band's more plaintive, piano-driven songs, with Matt Berninger's lyrics capturing the quiet relief of having one steady person to come home to - a hallmark of the band's knack for turning everyday adult unease into vivid, specific imagery.

guerilla toss|ceo of personal & pleasure.fact: Guerilla Toss formed in Boston in 2011 and relocated to Brooklyn in 2015 after singer Kassie Carlson signed the band to James Murphy's DFA Records. Carlson has described the title track's attitude as firing her own inner critic and reinstating herself as the slightly unhinged CEO of her own emotional start-up - a tongue-in-cheek self-care pep talk rather than anything else.

woods|be there still.fact: 'Be There Still' is track 10 on Woods' 2020 album Strange to Explain, the band's 99th release on their own Woodsist label. An alternate version of the song later appeared on the deluxe edition, More Strange, released the following year.

destroyer|el rito.fact: 'El Rito' is Destroyer's cover of a song by Spanish songwriter Antonio Luque of the band Sr. Chinarro, featured on the 2013 EP Five Spanish Songs. Dan Bejar said the original was one of Luque's most traditional flamenco-style songs, so he deliberately reworked it into a glammy, four-on-the-floor rock arrangement with fuzz guitar instead.

say she she|disco life.fact: Say She She is a disco-funk trio - Piya Malik, Sabrina Cunningham, and Nya Gazelle Brown - who met and built their sound across New York City, cutting their teeth with a residency at Brooklyn's Union Pool and playing their first show as a band at the venue Barbes. Drawing on '70s heroes like Chic and Nile Rodgers, the group records with analog gear and tape to keep their sound retro.

andrew bird|left handed kisses.fact: 'Left Handed Kisses' is a duet between Andrew Bird and Fiona Apple from Bird's 2016 album Are You Serious. Bird said the song began as an internal dialogue about his struggle to write a simple, uncomplicated love song, and he realized it needed to become a duet when another 'voice' crept into the lyrics - leading him to recruit Apple as a sparring partner. The pair also performed it together on The Ellen DeGeneres Show.

joy division|transmission.fact: 'Transmission' was Joy Division's debut single for Factory Records, released in October 1979, and was deliberately left off their album Unknown Pleasures because the band believed singles and albums should stay separate. The band also recorded it for a John Peel session at the BBC's Maida Vale studios, and its driving 'dance, dance, dance to the radio' refrain made it one of their most influential early tracks.

amber arcades|simple song.fact: 'Simple Song' is the sunny, horn-flecked opening track on Amber Arcades' 2018 album European Heartbreak. Its music video was released as the second installment of a trilogy that began with the clip for 'Goodnight Europe.'

ween|she wanted to leave (reprise).fact: 'She Wanted to Leave (Reprise)' closes out Ween's 1997 concept album The Mollusk, a nautical-themed record, reprising the earlier song's yarn about a sailor whose love is carried off by pirates. Musically, the reprise plays as the band's homage/parody of British prog-rock group the Moody Blues.

waxahatchee|sparks fly.fact: 'Sparks Fly' appears on Waxahatchee's 2017 album Out in the Storm, recorded by Katie Crutchfield with her twin sister Allison playing keyboards and singing harmonies. The lyrics describe staying up all night at a Berlin bar and watching the sunrise, building from a quiet acoustic strum into a huge, chorus-swirled finish.

devo|jocko homo.fact: DEVO's 'Jocko Homo' takes its title from a 1924 anti-evolution pamphlet called 'Jocko-Homo Heavenbound,' which fit the band's running concept of 'de-evolution.' Its famous call-and-response chorus, 'Are we not men? We are Devo!,' is a direct reference to a line from the 1932 film Island of Lost Souls, itself based on H.G. Wells' novel The Island of Doctor Moreau.

courtney barnett|sunfair sundown.fact: 'Sunfair Sundown' is the second track on Courtney Barnett's 2021 album Things Take Time, Take Time, and was inspired by a visit to Sunfair in the Mojave Desert - the last trip she took before the pandemic shut everything down. The album was recorded with producer/drummer Stella Mozgawa of Warpaint across sessions in Sydney, Northern NSW, and Melbourne.

yo la tengo|let's save tony orlando's ho.fact: The title of Yo La Tengo's 'Let's Save Tony Orlando's House' comes from a Simpsons episode, 'Marge on the Lam,' in which Troy McClure jokes about telethons including 'Let's Save Tony Orlando's House.' Bassist James McNew, a lifelong Simpsons fan, had a habit of naming the band's wordless instrumentals after random lines from the show, and this one stuck.

wilco|citizens.fact: 'Citizens' appears on Wilco's 2019 album Ode to Joy, recorded at the band's Chicago studio The Loft. For the record, classically trained drummer Glenn Kotche skipped playing a full kit and instead built his parts by recording individual percussion elements separately before stitching them together in the mix, giving the album's rhythms their distinct, orchestral feel.

mac demarco|my kind of woman.fact: 'My Kind of Woman' is the lead single from Mac DeMarco's 2012 sophomore album, 2, and is widely regarded as the record's standout, melodic peak. Unlike much of the album's loose, lo-fi style, the song leans into a warm, timeless pop sound that critics have compared to a modern indie-rock standard.

of montreal|jacques lamure.fact: 'Jacques Lamure' is the fourth track on of Montreal's 1999 concept album The Gay Parade, all of it written by frontman Kevin Barnes. The song is a whimsical character sketch of a volunteer fireman who works as a foreman at a clock factory, enjoys watching Westerns at the movies, and dreams of winning over a woman named Meg despite never working up the nerve to approach her.

radiohead|like spinning plates.fact: 'Like Spinning Plates,' from Radiohead's 2001 album Amnesiac, is built on the reversed backing track of an early electronic version of the then-unreleased song 'I Will.' Thom Yorke said that after hearing the tape played backward he thought the melody sounded better that way, so he learned to sing the lyrics backwards and then reversed that vocal take again to get the song's eerie, warped sound.

low|breakers.fact: The closest match in Low's catalog is 'Breaker,' the second track on their 2007 album Drums and Guns - the trio's first record to lean heavily on loops and samples. Built from synthetic percussion, handclaps, and Alan Sparhawk's jagged guitar skronk, it was recorded with Mimi Parker on drums and vocals and Matt Livingston on bass.

beirut|so many plans.fact: 'So Many Plans' is the lead single from Beirut's 2023 album Hadsel, named for the Norwegian island where frontman Zach Condon spent time in 2020. There, a local organ enthusiast introduced him to the pipe organ at the Hadselkirke church, whose sound became the foundation for the record; Condon called the song's lyric a 'covid-times lament' that turned into a gentle lullaby balancing acceptance, hope, and giving up.

cat power|werewolf.fact: Cat Power's 'Werewolf,' from her 2003 album You Are Free, is a cover of 'The Werewolf Song' by folk singer Michael Hurley, originally released on his 1964 debut, First Songs. Cat Power's version helped introduce a new generation of listeners, including fellow freak-folk artists, to Hurley's decades-spanning catalog.

fiona apple|valentine.fact: 'Valentine' is the third track on Fiona Apple's 2012 album The Idler Wheel Is Wiser Than the Driver of the Screw and Whipping Cords Will Serve You More than Ropes Will Ever Do. Apple recorded the whole album in secret without even telling her label, choosing to produce it herself with her touring drummer Charley Drayton rather than longtime collaborator Jon Brion - the result has no electric instruments on it at all. Despite the romantic-sounding title, Apple has said the song isn't about a lover but about a girl she admired and wished she could be more like.

real estate|darling.fact: 'Darling' is the opening track on Real Estate's 2017 album In Mind, the follow-up to 2014's Atlas. It was the band's first album recorded with new guitarist Julian Lynch, who joined after founding guitarist Matt Mondanile departed. True to the New Jersey band's laid-back style, the song opens with nearly a full minute of guitar jamming before any vocals come in.

doves|black and white town.fact: 'Black and White Town' was the lead single from Doves' 2005 album Some Cities, giving the Manchester-area band their second UK top-10 hit, peaking at No. 6. Frontman Jimi Goodwin has described its loose theme as cities changing over time - old, loved buildings torn down and replaced by generic new developments. It captures a restless feeling tied to watching a hometown's character disappear.

wednesday|twin plagues.fact: 'Twin Plagues' is the title track that opens Wednesday's breakout 2021 album of the same name, written by Karly Hartzman. Hartzman borrowed the phrase from author Richard Brautigan and uses it as a stand-in for the way certain personal events seem to recur throughout a life, like a cycle that can't quite be escaped. It set the tone for a record full of vivid, novelistic storytelling about growing up in North Carolina.

spiritualized|i'm your man.fact: 'I'm Your Man' is the second track on Spiritualized's 2018 album And Nothing Hurt. Unusually for a band known for lush, orchestral production, bandleader Jason Pierce recorded almost the entire album himself on a laptop in an upstairs room of his London home, teaching himself digital recording from scratch because there wasn't a budget for a proper studio. Despite the bedroom setup, he painstakingly layered strings and horns part by part to make the record sound as full as his earlier studio albums.

the cure|alone.fact: 'Alone' opens The Cure's 2024 album Songs of a Lost World, the band's first new album in 16 years and first new song since 2008's 4:13 Dream. Robert Smith has said the lyrics grew out of rediscovering the Ernest Dowson poem 'Dregs' in an old journal and borrowing its imagery. The album was recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales, and Smith has said that once 'Alone' was finished, he knew immediately it had to be the opening track because it unlocked the whole record for him.

st. vincent|flea.fact: 'Flea' was the second single from St. Vincent's 2024 album All Born Screaming, and it features Foo Fighters' Dave Grohl on drums alongside bassist Justin Meldal-Johnsen. Annie Clark has said she sent Grohl the song specifically because of its twisting, prog-style tempo changes, figuring the part would be right up his alley. It's one of the heavier, more rhythmically unusual tracks on the self-produced record.

fleet foxes|third of may - odaigahara.fact: 'Third of May / Odaigahara' was the lead single from Fleet Foxes' 2017 album Crack-Up, their first new music in six years. Frontman Robin Pecknold wrote it as a time-traveling meditation on his long friendship with guitarist Skyler Skjelset, whose birthday falls on May 3 - the same date their 2011 album Helplessness Blues was released. The title and some imagery also nod to Francisco Goya's 1814 painting The Third of May 1808, and each verse jumps to a different year in the band's history.

ramones|havana affair.fact: 'Havana Affair' appears on the Ramones' self-titled 1976 debut album, playing a Cold War-era spy storyline for laughs, with the narrator boasting about becoming 'a guide for the CIA' in pre-revolution Havana. Johnny Ramone was such a fan of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' cover version that he chose to open the 2003 Ramones tribute album We're a Happy Family with it.

the smile|the opposite.fact: 'The Opposite' is the second track on The Smile's 2022 debut album A Light for Attracting Attention, the trio project formed by Radiohead's Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood with drummer Tom Skinner. It's cheekily sequenced right after the album's opening track, 'The Same' - two songs with deliberately contrasting titles. Musically it locks into a tight, math-rock-style groove built from Greenwood's interlocking, finger-tapped guitar lines under Yorke's vocal.

the war on drugs|eyes to the wind.fact: 'Eyes to the Wind' appears on The War on Drugs' 2014 breakthrough album Lost in the Dream, and frontman Adam Granduciel has called it his favorite song on the record. It's a reflective, anthemic track about returning home and realizing how much you've changed while you were away. The album took about 18 months to record and was shaped partly by Granduciel's love of Raymond Carver's spare short stories.

the magnetic fields|the book of love.fact: 'The Book of Love' is track 12 on disc one of The Magnetic Fields' sprawling 1999 concept album 69 Love Songs, written by Stephin Merritt. On the surface it's a dry, deadpan send-up of love-song cliches - opening with the line 'The book of love is long and boring' - but many listeners read it as a sincere marriage proposal hidden inside a joke, which is part of why it has become one of the most popular wedding songs of the 2000s and has been covered by numerous artists since.

father john misty|q4.fact: 'Q4' appears on Father John Misty's 2022 album Chloe and the Next 20th Century, and it tells a satirical story about a fictional novelist, Simone Caldwell, whose own literary work keeps getting passed over by publishers while flashier, lesser books get showered with praise. The title refers to the fourth financial quarter - the song is a dry commentary on how the publishing and entertainment industries commodify art, framing a writer's worth in the cold language of business and sales projections.

bat for lashes|marilyn.fact: 'Marilyn' is a track from Bat for Lashes' (Natasha Khan) 2012 album The Haunted Man, inspired by Marilyn Monroe as a symbol of old-Hollywood glamour and transformation. Khan sings to the icon almost like an invocation, asking to borrow some of her star power. Beck contributes guitar and synths on the track.

joanna newsom|colleen.fact: 'Colleen' is a then-unreleased Joanna Newsom song that surfaced on the Joanna Newsom and the Ys Street Band release, from the same era as her acclaimed 2006 album Ys. Like the mythic storytelling on Ys, 'Colleen' unfolds as a kind of fairy tale, following a young mermaid or sea-nymph who has forgotten who she really is. It's built in the same dense, harp-driven, novelistic style that made Ys a cult favorite.

operation ivy|unity.fact: 'Unity' is a track from Operation Ivy's sole studio album, Energy (1989). The Berkeley ska-punk band broke up that same year after barely two years together, but two of its members, Tim Armstrong and Matt Freeman, went on to form Rancid. 'Unity' became one of the band's most enduring songs - it's been covered by other bands over the years, and original singer Jesse Michaels reunited with Armstrong and Freeman to perform it live at San Francisco's Warfield Theatre in 2006.

local natives|empty mansions.fact: 'Empty Mansions' appears on Local Natives' 2023 album Time Will Wait for No One, the band's fifth record. It was recorded across a string of historic Los Angeles studios with producer John Congleton, during a stretch the band has described as a period of major life changes - some members becoming fathers, others moving through isolation and loss - which shaped the album's emotional highs and lows.

kurt vile|baby's arms.fact: 'Baby's Arms' opens Kurt Vile's 2011 album Smoke Ring for My Halo, recorded with producer John Agnello. The gentle, fingerpicked acoustic arrangement led critics to compare Vile's delivery to a young Leonard Cohen or Nick Drake. It's a comfort-and-solace song, setting a softer tone before the record's rockier tracks kick in.

elliott smith|bled white.fact: 'Bled White' is track seven on Elliott Smith's 1998 album XO, his first release on a major label (DreamWorks) after years on indie Kill Rock Stars. Drummer Joey Waronker, known for his work with R.E.M. and Beck, played on the track. The song nods to Smith's adopted hometown of Portland, Oregon, and it was later covered by the UK band Yuck.

beach house|dive.fact: 'Dive' comes from Beach House's 2018 album 7, released on Sub Pop. The track slow-builds from hazy synths into a churning, shoegaze-leaning climax with rolling percussion, a bigger sonic swing than the duo's earlier dream-pop work. Lyrically it plays with the tension between wanting to open up and the instinct to hold back, captured in the repeated line 'tell her something, tell her nothing.'

bon iver|29 #strafford apts.fact: '29 #Strafford APTS' appears on Bon Iver's 2016 album 22, A Million. The quirky title is meant to be read aloud exactly as written - '29 hashtag Strafford apartments' - a nod to a real address. Musically it's one of the more conventional folk-guitar moments on an otherwise glitchy, heavily processed record.

yard act|the trench coat museum.fact: 'The Trench Coat Museum' was produced by Remi Kabaka Jr., best known for his longtime work with Gorillaz. Yard Act frontman James Smith wrote it as a reflection on ego, vanity, and how quickly public perception can shift after a band's rapid rise to fame. The accompanying music video leans into that theme, set decades in the future inside a surreal, dystopian museum exhibit.

madi diaz|fatal optimist.fact: 'Fatal Optimist' is the title track of Madi Diaz's follow-up to her acclaimed 2023 album Weird Faith. Diaz has described 'fatal optimism' as the hope you keep choosing even knowing a relationship might not work out - the willingness to be vulnerable despite the risk. It's framed as something of a flip side to the hopeful love songs on Weird Faith.

jeff rosenstock|healmode.fact: 'HEALMODE' appears on Jeff Rosenstock's 2023 album HELLMODE, and its title is a deliberate, hopeful wordplay counterpoint to the album name. Rosenstock wrote it after his band's first tour since 2019, reflecting on having moved away from California to escape wildfires and drought, and expressing gratitude for one person in his life. It's a notably quieter, acoustic-leaning track compared to his usual ska-punk energy.

pixies|here comes your man.fact: Black Francis wrote 'Here Comes Your Man' as a teenager, inspired by the small earthquakes he experienced growing up in California, and called it 'hobo film noir' about train-hopping drifters. The band was initially reluctant to release it, feeling it was 'too pop' for their sound, so it sat unused for years. It finally appeared, produced by Gil Norton, as a single from 1989's Doolittle and became one of the Pixies' biggest songs.

jay som|superbike.fact: 'Superbike' was the lead single from Jay Som's 2019 album Anak Ko, which Melina Duterte wrote, recorded, and produced entirely herself during a solo retreat in Joshua Tree. The lyrics imagine a motorcycle as an escape fantasy from heartbreak. Duterte has said she aimed for a sound combining the Cocteau Twins with Alanis Morissette.

khruangbin|white gloves.fact: 'White Gloves' appears on Khruangbin's 2015 debut, The Universe Smiles Upon You, recorded in a remote barn in the Texas countryside. The Houston trio takes its name from the Thai word for 'airplane' (literally 'engine fly'), a tribute to the 1960s-70s Thai funk records that first drew guitarist Mark Speer and drummer DJ Johnson together before bassist Laura Lee joined. That global, crate-digging influence runs through the band's whole catalog.

broken social scene|superconnected.fact: 'Superconnected' comes from Broken Social Scene's self-titled 2005 album, the sprawling Canadian collective's third full-length. Core members Kevin Drew and Brendan Canning were joined by contributors including Leslie Feist, Amy Millan, and k-os, and longtime producer David Newfeld was credited as an official band member for the first time. The record is considered a high point of the band's dense, layered, orchestral-meets-indie-rock sound.

cherry glazerr|big bang.fact: Cherry Glazerr's 'Big Bang' pairs a heavy emotional subject - the long, drawn-out end of a relationship - with deliberately euphoric production. Frontwoman Clementine Creevy said she wanted an early-2000s pop feel, blending acoustic guitar with bass synths and 808 hits, citing DJ Koze, Caribou, Yaeji, and Kaytranada as touchstones. The result turns heartache into something danceable rather than heavy.

yo la tengo|sinatra avenue drive.fact: Yo La Tengo's 'Sinatra Drive Breakdown,' from 2023's This Stupid World, is named after a real waterfront boulevard in the band's longtime home base of Hoboken, New Jersey - fittingly, Frank Sinatra's own hometown. Musically it's a noisy, extended jam built on warped, distorted guitar, blending the trio's early jangle-pop roots with denser, heavier riffing. It stands as one of the rawer, more improvisational moments from a band nearing 40 years together.

softcult|shortest fuse.fact: 'Shortest Fuse' comes from the 2024 EP Heaven by Softcult, the Canadian duo of twin sisters Phoenix and Mercedes Arn-Horn. Before forming Softcult in 2020, the twins fronted the pop-punk band Courage My Love. Softcult blends grunge, shoegaze, dream pop, and riot-grrrl influences, and true to their DIY ethic, the sisters write, produce, and engineer all of their own music.

animal collective|floridada.fact: Animal Collective's 'FloriDada' was the lead single from 2016's Painting With. Avey Tare has said the idea sparked from hearing a Los Angeles radio segment called 'Dumb Things People Are Doing in Florida,' though the song isn't really about the state - it's about resisting tidy geographic and cultural stereotypes. The title's Dada reference ties into the album's broader art-movement inspiration, with lyrics stacking up odd, mixed-up details like 'the fair hair of Sweden' and 'a dancer from Ghana.'

ween|tried and true.fact: 'Tried and True' appears on Ween's 2003 album Quebec, the eighth LP from the New Hope, Pennsylvania duo of Gene Ween and Dean Ween. Amid the band's usual genre-hopping and irreverent humor, the track stands out as one of their more straightforwardly sincere, melodic songs. It's remained a fan favorite and a staple that showcases a more earnest side of the band's songwriting.

savages|t.i.w.y.g..fact: 'T.I.W.Y.G.' (short for 'This Is What You Get') is a track from Savages' 2016 album Adore Life, the follow-up to their debut Silence Yourself. Singer Jehnny Beth opens the song with the line 'This is what you get when you mess with love,' and the band has said the whole record is ultimately about love's power to transform and change people. Drummer Fay Milton drives the track, building from tense hi-hat taps into a full post-punk release.

black belt eagle scout|scorpio moon.fact: 'Scorpio Moon' appears on Black Belt Eagle Scout's 2019 album At the Party With My Brown Friends, by Swinomish/Inupiaq musician Katherine Paul. Paul has said the 'party' in the title symbolizes the world, and her 'friends' represent fellow Indigenous people and people of color. Much of the album's sound traces back to music she grew up with on the reservation, including her family's drum group, the Skagit Valley Singers.

t. rex|20th century boy.fact: T. Rex recorded '20th Century Boy' in Tokyo in December 1972, in a rare session producer Tony Visconti didn't personally attend (though he remained officially credited). Backing vocals, handclaps, acoustic guitar, and saxophone were added later back in England. Despite being considered for the closing slot on the album Tanx, it was left off entirely and released as a standalone single in 1973, only showing up on Tanx as a bonus track on later reissues.

beck|blue moon.fact: Beck's 'Blue Moon,' the lead single from 2014's Morning Phase, borrows its title from the classic Rodgers and Hart standard. Beck has said part of the song's inspiration came from reading Peter Guralnick's two-volume Elvis Presley biography, reflecting on who Elvis was starting out versus who he became later in life. The song was actually an old, nearly forgotten demo that Beck rediscovered and added to the album at the last minute.

lcd soundsystem|new body rhumba.fact: 'New Body Rhumba' was LCD Soundsystem's first new song in five years, written specifically for the soundtrack of Noah Baumbach's 2022 film White Noise. Frontman James Murphy, who had previously scored Baumbach's films Greenberg and While We're Young, wrote and produced the track with drummer Pat Mahoney and keyboardist Nancy Whang.

new order|the village.fact: 'The Village' appears on New Order's 1983 album Power, Corruption & Lies. Its title was inspired by the British TV series The Prisoner, though the band says any resemblance between the lyrics and the show's imagery was coincidental. It was also the first New Order song built around more than one sequenced bassline, showing off the studio technology the band leaned on heavily that year.

iron & wine|waves of galveston.fact: 'Waves of Galveston' started life as an outtake from Iron & Wine's Ghost on Ghost sessions, written when The A.V. Club's 'State Songs' project tasked Sam Beam with writing a song about Texas. It remained one of his live staples for years before finally getting an official studio release on the 2018 Weed Garden EP.

radiohead|reckoner.fact: 'Reckoner' grew out of sessions for an unfinished Radiohead track called 'Feeling Pulled Apart by Horses' and was reworked for years before landing on In Rainbows. All five band members played percussion together to record its cathartic rhythm track at an English country house, and the album's title itself comes from a lyric in the song.

boygenius|emily i'm sorry.fact: 'Emily I'm Sorry' is one of three boygenius songs featured in 'the film,' a 14-minute short directed by Kristen Stewart and released alongside their debut album the record. In its segment, Phoebe Bridgers sings lead while monster trucks circle around her, with bandmates Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus joining her for a fiery finale.

grizzly bear|yet again.fact: 'Yet Again' was the second single from Grizzly Bear's 2012 album Shields and was one of only two songs recorded during the band's initial sessions in Marfa, Texas. The single's cover art features Untitled #17, a 1981 gouache-and-crayon piece by American painter Richard Diebenkorn, which also appears in the Shields liner notes.

belle and sebastian|i'll be your pilot.fact: 'I'll Be Your Pilot' is Stuart Murdoch's tender ode to his young son Denny, written for Belle and Sebastian's How to Solve Our Human Problems EP trilogy. Murdoch said becoming a father made him feel like the pilot character from Antoine de Saint-Exupery's The Little Prince, which inspired the song's desert and flying imagery.

anna burch|tell me what's true.fact: 'Tell Me What's True' comes from Anna Burch's 2018 album If You're Dreaming, recorded with producer Sam Evian at his home studio in New York's Catskill Mountains. Burch self-directed the song's music video, filmed in Hamtramck, Michigan, riffing on a scene from Martin Scorsese's 1974 film Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore of someone auditioning in a cowboy bar.

talking heads|blind.fact: 'Blind' opens Talking Heads' final studio album, Naked (1988), which the band built out of improvisational jam sessions in Paris with a large cast of guest musicians, including former Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr and singer Kirsty MacColl, before David Byrne added lyrics and vocals back in New York.

arlo parks|weightless.fact: 'Weightless' was the first single from Arlo Parks's second album, My Soft Machine, co-written and produced with Paul Epworth, the British producer behind hits for Adele, Florence and the Machine, and Coldplay. Parks said she wanted the track's faster tempo and bolder synths to 'throw people off balance,' a deliberate departure from the sparser sound of her debut.

hatchie|without a blush.fact: 'Without A Blush' was the lead single from Hatchie's debut album Keepsake (2019) on Heavenly Recordings, pairing jagged, industrial-tinged guitars with chiming, bell-like synth tones. Its music video, directed by Joe Agius, was shot in a candlelit warehouse filled with rows of red roses.

jonathan richman & the modern lovers|dan.fact: 'Dancin' Late at Night' appears on Modern Lovers 88, from a period when Jonathan Richman steered his band away from its earlier Velvet Underground-indebted sound toward a gentler blend of pop and 1950s rock and roll. The track itself chugs along with an upbeat feel critics have compared to a mix of Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, and the Ventures.

tame impala|the less i know the better.fact: Kevin Parker wrote and recorded nearly all of Currents alone in a home studio in Fremantle, Australia, and the song's instantly recognizable bassline isn't a bass at all — it's a guitar run through an octave-down pedal and guitar synth effects. Parker has said the core of the song, including that riff and the vocal melody, came together in about fifteen minutes. He briefly gave the track away to collaborator Mark Ronson before asking for it back, a decision that helped make it Tame Impala's signature song.

the decemberists|the crane wife 3.fact: The Crane Wife trilogy that closes the album is based on Tsuru no Ongaeshi, a centuries-old Japanese folktale about a man who nurses an injured crane back to health, only for a mysterious woman to later arrive and become his wife. Colin Meloy discovered the story in the children's section of a Portland bookstore and built the album's title and closing suite around it. The Crane Wife 3 picks up the man's side of the tale after the woman's secret is revealed.

angel olsen|all the flowers.fact: All the Flowers comes from Olsen's 2022 album Big Time, which she co-produced with Jonathan Wilson at his Fivestar Studios in Topanga Canyon, California. Wilson played an array of instruments across the sessions, including lap steel, mellotron, zither and mandolin, and Nashville musician Spencer Cullum added pedal steel, giving the record its warm, Americana-leaning sound. The album marked a deliberate shift toward country and classic pop influences for Olsen.

idles|mr. motivator.fact: The title nods to the real "Mr Motivator," British fitness instructor Derrick Evans, who became a UK breakfast-TV fixture in the 1990s leading brightly dressed, high-energy workout segments on GMTV. IDLES borrowed his name for a song that piles up over-the-top pop-culture pump-up lines as a tongue-in-cheek call to self-improvement. It was released as the first single from their 2020 album Ultra Mono.

chairlift|bruises.fact: Chairlift recorded Bruises in keyboardist Patrick Wimberly's Brooklyn basement during all-night sessions after scrapping an earlier, more polished studio version they weren't happy with. The stripped-down version ended up being chosen by Apple to soundtrack a 2008 iPod Nano commercial, turning the then-unknown band into a sudden commercial breakout. It remains the trio's best-charting single.

the wedding present|brassneck.fact: Brassneck opens The Wedding Present's 1989 album Bizarro and takes its title from a British slang term for shameless cheek or nerve. It became the Leeds band's highest-charting UK single to date, reaching number 24. The band also changed a key closing lyric for the single edit, swapping the album version's "I don't trust you anymore" for "I don't love you anymore" on the 7-inch release.

kurt vile|chazzy don't mind.fact: The title nods to "Chazzy," a nickname for the Seattle band Chastity Belt, whose singer Julia Shapiro provides guest vocals on the track. Vile has said Courtney Barnett introduced him to Chastity Belt's music while touring together, and he wanted the band on his 2022 album (watch my moves) after connecting with their lyrics. The song blends Vile's laid-back guitar style with Shapiro's deadpan delivery.

the apples in stereo|go.fact: Go opens The Apples in Stereo's 2000 album The Discovery of a World Inside the Moone, one of the earliest releases from Robert Schneider's Elephant 6 Recording Company collective. Schneider's songwriting on the record leans on the lush, layered pop production techniques associated with the Beach Boys and other 1960s studio pop. The album's title and concept riff on an old hoax about a fictional civilization discovered on the moon.

beach fossils|seconds.fact: Seconds is a single from Beach Fossils' 2023 album Bunny, their first full-length in six years. Frontman Dustin Payseur wrote it around the bittersweet feeling of loving someone more than they love you back, pairing the downbeat theme with jangly, upbeat guitar hooks. The contrast between wistful lyrics and sunny instrumentation is a signature of the band's sound.

portishead|the rip.fact: The Rip, from Portishead's 2008 album Third, opens as a sparse acoustic-guitar folk ballad before shifting halfway through into a pulsing electronic arpeggio passage. The band has noted that their vintage Siel Orchestra synthesizer's built-in sequencer wasn't advanced enough to play the arpeggio pattern they wanted, so they had to find workarounds in the studio. The song was released as the album's second single.

beck|saw lightning.fact: Saw Lightning, the lead single from Beck's 2019 album Hyperspace, was co-written and produced with Pharrell Williams, who also plays drums and keyboards and contributes an ad-libbed vocal breakdown on the track. Beck has said he'd wanted to make a record with Pharrell and the Neptunes ever since their sound first broke through around the time of his own Midnite Vultures, making the collaboration two decades in the making. The song later soundtracked a Beats by Dre commercial.

built to spill|liar.fact: Liar appears on Built to Spill's 2006 album You in Reverse, their first new album in four years. The band aimed for a looser, more live-sounding record this time, recording at Steve Lobdell's Audible Alchemy studio to capture the feel of their in-person jams rather than layering parts track by track. Doug Martsch's extended, winding guitar lines became a hallmark of the album's more improvisational approach.

courtney barnett|if i don't hear from yo.fact: This was the final single Courtney Barnett released before her 2021 album Things Take Time, Take Time. It captures the nervous, self-doubting feeling of having a crush that seems mutual but hasn't actually been confirmed by either person. Barnett co-founded the independent label Milk! Records with fellow Australian musician Jen Cloher, and the two have appeared on each other's records over the years.

the strokes|selfless.fact: Selfless, from The Strokes' 2020 album The New Abnormal, is built around a delicate string arrangement that gives the track an unusually dreamy, atmospheric quality for the band. It's introduced by a short snippet of studio chatter and a brief preview of the song bleeding in at the end of the preceding track. Singer Julian Casablancas leans into a softer falsetto for the song, a departure from the band's usual rougher vocal style.

pixies|monkey gone to heaven.fact: Monkey Gone to Heaven, from 1989's Doolittle, was the first Pixies song to feature outside musicians, bringing in two cellists and two violinists for its string arrangement. The lyrics mix environmental imagery with a bit of biblical numerology ("if man is five, then the devil is six, then God is seven"). It was released as the album's lead single ahead of Doolittle.

r.e.m.|what's the frequency, kenneth?.fact: The title comes from a bizarre real-life incident in October 1986, when a stranger confronted CBS news anchor Dan Rather on a New York City street while repeatedly demanding, "Kenneth, what is the frequency?" The attacker's identity and motive stayed a mystery for years, which fascinated Michael Stipe enough to build a song around the odd phrase for R.E.M.'s 1994 album Monster. Rather later took the strange tribute in stride, even joining the band onstage to sing along to it.

spirit of the beehive|i've been evil.fact: "I've Been Evil" appears on Spirit of the Beehive's 2024 album "You'll Have to Lose Something" (Saddle Creek), the Philadelphia band's first full-length written after its two founding members and co-vocalists, Zach Schwartz and Rivka Ravede, ended their real-life relationship. The pair kept writing and recording together anyway, channeling the aftermath into the record's hushed, steady guitar textures.

adrianne lenker|indiana.fact: "Indiana" is track seven on Adrianne Lenker's second solo album, "Hours Were the Birds," recorded in 2013 at Terrarium Studios back in her hometown of Minneapolis with producer Rob Oesterlin. The stripped-down, all-acoustic-guitar record was self-released in January 2014 before Saddle Creek Records reissued it in 2018.

the hold steady|lord, i'm discouraged.fact: "Lord, I'm Discouraged" is the tenth track on The Hold Steady's 2008 album "Stay Positive," recorded in Hoboken, New Jersey, and at Wild Arctic Studio in Queens, New York, with producer John Agnello during January and February of that year. It's one of the more musically expansive, bluesy numbers on a record where the band stretched beyond their earlier bar-rock sound.

lucy dacus|going going gone.fact: "Going Going Gone," from Lucy Dacus's 2021 album "Home Video," features backing vocals from her boygenius bandmates Phoebe Bridgers and Julien Baker. The song looks back at an awkward teenage fling, fitting the album's larger theme of revisiting childhood and adolescence through old memories.

m83|we own the sky.fact: "We Own the Sky" comes from M83's fifth album, "Saturdays = Youth" (2008), a record the French project built as a tribute to 1980s teen movies and new-wave radio. It was released as a single in December 2008 following the album.

parquet courts|almost had to start a fig.fact: This title is actually two separate Parquet Courts songs run together: "Almost Had to Start a Fight" and "In and Out of Patience," both from the band's 2018 album "Wide Awake!" Producer Danger Mouse, who helmed the record, insisted the two tracks be spliced into one two-part song, which is why they're often logged and listed as a single combined title.

andy shauf|catch your eye.fact: "Catch Your Eye" is from Andy Shauf's 2023 album "Norm," which he wrote, performed, and self-produced entirely alone in his garage studio. The record's narrative concept, centered on a character named Norm, grew out of Shauf's fascination with David Lynch's "Mulholland Drive."

bully|let you.fact: "Let You" is track six on Bully's third album, "SUGAREGG" (2020), recorded with producer Graham Walsh at Palace Studios in Toronto. The bass-driven track marked a new, more collaborative studio approach for frontwoman Alicia Bognanno after two self-produced records.

squid|undergrowth.fact: "Undergrowth" was one of three advance singles from Squid's second album, "O Monolith" (2023). Much of the record was written during a stay in rural Wiltshire at Real World Studios, the residential studio complex founded by Peter Gabriel.

songs ohia|just be simple.fact: "Just Be Simple" appears on "Magnolia Electric Co." (2003), the last album Jason Molina released under the Songs: Ohia name before adopting Magnolia Electric Co. as his band's name for every record that followed. The spare, tenor-guitar-driven track is typical of Molina's intimate indie-folk arrangements.

the mountain goats|make you suffer.fact: "Make You Suffer" is from The Mountain Goats' 2022 album "Bleed Out," produced entirely by Bully's Alicia Bognanno and tracked in about a week at Sylvan Esso's Betty's studio near Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Frontman John Darnielle drew lyrical inspiration from vintage action movies of the 1960s through '80s.

david vandervelde|nothin' no.fact: "Nothin' No" opens David Vandervelde's 2007 debut, "The Moonstation House Band," which he recorded as a teenager at former Wilco multi-instrumentalist Jay Bennett's Chicago studio, the Clubhouse. Bennett co-wrote and played bass on the track, giving Vandervelde access to vintage gear previously used on Wilco's "Yankee Hotel Foxtrot" and "Being There."

this mortal coil|song to the siren.fact: "Song to the Siren" was written in 1967 by Tim Buckley and his high-school friend and lyricist Larry Beckett, first appearing on Buckley's 1970 album "Starsailor." This Mortal Coil's 1983 cover, sung by Cocteau Twins' Elizabeth Fraser, was built around a guitar part Robin Guthrie improvised in a single take after hearing Buckley's original just once through headphones; the single spent 101 weeks on the UK independent chart.

the antlers|director.fact: "Director" appears on The Antlers' 2014 album "Familiars," the follow-up to their breakout concept record "Hospice." On the track, frontman Peter Silberman sings in a falsetto that drew comparisons to Jeff Buckley, building toward a cymbal-heavy instrumental break.

car seat headrest|vincent.fact: "Vincent" is the sprawling, nearly eight-minute second track on Car Seat Headrest's 2016 album "Teens of Denial," recorded at Soundhouse studio in Seattle with producer Steve Fisk, known for earlier work with Nirvana, Beat Happening, and Soundgarden. It was released as an advance single in February 2016, months ahead of the full album.

modest mouse|trailer trash.fact: "Trailer Trash" is a standout deep cut from Modest Mouse's 1997 album "The Lonesome Crowded West," released on the independent label Up Records before the band's major-label breakthrough. Pitchfork later ranked the song 63rd on its list of the 200 best songs of the 1990s.

yo la tengo|fallout.fact: "Fallout" was the lead single from Yo La Tengo's 2023 album "This Stupid World," which longtime trio Ira Kaplan, Georgia Hubley, and James McNew made entirely by themselves without an outside producer or mixer. They wanted the record to sound as live and unfiltered as their concerts.

woods|pushing onlys.fact: "Pushing Onlys" opens Woods' 2011 album "Sun and Shade," a notably poppier, more polished turn for the Brooklyn band. Frontman Jeremy Earl sings the track in his signature falsetto about getting older.

joanna newsom|inflammatory writ.fact: "Inflammatory Writ" was one of only three brand-new compositions on Joanna Newsom's 2004 debut, "The Milk-Eyed Mender" (the rest were older songs she re-recorded). It's a playful, country-tinged tune built around upright piano rather than her signature harp, widely noted as one of the album's funniest, most tongue-in-cheek moments.

phoebe bridgers|i can't wait.fact: "I Can't Wait" is from Phoebe Bridgers' 2026 album "Lost Weekend," co-produced by Bridgers with Tony Berg, Ethan Gruska, and Jack Antonoff. Its music video, directed by Chris Maggio and Pablo Rochat, follows a single housefly buzzing through Los Angeles, landing on faces, chasing light sources, and darting inside a guitar.

frankie cosmos|empty head.fact: "Empty Head" is a 2019 single by Frankie Cosmos, the project of prolific New York singer-songwriter Greta Kline. The breezy, lo-fi indie-pop track is built around the idea of quieting an overactive mind, with Kline singing that it's okay not to have something profound to say all the time.
