It's a good example of the deceptively simple, diary-style songwriting that has made Kline one of indie rock's most prolific tunesmiths.

sparks|this town ain't big enough for bo.fact: Sparks' breakout 1974 single began as brothers Ron and Russell Mael's idea to have Russell recite movie-dialogue clichés between verses; they ended up keeping only the title line. Producer Muff Winwood added the song's distinctive Western-movie gunshot sound effects during the Kimono My House sessions in London. The single reached #2 on the UK singles chart and introduced British audiences to the duo's theatrical performance style via an appearance on Top of the Pops.

radiohead|morning mr magpie.fact: The title of this In Rainbows (2007) track nods to an old British superstition about magpies: spotting a lone magpie is considered bad luck, so tradition holds that you should greet it ("Good morning, Mr. Magpie, how's your wife?") to ward off misfortune. The custom is tied to the children's rhyme "One for Sorrow," which assigns a fortune to the number of magpies spotted. It's a bit of British folklore tucked into one of the album's more skeletal, guitar-driven arrangements.

broken social scene|7/4 (shoreline).fact: True to its title, this standout from Broken Social Scene's 2005 self-titled album is built on an unusual 7/4 time signature. Despite the odd meter, the Toronto collective's arrangement feels effortlessly propulsive, making it one of the band's most accessible songs. It's often cited by musicians as a go-to example of a danceable, listener-friendly odd-time track.

big thief|heavy bend.fact: "Heavy Bend" appears on Big Thief's 2019 album U.F.O.F., recorded with longtime producer Andrew Sarlo at Bear Creek Studios, a converted barn on a farm outside Woodinville, Washington. The rural, intimate setting fed into the hushed, atmospheric sound that defines the record. U.F.O.F. was the first of two Big Thief albums released that year, paired later with the louder Two Hands.

destroyer|cover from the sun.fact: "Cover from the Sun" is track four on Destroyer's 2017 album ken. Unlike the full-band approach of its predecessor, Poison Season, ken was produced by the band's own drummer, Josh Wells (also of Black Mountain), and recorded in a rehearsal space nicknamed the Balloon Factory. Dan Bejar still brought in bandmates for guest appearances throughout the sessions.

deerhunter|nothing ever happened.fact: The lead single from Deerhunter's 2008 album Microcastle, this nearly six-minute track stretches into an extended, motorik groove clearly inspired by the German band Neu! It marked a shift toward a more accessible, guitar-driven rock sound compared to the hazier Cryptograms. The song is widely regarded as the album's centerpiece.

rancid|ruby soho.fact: Written by Tim Armstrong, Lars Frederiksen, and Matt Freeman, "Ruby Soho" was the third single from Rancid's 1995 album ...And Out Come the Wolves. The song is about the strain touring puts on relationships, with the narrator heading off to another "destination unknown" and a girl he leaves behind. It became one of Rancid's biggest hits, reaching #13 on the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks chart.

american football|honestly?.fact: "Honestly?" is the third track on American Football's self-titled 1999 debut (retroactively called LP1), recorded with producer Brendan Gamble at Private Studios in the band's college town of Urbana, Illinois. Mike Kinsella's lyrics capture the hazy uncertainty of looking back on teenage feelings. The album became a foundational text of the emo revival more than a decade after its release.

japanese breakfast|machinist.fact: "Machinist" was the first single from Michelle Zauner's Japanese Breakfast album Soft Sounds from Another Planet (2017). Set to a synth-pop groove, the song tells a tongue-in-cheek, B-movie-style sci-fi story about a woman who falls for a robot, closing out with an unexpected saxophone solo. The music video leans further into the retro space-opera concept.

of montreal|gronlandic edit.fact: "Gronlandic Edit" appears on of Montreal's 2007 album Hissing Fauna, Are You the Destroyer?, which bandleader Kevin Barnes recorded almost entirely by himself while living in Norway. The track blends glam-rock guitar with dance grooves indebted to Prince and Sly & the Family Stone, giving it an indie-disco bounce that made it a live-set favorite. It's considered one of the catchiest moments on an album that marked a major sonic shift for the group.

bush tetras|too many creeps.fact: Guitarist Pat Place wrote the lyrics to "Too Many Creeps" in minutes while working the box office at a cinema on New York's Bleecker Street, annoyed by passersby's unsolicited comments. Released as a single in 1980 on 99 Records, it became a downtown dance-punk anthem for the band, a No Wave-adjacent group formed in New York in 1979. The single reached #57 on Billboard's club play chart.

amber arcades|oh my love (what have we d.fact: "Oh My Love (What Have We Done)" is the third track on European Heartbreak (2018), the second album by Amber Arcades, the project of Dutch singer-songwriter Annelotte de Graaf. The song stands out on the record for its use of horns, giving it a bittersweet, brass-flecked pop texture distinct from her jangly earlier work. De Graaf wrote and recorded the album while balancing her music career with law studies and human-rights work.

the decemberists|this is why we fight.fact: "This Is Why We Fight" closes out The Decemberists' 2011 album The King Is Dead, which the band recorded in just six weeks in a barn at Pendarvis Farm outside Portland, Oregon. Aiming for a more concise, Americana-leaning sound, the band drew on R.E.M., Neil Young, and the Byrds, and brought in R.E.M.'s Peter Buck as a guest guitarist on several tracks. The stripped-down approach was a deliberate departure from the band's earlier prog-folk epics.

battles|atlas.fact: "Atlas" is the breakout instrumental from Battles' 2007 debut album Mirrored. Singer-guitarist Tyondai Braxton's vocals were run through pitch-shifting effects to create the track's unmistakable helium-like chant, layered over a shuffling groove based on "schaffel," a rhythm style born in German techno clubs. The song became an unlikely radio and blog hit for the experimental math-rock group.

sleater-kinney|the day i went away.fact: "The Day I Went Away" appears on Sleater-Kinney's self-titled 1995 debut album, one of only two songs on the record to run past the three-minute mark at a time when the band's songs were typically short and fast. The album was recorded on a tight budget in the earliest days of the Olympia, Washington trio, before Janet Weiss joined on drums. It's a touchstone for fans tracing the band's evolution toward more expansive songwriting.

metric|help i'm alive.fact: "Help I'm Alive" is the breakout single from Metric's 2009 album Fantasies, written by Emily Haines and James Shaw and recorded in Austin, Texas. It made Metric the first fully self-released act to crack the Top 20 of the US Alternative radio chart, a landmark for the Toronto band's independent, DIY approach. Fantasies went on to win the 2010 Juno Award for Alternative Album of the Year.

fugazi|repeater.fact: "Repeater" is the title track and opener of Fugazi's 1990 debut full-length, written not long after guitarist-vocalist Guy Picciotto joined the band, bringing his trebly Rickenbacker guitar sound into the mix. The song's driving riff and drum attack were partly inspired by Public Enemy's "Rebel Without a Pause." Self-released on Ian MacKaye's Dischord Records with no major-label push, Repeater sold over 300,000 copies through constant touring and word of mouth.

angel olsen|white fire.fact: "White Fire" is the emotional centerpiece of Angel Olsen's 2014 album Burn Your Fire for No Witness, and its key lyric actually gave the record its title. Olsen told Billboard it was one of the last songs she wrote for the album and almost didn't share it, written from the perspective of an older version of herself looking back rather than addressed to a former partner like most of the record's other songs.

wilco|everyone hides.fact: "Everyone Hides" appears on Wilco's 2019 album Ode to Joy and was recorded at the band's own studio, The Loft, in Chicago. Its music video has the band literally playing a game of hide-and-seek around The Loft and the surrounding neighborhood, including a hiding spot inside the building pictured on the cover of their classic album Yankee Hotel Foxtrot.

t. rex|children of the revolution.fact: Marc Bolan wrote and T. Rex producer Tony Visconti helmed "Children of the Revolution," which became a UK number 2 hit in September 1972. An earlier version featuring Elton John on piano and Ringo Starr on drums was filmed for Starr's documentary "Born to Boogie," but the single itself was re-recorded in the studio without either guest musician.

mac demarco|goodbye weekend.fact: "Goodbye Weekend" comes from Mac DeMarco's 2014 album Salad Days, which he recorded almost entirely by himself in about a month inside his Brooklyn apartment, right after a year and a half of near-constant touring. The track is one of the few on the record where DeMarco name-checks his own nickname, "Macky," and it closes with one of the album's more extended guitar solos.

built to spill|strange.fact: "Strange" opens Built to Spill's 2001 album Ancient Melodies of the Future and features Sam Coomes of the band Quasi guesting on Roxichord organ. Frontman Doug Martsch has said the songs on this album were some of the simplest he'd written in years, marking a deliberate shift toward more concise songwriting.

the national|eucalyptus.fact: Guitarist Bryce Dessner sent an early demo of "Eucalyptus" to Matt Berninger so long before the song was finished that Berninger had nearly forgotten about it. Berninger eventually wrote lyrics for it and asked to debut it at soundcheck hours before a show at New York's Capitol Theatre; the band had never even rehearsed it with a full demo, and part of what ended up on the First Two Pages of Frankenstein (2023) album was captured live that night.

beirut|santa fe.fact: Beirut frontman Zach Condon grew up in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and told Mojo the 2011 song is a "positive song about the hometown I once felt such a distance from," written after visiting as an adult with a more established career. The song's distinctive electric organ part actually came from an old instrument Condon was recording at his parents' house over a Christmas visit, originally meant for a documentary soundtrack before he repurposed it here.

cocteau twins|bluebeard.fact: "Bluebeard," the second single from Cocteau Twins' 1993 album Four-Calendar Café, marked a notable turning point for singer Elizabeth Fraser: after years of singing largely wordless "mouth music," her vocals on this track became far more intelligible and lyric-driven than on the band's earlier dream-pop releases. It remains one of the clearest examples of the group's evolving vocal approach in the early '90s.

iron & wine|sundown (back in the briars).fact: "Sundown (Back in the Briars)" appears on Iron & Wine's 2002 debut The Creek Drank the Cradle, a collection of lo-fi home recordings Sam Beam originally made just as demos to send to Calexico's Joey Burns and John Convertino in hopes they'd serve as his rhythm section. Instead, Beam wound up writing, performing, recording, and producing every track entirely by himself in a home studio.

the kills|cheap and cheerful.fact: "Cheap and Cheerful" comes from The Kills' 2008 album Midnight Boom, which the duo recorded with producer Alexander "Armani XXXchange" Epton after relocating from a Los Angeles studio to the quieter Key Club Recording Company in Benton Harbor, Michigan. The band has said they drew inspiration from old TV documentaries about 1960s youth culture, aiming to write "modern playground songs."

nick cave & the bad seeds|where the wild.fact: Nick Cave had reportedly wanted to write a song for Kylie Minogue for about six years before sending her the tape that became this 1995 duet, produced by Tony Cohen and Victor Van Vugt. It became the only Nick Cave & The Bad Seeds track to crack the Australian top 10, and although it never appeared on one of Minogue's own studio albums, it has since been included on three of her greatest-hits compilations.

ibibio sound machine|pull the rope.fact: The title track of Ibibio Sound Machine's 2024 album Pull the Rope, produced by Ross Orton and Max Grunhard, uses a tug-of-war image to describe finding common ground across differences. For the big chorus vocals, the band brought in friends Richmond Kessie and Helen McDonald, plus keyboardist Max Kerman's mother, to beef up the backing harmonies.

fiona apple|left alone.fact: Fiona Apple has said her favorite lyric she's ever written is "the ants weigh more than the elephants," from "Left Alone" on 2012's The Idler Wheel. She's credited the line to a David Attenborough nature documentary she saw about how, collectively, ants' total biomass actually outweighs that of elephants worldwide.

arctic monkeys|crying lightning.fact: "Crying Lightning" was recorded for Arctic Monkeys' 2009 album Humbug at Rancho De La Luna and Pink Duck Studios with Queens of the Stone Age's Josh Homme producing. Homme pushed the band to try guitar solos, something they'd rarely attempted before, making the track one of the clearest examples of his influence on the record.

real estate|paper cup.fact: "Paper Cup," a single from Real Estate's 2020 album The Main Thing, features guest vocals from Amelia Meath of Sylvan Esso over lush strings and backing harmonies. Frontman Martin Courtney has described the song as reflecting on getting older while still working as a touring musician.

galaxie 500|tell me.fact: "Tell Me" appears on Galaxie 500's 1988 debut Today, which producer Kramer recorded for the famously tiny budget of about $750. The band tracked the record in just three days at Noise New York, cutting basic tracks in roughly four hours on day one and most vocals and leads in single takes on day two.

wednesday|pick up that knife.fact: "Pick Up That Knife," from Wednesday's 2025 album Bleeds, grew out of an unglamorous real-life memory: pedal steel player Xandy Chelmis getting sick in the mosh pit during Death Grips' set at Primavera Sound in 2023. Frontwoman Karly Hartzman has pointed to that chaotic moment as part of the spark for the song.

spiritualized|let it bleed (for iggy).fact: "Let It Bleed (For Iggy)" is a sprawling, blues-tinged track from Spiritualized's 2022 album Everything Was Beautiful, released on Fat Possum Records, and is explicitly dedicated to Iggy Pop as a tribute to his lasting influence on bandleader Jason Pierce. It's built around Pierce's broader exploration of how music tries to communicate feelings that words alone can't fully express.

my bloody valentine|only shallow.fact: "Only Shallow" opens My Bloody Valentine's notoriously painstaking 1991 album Loveless, whose recording was so drawn-out that engineer Alan Moulder left partway through to work with other bands before returning months later. Guitarist Kevin Shields has said he had to be kept lightly damp with a water mister during tracking just to stop static from ruining the recordings.

sylvan esso|die young.fact: "Die Young" appears on Sylvan Esso's 2017 album What Now. Vocalist Amelia Meath wrote it as an experiment to see if she could pull off a straightforward love song, inspired by how falling in love had reshaped plans she'd made for her own life. Lines like "I had a plan, you ruined it completely" turn a wry joke into an upbeat synth-pop anthem.

wild nothing|a woman's wisdom.fact: "A Woman's Wisdom" is track three on Wild Nothing's third album, Life of Pause (2016, Captured Tracks). It finds songwriter Jack Tatum pivoting from the band's shimmery '80s dream-pop toward a warmer blend of '70s AM-radio soul, funk, and R&B, with disco-tinged synth lines underpinning his breathy vocal. Critics compared the track's style to a mix of Jim O'Rourke and Tobias Jesso Jr.

black flag|tv party.fact: Written by guitarist Greg Ginn, "TV Party" first appeared on Black Flag's 1981 album Damaged. The band re-recorded it twice more: once for a 1982 promotional EP with new drummer Emil Johnson (slower tempo, added hand claps), and again in 1984 for director Alex Cox's cult film Repo Man and its soundtrack. Each version namechecks different TV shows that were popular when it was recorded.

toro y moi|girl like you.fact: "Girl Like You" is the lead single from Toro y Moi's fifth album, Boo Boo (2017), written, produced, and performed entirely by Chaz Bundick. The song's hazy opening sound was simply a factory preset on his synthesizer that he liked so much he left it in the final mix. It marked a playful, groove-driven turn after the more downtempo What For.

the jesus and mary chain|something's wro.fact: "Something's Wrong" is track B6 on The Jesus and Mary Chain's 1985 debut, Psychocandy. The album is built on layers of guitar feedback and distortion that brothers William and Jim Reid buried beneath Phil Spector-style "wall of sound" melodies. That noisy, lo-fi production approach became hugely influential on later shoegaze and noise-pop bands.

sebadoh|flame.fact: "Flame" was written by Lou Barlow and released as a single in January 1999 off Sebadoh's self-titled album The Sebadoh. Produced by Eric Masunaga and Rich Costey, it became the band's highest-charting UK single, reaching number 30 on the UK Singles Chart.

ethel cain|nettles.fact: "Nettles" is the lead single from Ethel Cain's 2025 album Willoughby Tucker, I'll Always Love You, a prequel to her 2022 debut Preacher's Daughter. For the track's atmosphere, Cain tracked down the same vintage synthesizers composer Angelo Badalamenti used to create the iconic Twin Peaks theme. She wrote and recorded the song in the same Alabama house where she had finished Preacher's Daughter.

beastie boys|jimmy james.fact: "Jimmy James," the opening track on Beastie Boys' 1992 album Check Your Head, is named after a stage pseudonym Jimi Hendrix used early in his career while fronting Jimmy James and the Blue Flames. The group originally built the song almost entirely from Hendrix samples, but when the Hendrix estate denied clearance, they re-recorded it keeping only a few approved samples.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|shangha.fact: "Shanghai," written by Stu Mackenzie and Ambrose Kenny-Smith, appears on King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2021 album Butterfly 3000. The track is built around hypnotic synth loops and Kenny-Smith's falsetto verses before the band stretches it into an extended jam on the main riff, a staple of their live shows.

damien jurado|ohio.fact: "Ohio" appears on Damien Jurado's 1999 album Rehearsals for Departure, an early breakthrough record produced by Ken Stringfellow of The Posies. The hushed, acoustic-leaning album helped establish Jurado's reputation as a literary, understated singer-songwriter on Seattle's Sub Pop label.

perfume genius|without you.fact: "Without You" appears on Perfume Genius's 2020 album Set My Heart on Fire Immediately. The strummy, major-key track finds Mike Hadreas singing about the ache of distance from someone important to him, part of a record he described as being about the strange, meaningful connections people share. Musically it's one of the album's warmest, most straightforwardly uplifting songs.

khruangbin|evan finds the third room.fact: "Evan Finds the Third Room" appears on Khruangbin's 2018 album Con Todo El Mundo. Its title nods to scholar Homi K. Bhabha's "third space" theory, describing a space where different cultures blend into something new. The band later released a dub version of the track titled "A La Sala," Spanish for "to the living room."

the english beat|mirror in the bathroom.fact: "Mirror in the Bathroom," written by Dave Wakeling, was released in 1980 as a single from The Beat's debut album I Just Can't Stop It. It reached number 4 on the UK singles chart, the band's biggest hit until 1983, and NME ranked it the third-best track of that year. The song's skittering ska-pop sound, built around David Steele's bassline, became one of the defining singles of the 2 Tone era.

tame impala|disciples.fact: "Disciples" is a sub-two-minute track from Tame Impala's 2015 album Currents, first previewed by Kevin Parker during a Reddit AMA. The song features guitar work from veteran musician Todd Rundgren, whose 1973 album A Wizard, a True Star had already shaped Parker's songwriting on the earlier record Lonerism.

nation of language|inept apollo.fact: "Inept Apollo" is a single from Nation of Language's 2025 album Dance Called Memory, their first release since signing to Sub Pop. The Brooklyn trio built the track around layered analog synths and singer Ian Devaney's echoing vocals, continuing their run of records steeped in early-'80s New Wave acts like Kraftwerk.

r.e.m.|e-bow the letter.fact: "E-Bow the Letter" was the first single from R.E.M.'s 1996 album New Adventures in Hi-Fi, written by all four band members and produced by Scott Litt with R.E.M. Its title comes from the E-Bow, an electronic device Peter Buck used to bow his guitar strings into sustained, droning notes. The track is a duet featuring punk-poet Patti Smith on vocals, which guitarist Peter Buck later called a career highlight.

radiohead|tinker tailor soldier sailor r.fact: This track from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool borrows its title from a traditional English counting rhyme once used in children's fortune-telling games, such as counting cherry stones or buttons to predict a future profession. Director Richard Ayoade, known for the films Submarine and The Double, made a short companion video for the song.

big star|thirteen.fact: "Thirteen," written primarily by Alex Chilton with a credit to Chris Bell, was recorded in late 1971 at Ardent Studios in Memphis for Big Star's debut album #1 Record. Rolling Stone later ranked it among the 500 greatest songs of all time, calling it one of rock's most beautiful depictions of early adolescence. It's Big Star's most-covered song, with versions by Elliott Smith, Garbage, and Wilco among dozens of others, and Chilton himself singled out Garbage's cover as a favorite.

jose gonzalez|crosses.fact: "Crosses" was the title track of José González's debut EP, released in June 2003, and was later folded into his first full-length album, Veneer, that October. The stripped-down acoustic track later gained wider exposure when it soundtracked the season-two finale of the TV series The O.C.

just mustard|endless deathless.fact: "Endless Deathless" is the title track from Just Mustard's third album, which the Dundalk, Ireland band recorded together at Black Mountain studio near their hometown. The group - vocalist Katie Ball, David Noonan, Mete Kalyoncuoğlu, Rob Clarke and Shane Maguire - blends shoegaze noise with dance-leaning beats, a sound that later led to them supporting The Cure on a run of outdoor stadium shows.

father john misty|true affection.fact: "True Affection" marked a notable departure for Father John Misty, built entirely around drum machines and pulsing synthesizers rather than his usual folk-rock arrangements. Produced by Josh Tillman with Jonathan Wilson for 2015's "I Love You, Honeybear," the electronic-heavy track has drawn comparisons to Sufjan Stevens's "Age of Adz" and Beck.

vampire weekend|mansard roof.fact: "Mansard Roof" was Vampire Weekend's debut single, released in October 2007 and later placed as the opening track of their self-titled 2008 album. Written by Ezra Koenig and Rostam Batmanglij, the song takes its name from the distinctive sloped mansard-style roofs common in the coastal Northeast, setting the scene for the band's architecture-referencing lyrical style.

cherry glazerr|ready for you.fact: "Ready For You" appears on Cherry Glazerr's 2023 album "I Don't Want You Anymore," built around a big, staticky guitar riff that leans into the record's harder rock sound. The band shot the song's music video, directed by Sarah Ritter, in the Joshua Tree desert using an old car and motel room, performing part of it inside a moving U-Haul truck in 118-degree heat.

yeah yeah yeahs|soft shock.fact: "Soft Shock" comes from Yeah Yeah Yeahs' 2009 album "It's Blitz!" and finds Karen O trading her usual yelps for gentle crooning reminiscent of the band's hit "Maps." The track builds from a hushed, atmospheric ballad into a more forceful climax, with Nick Zinner layering in backmasked guitars as the song progresses.

weyes blood|a lot's gonna change.fact: "A Lot's Gonna Change" opens Weyes Blood's 2019 album "Titanic Rising," which Natalie Mering recorded with producer Jonathan Rado of Foxygen. The track pairs lush baroque strings and piano with a maximalist arrangement that still leaves room for Mering's vocals, setting the cinematic tone for the rest of the record.

beach house|you came to me.fact: "You Came to Me" appears on Beach House's debut album "Devotion," recorded at the Lord Baltimore studio in the summer of 2007 and released in 2008 on Carpark Records. AllMusic described it as a "stunner" of dark chamber pop, and the duo made a music video for the track as part of the album's promotion.

jungle|keep moving.fact: "Keep Moving" was the lead single from Jungle's 2021 album "Loving in Stereo," premiering on BBC Radio 1's Annie Mac show before release. The band paired the disco-leaning track with a West Side Story-inspired music video, choreographed and directed alongside longtime collaborator Charlie Di Placido.

the olivia tremor control|the opera hous.fact: "The Opera House" opens The Olivia Tremor Control's 1996 album "Dusk at Cubist Castle," a record the Elephant 6 band recorded and mixed entirely on four- and eight-track tape. Co-founder Will Cullen Hart has said at least eight different people played guitar on this one opening track alone.

fugazi|waiting room.fact: "Waiting Room" was recorded in June 1988 at Inner Ear Studios in Arlington, Virginia, and first appeared on Fugazi's self-titled debut EP before being compiled onto 1989's "13 Songs." Ian MacKaye wrote it about being determined not to repeat the mistakes of his short-lived previous band, Embrace, and its funk-, reggae- and hip-hop-inflected groove made it one of Fugazi's most widely covered songs despite never being released as a single.

flock of dimes|keep me in the dark.fact: "Keep Me in the Dark" is track two on Flock of Dimes' 2025 album "The Life You Save," produced by Jenn Wasner and recorded at Betty's studio in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, and Montrose Recording in Los Angeles with additional production from Nick Sanborn. Its music video, directed by frequent collaborator Spencer Kelly, surrounds Wasner with projections of her younger self.

elliott smith|say yes.fact: "Say Yes" closes Elliott Smith's 1997 album "Either/Or" and was written about his then-girlfriend Joanna Bolme; Smith even left in the sound of himself clearing his throat at the start of the take for an unpolished, intimate feel. The song later gained wider recognition after director Gus Van Sant used it, along with two other Either/Or tracks, in the "Good Will Hunting" soundtrack.

anna burch|can't sleep.fact: "Can't Sleep" opens Anna Burch's 2020 album "If You're Dreaming," setting a restless tone for the record. Burch has said the song grew directly out of a real bout of insomnia, part of a broader thread of anxious energy that runs through the album's lyrics.

talking heads|lifetime piling up.fact: "Lifetime Piling Up" was written by all four members of Talking Heads - David Byrne, Chris Frantz, Jerry Harrison and Tina Weymouth - as an outtake from the sessions for their 1988 album "Naked." It stayed unreleased until it surfaced on the 1992 compilation "Popular Favorites 1976-1992: Sand in the Vaseline," where it reached number 11 on the Billboard Alternative Airplay chart.

hatchie|the rhythm.fact: "The Rhythm" was released on April 21, 2022, as a single ahead of Hatchie's second album, "Giving the World Away," which arrived the following day through Secretly Canadian. The song reflects the Australian artist's shift toward a brighter, more polished synth-pop sound compared to her shoegaze-indebted debut EP.

yeasayer|sunrise.fact: "Sunrise" opens Yeasayer's 2007 debut album "All Hour Cymbals" and originally served as the b-side to the single "2080." The track builds from choral harmonies and handclaps into a dense, percussion-heavy climax, reflecting the gospel and world-music influences the Brooklyn band wove into their early sound.

boygenius|salt in the wound.fact: "Salt in the Wound" comes from boygenius's self-titled 2018 EP, which Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus wrote and recorded together in just five days at Sound City Studios. Each member arrived with one finished song and one half-formed idea, and the trio fleshed out all six tracks collaboratively. The track layers Dacus's lead vocal with Bridgers's higher harmonies and a towering guitar solo from Baker.

diiv|trillions.fact: "Trillions" is a single from DIIV's fifth album, ZIRP!, released via Fantasy Recordings in 2026. The album's title refers to "zero interest rate policies," the economic backdrop the band says shaped a culture of financial speculation and startup excess over the past decade. The track continues DIIV's collaboration with producer A. G. Cook, known for his work with Charli XCX and Caroline Polachek, and is among the most overtly pop-leaning songs the band has released.

grizzly bear|four cypresses.fact: "Four Cypresses," from Grizzly Bear's 2017 album Painted Ruins, began with drummer Chris Bear's unusual rolling beat and chord change, around which singer Daniel Rossen then built a melody and lyric. The music video pairs the song with home-movie footage from Rossen's own childhood, presented with lyrics styled like old VHS captions, exploring themes of impermanence.

the stone roses|made of stone.fact: "Made of Stone" was released in March 1989 and recorded across three studios -- Battery, Konk (owned by Kinks frontman Ray Davies), and Rockfield in Wales -- with the Stone Roses working through the night rather than during the day to nail the track. Produced by John Leckie, the song later re-entered the UK singles chart on six separate occasions between 1989 and 2022, and it also marked the band's national television debut on BBC's The Late Show that September.

wishy|covergirl.fact: "Covergirl" appears on Triple Seven (2024), the debut album from Indianapolis band Wishy. Co-founders Kevin Krauter (formerly of the band Hoops) and Nina Pitchkites met in high school and started Wishy together in 2021 after Pitchkites moved back to Indiana from Philadelphia. The song's hazy, drum-driven sound has drawn comparisons to shoegaze acts like My Bloody Valentine.

cocteau twins|love's easy tears.fact: "Love's Easy Tears" was the title track of a 1986 EP released on 4AD -- the band's eighth EP overall and their last for that label until 1993. It marked Cocteau Twins' first full-trio recording without outside guests in some time, with bassist Simon Raymonde and guitarist Robin Guthrie crafting one of Guthrie's signature crystalline feedback washes for the chorus.

alex g|immunity.fact: "Immunity" appears on Alex G's 2022 album God Save the Animals. Philadelphia songwriter Alex Giannascoli wrote and demoed the record alone during pandemic lockdown before bringing it into several studios around his hometown to finish. The song's piano shifts from a major key into a minor one near the end, and it closes out with an unexpected instrumental jam of wobbly guitars and staccato piano.

elbow|asleep in the back.fact: "Asleep in the Back" became Elbow's first UK Top 20 single, and oddly wasn't on the original 2001 release of the album of the same name -- it was written and added only after the record was already finished, then included as a bonus track on later pressings. Singer Guy Garvey called it "sonically one of the most interesting" tracks the band made with producer Ben Hillier, and Australian band Gang of Youths later covered it for their 2021 EP Total Serene.

the black keys|i forgot to be your lover.fact: The Black Keys' version is a cover of William Bell's 1968 soul single, co-written by Bell and Booker T. Jones, which reached No. 45 on the charts. The song later became the foundation for Billy Idol's 1986 hit "To Be a Lover," though The Black Keys' rendition -- from their 2024 album Ohio Players -- stays closer to Bell's original, dressing it in orchestral strings and organ.

my bloody valentine|slow.fact: "Slow" first appeared on My Bloody Valentine's 1988 EP You Made Me Realise, released the same year as their debut album Isn't Anything. Critics point to the track as proof of the band's reinvention away from the jangly C86 indie-pop sound of their earliest records, pushing toward the noisier, more intense style that would go on to help define shoegaze.

angel olsen|waving, smiling.fact: "Waving, Smiling" is one of two new songs included on Angel Olsen's 2020 release Whole New Mess, a stripped-down companion album featuring alternate versions of songs that would later appear on All Mirrors. Built around a simple fingerpicking pattern with a classic-soul feel, Olsen described the song as capturing a peaceful, bittersweet sense of closure.

the cure|a fragile thing.fact: "A Fragile Thing" appears on The Cure's 2024 album Songs of a Lost World, the band's first studio record in sixteen years. Robert Smith revealed the song was originally written under the working title "Kill the Sun" and changed considerably before reaching its final form; the band had already debuted it live back in November 2022, where it became a staple of their tour.

the dandy warhols|danzig with myself (fe.fact: The title started as a studio joke -- guitarist/frontman Courtney Taylor-Taylor said the song's central riff sounded like something out of Misfits or Danzig, and the nickname stuck as a working title until it became permanent. Pixies frontman Frank Black joined almost by chance: Taylor-Taylor was simply checking in with him while he happened to be in Zurich, and the visit turned into a studio session for the track, which appears on the Dandy Warhols' 2024 album Rockmaker.

the beths|do you want me now.fact: "Do You Want Me Now" appears on The Beths' 2020 album Jump Rope Gazers. The New Zealand band built the mid-tempo track around Beach Boys-style backing harmonies and country-leaning guitars, a notable departure from their usual power-pop sound, to match frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes's reflection on the strange, stilted limbo of a long-distance relationship.

belly|feed the tree.fact: "Feed the Tree," from Belly's 1993 debut album Star, hit No. 1 on the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks chart. Songwriter Tanya Donelly originally wrote it as a possible contribution to a second Breeders album, but when bandmate Kim Deal committed to a long Pixies tour, Donelly started Belly instead rather than wait around. Paul McCartney reportedly sent Donelly a personal note congratulating her on the song.

m83|blister sunrise.fact: "Blister Sunrise" is the opening track on M83's tenth studio album, I Wrote You a Letter, released September 25, 2026. Frontman Anthony Gonzalez put the song out as the album's lead single three weeks earlier and recorded the record with collaborators Joe Berry, Clement Libes, and Benoit de Villeneuve. The track opens abruptly, almost as if starting mid-song, layering synths, percussion, and strings under distant-sounding vocals.

animal collective|summertime clothes.fact: "Summertime Clothes," from Animal Collective's 2009 album Merriweather Post Pavilion, was originally titled "Bearhug" while the band was writing it. The record was written and recorded in about a month at Sweet Tea Recording Studio in Oxford, Mississippi, with Avey Tare and Panda Bear trading vocals over swirling synths and a bouncing low end meant to evoke a carefree summer feeling.

adrianne lenker|fool.fact: "Fool" was one of the very first songs tracked for Adrianne Lenker's 2024 album Bright Future, recorded late at night with producer Philip Weinrobe. Weinrobe said the song shows "a different side" to Lenker's writing, since she's often associated with melancholy but "can do unbridled ecstatic happiness just as deftly as every other emotion." Lenker herself described it as "a buoyant questioning of creaturey loopiness," and on the recording she can be heard audibly laughing when she slips into the line "we could be friends."

alvilda|angoisse.fact: ALVILDA is a Paris quartet — Nina, Mel, Eva and Sandra — who sing entirely in French and blend the melodic charm of 1960s girl-group pop with late-1970s power pop and punk energy. "Angoisse" was the bouncy, new-wave-leaning lead single from their debut full-length, C'est Déjà L'heure, released through UK punk label Static Shock Records.

amyl and the sniffers|chewing gum.fact: "Chewing Gum" was the lead single announcing Amyl and the Sniffers' 2024 album Cartoon Darkness. Frontwoman Amy Taylor said the song is about actively choosing fun and freedom over always being "right," summed up in the chorus line about choosing to be young and choosing bad decisions because life is short. Taylor described the song's outlook as neither pure nihilism nor pure hedonism, but "the chaos between the two."

andrew bird|fake palindromes.fact: "Fake Palindromes" is the most straightforwardly rock-oriented track on Andrew Bird's 2005 breakthrough The Mysterious Production of Eggs, built on thrumming bass, psychedelic guitar, and echo-drenched fiddle. It's a showcase for Bird's dual musical identity: a classically trained violinist who is equally famous for his operatic, full-bodied whistling, which he says is deliberately pitched to cut through his own mid-range instruments.

beach house|sparks.fact: "Sparks," the opening track on Beach House's 2015 album Depression Cherry, began almost by accident: during a Bristol, England soundcheck, Victoria Legrand's voice looped through the PA, and the duo were so struck by the ethereal sound that they recorded it on their phones. That accidental loop became the vocal hook that runs through the finished song.

beastie boys|intergalactic.fact: "Intergalactic" was the lead single from Beastie Boys' 1998 album Hello Nasty and became the trio's biggest UK hit, reaching No. 5 there and No. 28 on the US Hot 100. Its Adam Yauch-directed video, shot in Tokyo's Shibuya and Shinjuku districts, is an homage to Japanese tokusatsu and kaiju shows, with a giant robot battling a trident-wielding, cephalopod-headed monster. The song went on to win the Grammy for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group.

beck|chemical.fact: "Chemical," from Beck's 2019 album Hyperspace, was co-written and co-produced with Pharrell Williams, who processes and contorts Beck's voice throughout the track. Beck framed the song's central idea — treating love itself as "a chemical" reaction a person can't fully control — with a cold, almost scientific detachment, calling the result "a lullaby delivered from a space shuttle with just one person on it."

beck|die waiting.fact: "Die Waiting" is a duet between Beck and Sky Ferreira from his 2019 album Hyperspace, built around a mystic, slowly building guitar riff layered with electronics. The song is a devotional, patience-themed ballad, with the two trading lines about waiting out hard times for someone they love.

belle and sebastian|safety valve.fact: "Safety Valve" is actually older than Belle and Sebastian itself — Stuart Murdoch wrote it before the band had formed. It sat unreleased for decades until it finally surfaced on the soundtrack to the 2019 film Days of the Bagnold Summer, giving fans a glimpse of Murdoch's songwriting style in its earliest, twee-pop form.

big thief|strange.fact: "Strange," from Big Thief's 2019 album U.F.O.F., was described by Stereogum as "a jaunty funhouse of a song that unwinds like a twisted nursery rhyme." The track leans into surreal, dreamlike nature imagery — at one point picturing a luna moth crying "lime green tears" — as the arrangement gradually dissolves into a hazy, psychedelic mist of reverb and bubbling bass.

black country, new road|besties.fact: "Besties" marked Georgia Ellery's (also of Jockstrap) debut turn as lead vocalist for Black Country, New Road, serving as the lead single from their 2025 album Forever Howlong. Opening on a distinctive harpsichord line, the light-hearted, tongue-in-cheek track plays with the blurry space between close friendship and unrequited romantic feeling.

blonde redhead|23.fact: "23," the title track of Blonde Redhead's seventh album (2007), centers on the numerological pull of its titular number as a stand-in for fate and the passage of time. The band deliberately aimed for a more spontaneous, less overanalyzed songwriting approach on this record, trading the melancholy of their earlier album Misery for a more energetic, streamlined sound.

blonde redhead|spring and by summer fall.fact: "Spring and by Summer Fall," also from 2007's 23, pairs a dense, guitar-heavy, propulsive sound with lyrics that use the changing seasons as a metaphor for shifting relationships and self-identity. Its opening line — "I look in your eyes and can only see my own complexion" — sets up the song's theme of searching for yourself in how others reflect you back.

bonnie 'prince' billy|squid eye.fact: "Squid Eye," from Bonnie "Prince" Billy's 2019 album I Made a Place, tackles the real-world subject of rising sea levels, but with a playful touch — the lyrics joke about diving in like "Aquaman's kid" and having the eyes of a squid. Rather than despair, the song frames adapting to a changing world as an act of resilience, wonder, and even childlike fun.

boygenius|not strong enough.fact: On "Not Strong Enough," from boygenius' 2023 debut album The Record, Phoebe Bridgers revealed that the key lyric "not strong enough to be your man" was a direct nod to Sheryl Crow's 1994 hit "Strong Enough." The song became the first single by any of the three members' projects to top Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart.

broken social scene|the call.fact: "The Call" is co-written and lead-sung by guitarist Andrew Whiteman, from Broken Social Scene's 2026 album Remember the Humans — the band's first new album in roughly nine years. For it, the Toronto collective reunited with producer David Newfeld, who had helmed their beloved early-2000s records You Forgot It in People and Broken Social Scene.

built to spill|untrustable/part 2 (about.fact: The closing track on Built to Spill's 1997 album Perfect From Now On, "Untrustable/Part 2 (About Someone Else)," came out of a famously grueling recording process. Doug Martsch first tried overdubbing nearly every instrument himself, scrapped that, then re-recorded the album with bassist Brett Nelson and drummer Scott Plouf — only for those tapes to be ruined by heat in producer Phil Ek's car on the drive from Seattle to Boise, forcing the band to record the whole album a third time.

camper van beethoven|take the skinheads.fact: Despite its provocative title, "Take the Skinheads Bowling" is a deliberately absurdist nonsense song — frontman David Lowery and co-founder David McDaniel spent weeks riffing on implausible, meaningless lyrics specifically to undermine any "real" interpretation. The band has said the joke was in the mundane image itself: taking feared skinhead figures bowling humanizes them into just "kids in odd clothing," and the throwaway track unexpectedly became the band's signature song.

car seat headrest|devereaux.fact: "Devereaux" is track two on Car Seat Headrest's 2025 rock opera "The Scholars," a concept album set at the fictional Parnassus University that frontman Will Toledo built in the tradition of classic story-cycle records like The Who's "Tommy" and David Bowie's "Ziggy Stardust." The track rides a chugging, propulsive rhythm into a big singalong chorus.

car seat headrest|the catastrophe (good.fact: "The Catastrophe (Good Luck With That, Man)" was the third single from Car Seat Headrest's 2025 rock opera "The Scholars." Written from the perspective of several members of a fictional band, the five-and-a-half-minute power-pop track mixes acoustic and distorted guitars and packs in references ranging from the Roman Empire to the Old Testament to the Edsels' doo-wop hit "Rama Lama Ding Dong."

cheekface|there is a god.fact: "There Is A God" opens Cheekface's 2026 album "Podium." True to the LA trio's deadpan, wordplay-heavy style, singer Greg Katz builds the song's title around a slant rhyme, landing on "Erewhon" (the LA grocery chain) paired with "there is a God."

david nance|mock the hours.fact: "Mock the Hours" is the title track and lead single from David Nance & Mowed Sound's 2024 album, released on Jack White's Third Man Records. The band -- Nance on vocals and guitar alongside Kevin Donahue, James Schroeder, Derrick Higgins, and Sam Lipsett -- built the song around a big drum-and-piano drone rhythm topped with what reviewers called the album's biggest chorus.

deafheaven|shellstar.fact: "Shellstar" opens Deafheaven's 2021 album "Infinite Granite," the record on which the blackgaze band shifted toward shoegaze and dream pop, with vocalist George Clarke singing in a clean falsetto for the first time. The track moves from serene, bell-like guitar tones and choral backing vocals into a layered, wall-of-sound finale built on '90s alt-metal drum patterns.

dow jones and the industrials|ladies wit.fact: "Ladies with Appliances" comes from Dow Jones & The Industrials, a new-wave band from West Lafayette, Indiana active from 1979 to 1981, featuring Greg Horn, Chris Clark, Tim North, and keyboardist Brad Garton (nicknamed "Mr. Science"). The track appeared on the 1981 "Red Snerts" compilation from Gulcher Records, a document of the Indiana punk and new-wave scene the band helped pioneer alongside a split LP with the Gizmos.

dr. dog|the ark.fact: "The Ark" appears on Dr. Dog's 2008 album "Fate," posing the plain existential question "What does it mean to be here?" over a repeated, slightly discordant guitar lick the band leans into for comfort rather than tension. The song eases from bluesy sludge into a more stately arrangement as it closes.

dry cleaning|cruise ship designer.fact: "Cruise Ship Designer" was the second track revealed from Dry Cleaning's Cate Le Bon-produced 2026 album "Secret Love." Vocalist Florence Shaw says the song follows a well-paid, skilled cruise-ship and hotel designer who privately doubts his work has any real worth, but throws himself into the job's challenges anyway.

esther rose|safe to run.fact: "Safe to Run" is the title track of Esther Rose's 2023 album on New West Records, featuring guest vocals from Hurray for the Riff Raff's Alynda Segarra alongside Johnny "Up" Shadid's pedal steel and Nick Cohon's guitar. It's a hopeful-but-uneasy song about heading out into an uncertain world and wondering whether good intentions alone will be enough to carry you through.

foxwarren|yvonne.fact: "Yvonne" is a single from Foxwarren's 2025 album "2," the second record from the Canadian band led by singer-songwriter Andy Shauf alongside Dallas and Darryl Kissick, Avery Kissick, and Colin Nealis. The short, bossa-nova-tinged track layers seagull sounds and oblique strings under a soft lead vocal, and arrived with an animated video by artist Meghan Fenske.

gelli haha|johnny.fact: "Johnny" appears on "Switcheroo," the 2025 album from Gelli Haha -- the stage persona of LA artist Angel Abaya, built in collaboration with producer Sean Guerin. On the track, Gelli plays a torch singer leaning against a Casio keyboard, repeating the apology "sorry for acting cold (like ice cream)" until it starts to feel earned.

ging|can you see me.fact: "Can You See Me" appears on "We're Here, My Dear," the 2022 debut album released under the name Ging -- the recording identity Adam King Feeney adopted after retiring his longtime producer alias Frank Dukes, under which he'd made hits for Lorde, Camila Cabello, Post Malone, and The Weeknd. The album marked Feeney's shift from writing and producing for others to releasing music under his own voice.

greg freeman|gallic shrug.fact: "Gallic Shrug" is track four on Greg Freeman's 2025 album "Burnover," featuring pedal steel from Ben Rodgers. Freeman sings the title's gesture of indifference -- "all you get is a Gallic shrug" -- in a ragged, earnest falsetto that critics compared to Paul Westerberg at his most heartfelt.

hatchie|stay with me.fact: "Stay With Me," from Hatchie's 2019 debut album "Keepsake," started as a songwriting exercise for Harriette Pilbeam to try something more upbeat and dance-ready than her usual dream pop -- she'd written it with another artist in mind before realizing it fit her own record. She's called herself "a sucker for crying-in-the-club tracks," and it became one of her favorites on the album.

hayley williams|true believer.fact: Hayley Williams first released "True Believer," from her 2025 album "Ego Death at a Bachelorette Party," as an exclusive, passcode-gated track distributed through her hair-dye company Good Dye Young, before it reached streaming via her label Post Atlantic. She gave the song its live debut with a performance on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon" in October 2025.

heartworms|extraordinary wings.fact: "Extraordinary Wings" is a single from Heartworms -- the project of London artist Jojo Orme -- off her 2025 debut LP "Glutton for Punishment." The lyrics build a modern myth around flight and falling in the spirit of Icarus: the pull toward something extraordinary, shadowed by the fear of what it costs to reach that high.

hippo campus|forget it.fact: "Forget It," from Hippo Campus's 2024 album "Flood," came together after the band scrapped roughly five years of earlier material and started fresh, pouring more unguarded feelings into the new songs. The track turns on nostalgic questions about a first love -- who spoke first, what you were wearing -- regardless of whether you'll remember the details someday.

horsegirl|2468.fact: "2468" is a 2024 single from Horsegirl, the Chicago trio of Penelope Lowenstein, Nora Cheng, and Gigi Reece, released alongside the announcement of their Cate Le Bon-produced second album "Phonetics On and On." It marked a deliberate shift from the raw, bare-bones approach of their 2022 debut "Versions of Modern Performance," which the band had recorded live-to-tape with engineer John Agnello at Chicago's Electrical Audio.

horsegirl|julie.fact: "Julie," from Horsegirl's Cate Le Bon-produced 2025 album "Phonetics On and On," was originally written on acoustic guitar -- an instrument the band ultimately cut from the finished recording. The slower, more melancholic song reflects the loneliness of moving to a new city, paired with a video built around winter and unrequited love.

hotline tnt|julia's war.fact: "Julia's War" is the lead single from Hotline TNT's 2025 album Raspberry Moon, and it marks the first song the band recorded together as a full four-piece — frontman Will Anderson, guitarist Lucky Hunter, bassist Haylen Trammel, and drummer Mike Ralston — after earlier records had been largely a solo studio project. The band tracked the album with producer Amos Pitsch of Tenement. Anderson wanted the vocals to cut through clearly over the wall-of-guitar shoegaze sound, giving the song its earworm "na na na" chant.

hovvdy|forever.fact: "Forever" comes from Hovvdy's 2024 self-titled double album, a 19-song set released on Arts & Crafts. The song's music video, directed by Michael Rees, stars comedians Veronika Slowikowska and Kyle Chase. It was one of the songs the band used to announce the record.

iron and wine|what hurts worse.fact: "What Hurts Worse" opens Iron & Wine's 2018 EP Weed Garden, recorded at The Loft studio in Chicago with the same backing musicians — Joe Adamik, Jim Becker, Rob Burger, and Teddy Rankin-Parker — who played on the preceding album Beast Epic. It began as a leftover idea from the Beast Epic sessions that gained momentum on tour before the band finished it in the studio in early 2018. As with past Iron & Wine releases, frontman Sam Beam provided the cover artwork himself.

jenny hval|to be a rose.fact: "To Be a Rose" was the lead single from Jenny Hval's 2025 album Iris Silver Mist. Over a drum-machine beat, Hval half-speaks the line "A rose is a rose is a rose is a cigarette," nodding to Gertrude Stein's famous repeated-rose line. The accompanying video splices together tour footage Hval shot between 2015 and 2024, edited by Jenny Berger Myhre.

julien baker and torres|sylvia.fact: "Sylvia" is a track from Julien Baker & TORRES's 2025 collaborative country album Send a Prayer My Way. TORRES wrote it about adopting her dog Sylvia, recalling that while driving to pick the dog up from an upstate shelter, Dolly Parton's "Cracker Jack" came on the radio — a moment that felt like confirmation the dog was meant to be hers. The song celebrates the trust built in that relationship.

julie|flutter.fact: "flutter" was the debut single from the band julie, written and recorded in Los Angeles after members Keyan Pourzand and Alexandria Elizabeth moved there for architecture school. They finished recording it just before COVID lockdown and released it in 2020 hoping it might reach 1,000 streams; instead it went on to rack up more than 30 million plays, launching the band's career.

jungle|candle flame (feat. erick the arc.fact: "Candle Flame" was the lead single from Jungle's 2023 album Volcano, built around sped-up, soul-pitched vocal samples meant to capture the fire and passion of early love. The guest verse comes from Erick the Architect of the rap group Flatbush Zombies, whose energetic delivery added extra intensity to the track.

khruangbin|august 10.fact: "August 10," from Khruangbin's 2018 album Con Todo El Mundo, is a reworking of "August 12," the very first song the Houston trio ever wrote. To create it, the band listened to the original backwards, learned to play that reversed version, and recorded it roughly six years after the original, making it a deliberate piece of connective tissue between their first and second albums.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|deads.fact: "Deadstick" is the lead single from King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2025 album Phantom Island, and its title refers to the aviation term for a plane whose propeller has stalled mid-flight. The song features an elaborate horn arrangement by Chad Kelly, a member of the Los Angeles Philharmonic, which frontman Stu Mackenzie joked made the track sound "like the Blues Brothers on crack."

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|gila.fact: "Gila Monster" is a thrash-metal track from King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2023 concept album PetroDragonic Apocalypse, which frontman Stu Mackenzie has described as being about humankind and the planet wrapped in a mythology of "witches and dragons." On the song, co-vocalists Mackenzie and Ambrose Kenny-Smith trade lines before the whole band joins in on a chanted hook, making it one of the heaviest, most metal tracks in the group's catalog.

l.a. witch|the lines.fact: "The Lines" is a 2025 single from L.A. Witch's album DOGGOD, marking a shift toward colder post-punk and darkwave textures. Guitarist Sade Sanchez used chorus and flanger pedals along with vintage string machines like the Solina and Roland VP330 to get the track's wiry, European-leaning sound. Its music video features ASL interpreter and dancer Lark Detweiler signing out different meanings of the word "lines."

lcd soundsystem|new york i love you but.fact: "New York I Love You But You're Bringing Me Down" closes LCD Soundsystem's 2007 album Sound of Silver, and it was also the final song the band played at its original farewell concert at Madison Square Garden in 2011. Sound of Silver itself is dedicated to Dr. George Kamen, a New York psychiatrist and longtime friend of frontman James Murphy, and the album earned the band a Grammy nomination for Best Electronic/Dance Album.

lifeguard|it will get worse.fact: "It Will Get Worse" is the lead single from Ripped and Torn, the 2025 debut album by Chicago trio Lifeguard — Asher Case, Isaac Lowenstein, and Kai Slater. It's a fast, d-beat-driven punk track recorded with producer Randy Randall of the band No Age, capturing the energy of the house-party scene the band came up playing in.

m83|reunion.fact: "Reunion" was the second single from M83's 2011 double album Hurry Up, We're Dreaming, written by Anthony Gonzalez with Yann Gonzalez and Morgan Kibby, and produced by Gonzalez with Justin Meldal-Johnsen. Built on a yearning, 1980s-indebted guitar line and a driving drumbeat, the song uses imagery like a "lightning rod" to describe the joy of reconnecting with someone who feels renewing.

mamalarky|#1 best of all time.fact: "#1 Best of All Time" is a single from Mamalarky's 2025 album Hex Key, a fast, high-energy track that plays with the idea of competitiveness and betting on yourself even when the odds feel stacked against you. It followed the band's 2022 album Pocket Fantasy and helped introduce the more amped-up sound of Hex Key.

mamalarky|feels so wrong.fact: "Feels So Wrong" was the second single Mamalarky released after signing to Epitaph Records, a laid-back, sunny track leaning into 1970s AM-radio and yacht-rock textures reminiscent of Steely Dan. Bandleader Livvy Bennett wrote it around the idea that the things meant to make us feel good often bring less meaning than confronting what's actually hard. It appears on the band's 2025 album Hex Key.

matt berninger|bonnet of pins.fact: "Bonnet of Pins" is the lead single from Matt Berninger's second solo album, Get Sunk (2025), his first solo release since 2020's Serpentine Prison. Recorded with producer Sean O'Brien, the song builds from driving drums and guitars into a burst of horns and choral backing vocals under Berninger's baritone, with the album featuring guest contributions from musicians including Booker T. Jones and Meg Duffy of Hand Habits.

melody's echo chamber|the house that doe.fact: "The House That Doesn't Exist" is a 2025 single by Melody's Echo Chamber (the project of French musician Melody Prochet), released ahead of her fourth album, Unclouded. Built with producer Sven Wunder around swooping strings that climb and then resolve into a lower register, Prochet has described the song as turning the idea of a joyful human life in today's world into something that feels possible again. Its video was directed by longtime collaborator Diane Sagnier.

men i trust|i come with mud.fact: "I Come With Mud" opens Men I Trust's 2025 album Equus Asinus, from the Quebec City trio. The song begins with roughly ninety seconds of simple, repeated guitar chords before Emma Proulx's whispery vocals enter, setting a pastoral, Romantic-poetry-style tone — full of imagery about love and nature — that carries through the rest of the record.

mj lenderman|dancing in the club.fact: "Dancing in the Club" is MJ Lenderman's cover of a song by This Is Lorelei (Nate Amos), recorded with Amos's help in late 2024 and released on the 2025 deluxe edition of Amos's album Box for Buddy, Box for Star. Where the original is an upbeat synth-pop tune, Lenderman reworks it into a slower, twangy, acoustic version that became a regular part of his live sets.

mogwai|lion rumpus.fact: "Lion Rumpus" comes from Mogwai's 2025 album The Bad Fire (a Scottish term for Hell), built on big chord changes from keyboard and guitar and energized by drummer Martin Bulloch's fast playing. Its music video, directed by longtime collaborator Antony Crook, tells the story of Lawrence "Larry" Wilson, a man from Glasgow who moved to New York City and became a dog walker.

nation of language|now that you're gone.fact: "Now That You're Gone" is from Nation of Language's 2025 album Dance Called Memory, the band's full-length debut for Sub Pop. The track was recorded, produced, and mixed in New York by Nick Millhiser, a producer known for his work with LCD Soundsystem and Holy Ghost!, and mastered by Heba Kadry in Brooklyn.

pj harvey|the letter.fact: "The Letter" was the lead single from PJ Harvey's 2004 album Uh Huh Her, reaching No. 28 on the UK Singles Chart. For the first time since her 1993 demos collection, Harvey self-produced the record and played nearly every instrument herself, recording much of it alone on a four- and eight-track home setup before longtime collaborator Rob Ellis added drums.

puma blue|pretty.fact: "Pretty" was the lead single from Puma Blue's 2023 album Holy Waters, his first record made with a full live band rather than alone in his bedroom. It was recorded over two sessions at Echo Zoo Studios in Eastbourne, England, with a roster of co-producers including Andrew Sarlo (Bon Iver), Gabe Wax (Soccer Mommy), and Luke Smith (Foals, Depeche Mode).

radiohead|desert island disk.fact: "Desert Island Disk," from Radiohead's 2016 album A Moon Shaped Pool, takes its title from the BBC's long-running radio program Desert Island Discs. For this record, longtime producer Nigel Godrich changed his approach, capturing the band on tape as they worked through Thom Yorke's acoustic demos together for the first time, blending the group's early folk-leaning sound with its later electronic experimentation.

runo plum|sickness.fact: "Sickness" was the lead single Minneapolis musician Runo Plum used to announce their debut album Patching. The track, built around soft percussion and melancholic guitar, was co-produced with Lutalo and features contributions from instrumentalist Noa Francis.

sault|9.fact: "9" appears on SAULT's 2021 album Nine, a release the anonymous UK collective made available to buy or stream for only 99 days before pulling it. The song was co-written by singer Cleo Sol along with Dean "Inflo" Josiah and other members of the collective, and its buoyant guitar line offers an uplifting counterpoint to the album's heavier tracks.

siouxsie and the banshees|spellbound.fact: "Spellbound" was the first single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1981 album Juju, co-produced by the band with Nigel Gray. It was the first single to feature guitarist John McGeoch, who had joined after the band toured the UK in February 1981 to debut the new material, and the song reached No. 22 on the UK Singles Chart.

sprints|up and comer.fact: "Up and Comer" is a track from Irish band SPRINTS' 2024 debut album Letter to Self. Frontwoman Karla Chubb has said the song confronts the imposter syndrome and self-doubt she's felt since she first picked up an instrument, wondering if she'd always just be considered "good for a girl" rather than great, and she channels that frustration into one of the album's most ferocious tracks.

st. vincent|el mero cero.fact: "El Mero Cero" is a Spanish-language version of St. Vincent's "Big Time Nothing," one of several songs she re-recorded for Todos Nacen Gritando, a full Spanish-language companion to her 2024 album All Born Screaming. She made the companion record as a way of thanking her Latin American fans, releasing it about six months after the original English version came out.

sufjan stevens|so you are tired.fact: "So You Are Tired" was the lead single from Sufjan Stevens' 2023 album Javelin. The recording features a sizable cast of guest backing vocalists, including Bryce Dessner of the National, adrienne maree brown, Hannah Cohen, Pauline Delassus, Megan Lui, and Nedelle Torrisi, giving the song's back half a choir-like swell.

the antlers|hotel.fact: "Hotel" is the third track on The Antlers' 2014 album Familiars, a separate record from the band's earlier Hospice concept album. It was the second song released from Familiars, following lead single "Palace," and like the rest of the record it was mixed by Chris Coady; reviewers at the time noted the track's horn arrangement and groove marked a new, more upbeat direction for the band.

the avalanches|frontier psychiatrist.fact: "Frontier Psychiatrist," from The Avalanches' 2000 album Since I Left You, takes its title and several spoken-word samples from a 1960s comedy sketch called "Frontier Psychiatrist" by the duo Wayne and Shuster. The track is built from dozens of samples, reportedly more than any other song on the album, including a sampled horse whinny and a piece of music from the 1971 film Anna, all scratched together one phrase at a time by DJ Dexter Fabay.

the beths|whatever.fact: "Whatever" was the lead single from The Beths' debut EP Warm Blood, which the Auckland band independently released in March 2016 before they'd signed to a label. Produced by guitarist Jonathan Pearce, the song became an early breakout track that helped earn the four-piece glowing reviews from the New Zealand music press.

the last dinner party|nothing matters.fact: "Nothing Matters" was the debut single from UK band The Last Dinner Party, released in April 2023 ahead of their album Prelude to Ecstasy. Singer Abigail Morris originally wrote it as a slow, sad ballad, but the band reworked it into a maximalist anthem that went viral on TikTok and Instagram Reels, becoming the group's first UK Top 20 single at No. 16.

the linda lindas|no obligation.fact: "No Obligation" is the title track of The Linda Lindas' 2024 sophomore album. Bassist Eloise Wong wrote the song as the band's statement of purpose, opening with the line "I don't got no obligation" to declare that they make music for themselves rather than to meet anyone else's expectations.

the linda lindas|yo me estreso.fact: "Yo Me Estreso" is a Spanish-language song from The Linda Lindas' 2024 album No Obligation about the everyday experience of feeling stressed and anxious. Musically it was inspired by corridos tumbados, banda, and Duranguense styles filtered through the band's own punk sound, and its video features a guest appearance by "Weird Al" Yankovic on accordion.

the magnetic fields|100,000 fireflies.fact: "100,000 Fireflies" was the first single by The Magnetic Fields, taken from their 1991 debut album Distant Plastic Trees. It features the sparse, soprano vocals of Susan Anway, who sang on the band's early records but never performed live with them, and the song went on to become a cult favorite of 1990s mixtape culture, even earning a rocked-up cover from Superchunk.

the magnetic fields|california girls.fact: "California Girls," from The Magnetic Fields' 2008 album Distortion, is Stephin Merritt's tongue-in-cheek answer song to the Beach Boys' classic of the same name. For the whole record, Merritt aimed to sound "more Jesus and Mary Chain than Jesus and Mary Chain," running nearly every instrument, including guitars, piano, accordion, and strings, through tiny Smokey Amplifiers to build a deliberately overloaded wall-of-noise production.

the magnetic fields|i don't want to get.fact: "I Don't Want to Get Over You" appears on The Magnetic Fields' sprawling 1999 triple album 69 Love Songs, 69 tracks about love written and sung by frontman Stephin Merritt for Merge Records. Its deadpan baritone vocal and bittersweet melody made it one of the collection's most enduring cuts, later covered by artists including Ben Gibbard and Superchunk.

the reverend horton heat|psychobilly fre.fact: "Psychobilly Freakout" began as a 7-inch single released in December 1990 on Sub Pop's Singles Club, pressed in a limited run of 1,000 copies (250 on blue vinyl, the rest black) before landing on the band's 1992 debut album. The song later turned up in a Buell Motorcycles commercial and in the video games Guitar Hero II and Guitar Hero Smash Hits.

the smile|don't get me started.fact: "Don't Get Me Started" was recorded by The Smile — Radiohead's Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood with drummer Tom Skinner — across sessions in Oxford and at Abbey Road Studios, produced and mixed by Sam Petts-Davies, who also helmed the band's Wall of Eyes. It arrived on vinyl paired with a sister track, "The Slip," and its music video was directed by Weirdcore, the longtime visual collaborator of Aphex Twin.

the smile|zero sum.fact: "Zero Sum" was recorded during the same sessions that produced The Smile's 2024 album Wall of Eyes, but ended up instead on their follow-up record, Cutouts, released that October. The band had been playing the rhythmically busy, punk-funk track live for months before the studio version surfaced alongside a Weirdcore-directed video.

toro y moi|hollywood (feat. benjamin gib.fact: On "Hollywood," Toro y Moi's Chaz Bear teamed up with Death Cab for Cutie frontman Ben Gibbard, pairing a Blink-182-style guitar riff with a trap beat for an unusual genre mashup. The song appears on Bear's 2024 album Hole Erth, and Bear has said he'd long been a fan of Gibbard's music and it felt right to bring him onto the record.

toro y moi|tuesday.fact: "Tuesday" is the opening track and lead single from Toro y Moi's 2024 album Hole Erth, whose title nods to the countercultural 1960s-70s publication Whole Earth Catalog. The song blends Chaz Bear's longtime love of pop-punk with rap-rock, and its video was directed by India Sleem; the full album also features guest spots from Ben Gibbard, Don Toliver, Porches, and Kevin Abstract.

tv star|reality cheque.fact: "Reality Cheque" is the second track on TV Star's debut album Music For Heads, released via Father/Daughter Records. The Seattle/Tacoma band grew out of the Pacific Northwest DIY scene during the pandemic, and its lineup includes bassist Mark Palm, who also fronts the band Supercrush.

vampire weekend|capricorn.fact: "Capricorn" was the lead single from Vampire Weekend's 2024 album Only God Was Above Us, arriving five years after Father of the Bride. Frontman Ezra Koenig has said the wistful, string-laden track isn't about one specific person born under the sign, but uses Capricorn — the sign for people born at the very end of the year — as a lens for reflecting on time passing.

vampire weekend|mary boone.fact: "Mary Boone," from Vampire Weekend's Only God Was Above Us, builds its rhythm from a sample of Soul II Soul's 1989 hit "Back to Life (However Do You Want Me)" — the same drum loop Primitive Radio Gods used for their 1996 single "Standing Outside a Broken Phone Booth with Money in My Hand." The track layers in a full choir, strings, and warbling synths, and takes its title from a prominent figure in New York's 1980s art world.

vampire weekend|sympathy.fact: "Sympathy," from Vampire Weekend's 2019 album Father of the Bride, finds the band diving fully into dance music for the first time, with driving guitars and castanets giving it a sound critics compared to the dance-punk duo Basement Jaxx. When the band performed it on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, they reworked the all-hook dance track into a lush, propulsive, semi-acoustic arrangement.

water from your eyes|life signs.fact: "Life Signs" is the lead single from Water From Your Eyes' 2025 album It's a Beautiful Place, released via Matador Records. Written by the duo's Rachel Brown and Nate Amos and produced with engineer Howie Weinberg, the track opens with a nu-metal-style backbeat before pivoting into the band's signature dream-pop chorus; Amos has said it was the first WFYE song he wrote picturing the band playing venues bigger than a basement.

waxahatchee|bored.fact: Waxahatchee's Katie Crutchfield has said "Bored," from 2024's Tigers Blood, grew out of a soured platonic friendship and was written from a place of anger rather than her usual sadness or heartache. She's noted that writing from anger felt like a riskier departure for her, since her comfort zone as a songwriter usually sits somewhere between sadness and heartache.

westside cowboy|kick stones (the boys).fact: "Kick Stones (The Boys)" is the lead single and opening track from Westside Cowboy's debut album It Goes On, released via Island Records. The Manchester four-piece has said a live recording of The Velvet Underground's "What Goes On" was a reference point while writing the song, and its music video was filmed at an FC United of Manchester match, featuring the club's players, volunteers, and supporters.

whitney|damage.fact: "Damage" is a single from Whitney's 2025 album Small Talk, recorded by the duo of Max Kakacek (formerly of Smith Westerns) and Julien Ehrlich (formerly of Unknown Mortal Orchestra) without an outside producer, with friends dropping into the studio to add parts. Ehrlich has said the band spent a while trying to avoid writing another breakup song before accepting the song needed to be one, as long as it felt distinctly Whitney.

wilco|more....fact: "More..." is the second track on Wilco's surprise 2015 album Star Wars, which the band released as a free download with no advance notice and a title that has nothing to do with the film franchise. The song's acoustic-driven verses give way to gnarled, swirling guitar effects, a tonal shift that stood out on the brief, 11-track record.

wisp|see you soon.fact: "See You Soon" is the second single from Wisp's 2024 debut EP Pandora, released via Music Soup/Interscope. Built from a beat originally made by producer Grayskies, the shoegaze track pairs swirling, distorted guitars with Wisp's airy vocals, building toward a cathartic release in the chorus.

wisp|your face.fact: "Your Face" was Wisp's debut single, released in April 2023 — the song she's called "the one I owe for everything," since it launched her career. It went viral on TikTok and spent 15 weeks on Billboard's Hot Hard Rock Songs chart, peaking at No. 8, later becoming the lead single on her 2024 EP Pandora.

snail mail|light on our feet.fact: "Light on Our Feet" appears on Snail Mail's 2026 album Ricochet, released via Matador Records -- her first full-length in five years. The violin-and-strings-laden ballad draws an orchestral comparison to Smashing Pumpkins' Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness, part of an album the band has described as preoccupied with how time moves and what it leaves behind.

yeasayer|2080.fact: "2080" is a track from Yeasayer's 2007 debut album All Hour Cymbals, released as a single paired with "Sunrise" on the label We Are Free. The Brooklyn band, formed in 2006 by Chris Keating, Anand Wilder, and Ira Wolf Tuton, built the song's dense, layered sound from a blend of psychedelic, world-music, and funk-inspired textures that drew comparisons to Fleetwood Mac and Animal Collective. NPR featured it as a "Song of the Day" just weeks after its release.

mac demarco|a wolf who wears sheeps clot.fact: "A Wolf Who Wears Sheeps Clothes" is track nine on Mac DeMarco's 2017 album This Old Dog. The song takes the old fable of a predator disguised as something harmless and plays it almost literally, with DeMarco singing a gentle warning about not letting "the world outside the windowpane" get to your head. The album overall marked a more introspective turn for DeMarco, with songs reflecting on family and growing older.

new order|age of consent.fact: "Age of Consent" opens New Order's 1983 album Power, Corruption & Lies and was recorded at Britannia Row Studios in London. Driven by Peter Hook's melodic bass line, it's often cited as the bridge between the band's roots in Joy Division and their new synth-pop direction. The song was originally slated for the Wayne's World 2 soundtrack, but when the film's producers couldn't afford the licensing fee, a studio-musician cover was used in the movie instead.

stiff little fingers|alternative ulster.fact: Stiff Little Fingers formed in Belfast in 1977 out of a covers band called Highway Star, taking their new name from a song by English punk band the Vibrators. Their breakthrough single shares its title with Alternative Ulster, a Belfast punk fanzine started in 1977 by teenage writer Gavin Martin to chronicle the city's emerging punk scene. The song, released in 1978, became the band's signature anthem and anchored their debut LP, Inflammable Material.

kate bush|army dreamers.fact: "Army Dreamers" stood out on Kate Bush's 1980 album Never for Ever for being built around a hypnotic waltz rhythm, an unusual choice for a pop single. Released that September, it reached the UK Top 20. Its widely praised music video uses a visual trick in which the camera follows a young child who appears to age into a young adult within a single continuous shot.

mazzy star|be my angel.fact: "Be My Angel" appears on Mazzy Star's 1990 debut album, She Hangs Brightly. The band was formed in Santa Monica, California, around Hope Sandoval and David Roback, who had previously played in other Paisley Underground-scene bands including Rain Parade and Opal. The album blended dream pop, psychedelic rock, and folk influences and was first released on Rough Trade before being picked up by Capitol Records.

fiona apple|better version of me.fact: "Better Version of Me" appears on Fiona Apple's 2005 album Extraordinary Machine, which was Grammy-nominated for Best Pop Vocal Album. The album was actually recorded twice: an initial version produced by Jon Brion was shelved, and Apple re-recorded most of the songs, including this one, with producer Mike Elizondo for the final release.

beat happening|bewitched.fact: Beat Happening formed in Olympia, Washington in 1982 among students at Evergreen State College, and became pioneers of the lo-fi, twee-pop sound built on enthusiasm over technical polish. During the recording of "Bewitched," the opening track on their 1988 album Jamboree, guitarist Bret Lunsford's guitar string got caught on a protruding screw — rather than stop, he kept playing and hitting the string harder until it worked itself loose, and the take stayed on the record.

camera obscura|big love.fact: "Big Love" was the lead single from Camera Obscura's 2024 album Look to the East, Look to the West, the Scottish band's first new album in over a decade. The jangly, country-tinged track features pedal steel guitar from Tim Davidson, giving the Glasgow group's signature guitar-pop sound an extra twang.

squid|building 650.fact: "Building 650" is from Squid's 2025 album Cowards. Drummer and vocalist Ollie Judge wrote it after the English band's first trip to Japan, which happened just days after pandemic travel restrictions lifted in 2022 — he's said he wrote the lyrics about the particular feeling of being a stranger in an unfamiliar country, inspired partly by reading Ryu Murakami's novel In the Miso Soup and watching Lost in Translation on the flight over. Its music video was filmed on location in Japan.

beirut|caspian tiger.fact: "Caspian Tiger" by Beirut (the project of Zach Condon) was originally composed for the soundtrack of A Study of Losses, a production by the Swedish circus company Kompani Giraff. Named for an extinct tiger subspecies once found around the Caspian Sea, the track opens with solo piano before harp and brass enter, echoing the Renaissance and choral influences found throughout Condon's earlier work.

sports team|condensation.fact: "Condensation" is a single from Sports Team's 2025 album Boys These Days. The six-piece English band has said the song is literally about sweat — written after two years away from touring, it was meant to capture the physical feeling of being in a packed room with a crowd again. Musically, it leans into a bigger, Britpop-influenced sound reminiscent of bands like Blur.

katy kirby|cool dry place.fact: "Cool Dry Place" is the title track from Katy Kirby's 2021 debut album, released via Keeled Scales Records. The song builds from a whisper-sung, stripped-down opening into a sweeping folk-rock arrangement, with a deconstructed guitar solo that critics compared to Big Thief and Sandy (Alex G).
