Kirby has cited influences ranging from Leonard Cohen to contemporary indie-folk songwriters.

beck|dear life.fact: "Dear Life" opens Beck's 2017 album Colors, produced by Beck alongside Greg Kurstin. The track is built around a jaunty, jazz-tinged piano riff before opening up into rock guitar and vocal harmonies. It was released as an instant-download single when the album was announced, with an accompanying lyric video mixing live-action footage and psychedelic animation.

kilo kish|death fantasy (ft. miguel).fact: "Death Fantasy" is the third track on Kilo Kish's 2022 album American Gurl, featuring a guest vocal from Miguel and a music video directed by Dave Laven. The New York Times described its mood as more of a trance-like spell than a straightforward hook. The collaboration went well enough that Kilo Kish and Miguel teamed up again in 2025 for the song "Negotiate."

yo la tengo|did i tell you.fact: "Did I Tell You" first appeared on Yo La Tengo's 1987 album New Wave Hot Dogs, then was re-recorded as a hushed, late-night ballad for their 1990 covers-and-rarities album Fakebook. On the Fakebook version, Ira Kaplan's conversational lead vocal is paired with Georgia Hubley's airy backing harmonies, giving the song an intimate, heart-to-heart feel.

the beta band|dry the rain.fact: "Dry the Rain" opened The Beta Band's 1997 debut EP Champion Versions and later appeared on the compilation The Three EPs. Bassist Richard Greentree said the song was written to bridge folk music and hip-hop, and it builds from a simple acoustic opening into a brass-heavy, gospel-tinged finale featuring trumpet from Jonathan Levien. The track became the band's best-known song after a memorable cameo in the 2000 film High Fidelity.

mazzy star|flowers in december.fact: "Flowers in December" was the lead single from Mazzy Star's 1996 album Among My Swan, written by Hope Sandoval and David Roback and produced by Roback. It became the band's only UK Top 40 single, reaching No. 40, and its music video was directed by Kevin Kerslake.

youth lagoon|football.fact: "Football" is a 2024 single from Trevor Powers' project Youth Lagoon, reuniting him with producer Rodaidh McDonald. Powers has said the song uses sports as a metaphor, inspired by how throwing a ball was one of the few things he and his father connected over growing up, regardless of skill.

friendship|free association.fact: "Free Association" is the lead single from Friendship's album Caveman Wakes Up on Merge Records, with a video the band shot on Super 8 film on a closed boardwalk in Seaside Heights, New Jersey. Singer Dan Wriggins said he was inspired by folk singer Kath Bloom, and even borrowed the line "born with a weak heart" from David Byrne; the band also said the Mellotron sax and voice sounds on the track started as studio jokes they ended up keeping.

devo|gates of steel.fact: "Gates of Steel" began as an instrumental demo Mark Mothersbaugh recorded with Debbie Smith and Sue Schmidt of the band Chi-Pig, before Gerald Casale added lyrics he'd written separately. It was released as a single on October 6, 1980 from DEVO's album Freedom of Choice.

snocaps|heathcliff.fact: Snocaps is a band formed by twin sisters Allison Crutchfield (of Swearin') and Katie Crutchfield (Waxahatchee), along with MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook. "Heathcliff," the second track on their 2025 self-titled debut, was written and sung by Allison; the album was produced and almost entirely engineered by Cook, with all four musicians switching between instruments.

tame impala|i don't really mind.fact: "I Don't Really Mind" closes out Tame Impala's 2010 debut album InnerSpeaker, giving the record what's been called an "intergalactic bubblegum" finish. Kevin Parker recorded and produced the album himself in a mansion overlooking the Indian Ocean, and it was later mixed by Dave Fridmann, known for his work with MGMT and The Flaming Lips.

the xx|intro.fact: "Intro," the instrumental opening track of The xx's 2009 debut album xx, was composed by the band and produced by Jamie xx. It went on to soundtrack numerous TV commercials, served as the BBC's theme for the UK's 2010 general election coverage, and was later sampled by Rihanna on her 2011 album Talk That Talk.

the beths|jump rope gazers.fact: "Jump Rope Gazers" is the title track of The Beths' 2020 sophomore album. Singer Liz Stokes has described the title as an image of two people holding either end of a jump rope — connected, yet kept apart by the distance between them, which mirrors the song's theme of the push and pull in a relationship. The band performed it, complete with a clarinet solo, for NPR's Tiny Desk concert series.

the feelies|let's go.fact: "Let's Go" is track six on The Feelies' 1986 album The Good Earth, released on Coyote Records. The album was co-produced by R.E.M.'s Peter Buck, who had been a Feelies fan going back to his days working as a record store clerk.

superchunk|like a fool.fact: "Like a Fool" opens Superchunk's 1994 album Foolish, their first full-length for Merge Records, recorded at a breakneck pace at Pachyderm Studio with producer Brian Paulson. The band deliberately put it first because its clean, written-on-acoustic-guitar sound was a surprising change of pace from the crunchy power chords fans expected from them.

day wave|linger.fact: Day Wave, the project of Jackson Phillips, recorded a stripped-down cover of The Cranberries' "Linger" using just two guitars and a couple of voices. It appeared on the deluxe edition of his 2022 album Pastlife, closing the record out.

radiohead|lucky.fact: Radiohead recorded "Lucky" in just five hours on September 4, 1995, at producer Brian Eno's invitation, for The Help Album, a charity compilation benefiting War Child's work with children affected by the Bosnian war. The band considered it some of their best work at the time, and it was later included on their 1997 album OK Computer.

toro y moi|mirage.fact: "Mirage" opens Toro y Moi's fifth album Boo Boo (2017, Carpark Records). Chaz Bear has said he wrote the record as a form of personal therapy during a period of feeling self-conscious about fame after years of touring, drawing on influences like Travis Scott, Daft Punk, Frank Ocean, and Oneohtrix Point Never.

fleet foxes|montezuma.fact: "Montezuma" opens Fleet Foxes' 2011 album Helplessness Blues. The band dressed up the minimal, elegiac arrangement with unusual instrumentation for an indie-folk record, including zithers, tamburas, Tibetan singing bowls, and a Moog synthesizer.

waxahatchee|much ado about nothing.fact: "Much Ado About Nothing" is a Waxahatchee single Katie Crutchfield released in October 2024, in the same twangy folk-rock vein as her album Tigers Blood. It features MJ Lenderman on electric guitar along with Brad and Phil Cook, and later got a dedicated 7-inch release for Record Store Day 2025, backed with two more new recordings, "Mud" and "Next To Me."

the microphones|my roots are strong and.fact: "My Roots Are Strong and Deep" is track B2 on The Microphones' 2001 album The Glow Pt. 2, the project's third studio release. The song has a hymn-like quality, built around a clanging, unsteady piano sound and washes of distorted toy piano.

unknown mortal orchestra|necessary evil.fact: "Necessary Evil" is track 8 on Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2015 album Multi-Love, and its warm brass chorus was played by frontman Ruban Nielson's father, jazz musician Chris Nielson. The two have continued performing the song together since, including as part of a family trio (with Ruban's brother Kody on drums) at UMO's 2023 NPR Tiny Desk Concert.

the jesus and mary chain|never understan.fact: "Never Understand" was the debut single from The Jesus and Mary Chain, later included on their 1985 album Psychocandy. A demo tape of the song (along with "Upside Down") made its way to Primal Scream's Bobby Gillespie, who passed it to Alan McGee of Creation Records — leading McGee to become the band's manager and launch their career.

sharon van etten|one day.fact: "One Day" is the lead single from Sharon Van Etten's 2010 album Epic. The record's hazy, warm guitar sound carries an obvious Fleetwood Mac Rumours influence, and Van Etten even dedicated the album sleeve to the band, writing: "Dedicated to Fleetwood Mac. You changed my world."

yo la tengo|our way to fall.fact: "Our Way to Fall" appears on Yo La Tengo's 2000 album And Then Nothing Turned Itself Inside-Out, built around gently brushed drums, luminous organ, and Ira Kaplan's hushed vocal. The song later soundtracked a scene in the HBO series Six Feet Under, in the season 2 episode "Driving Mr. Mossback."

hot chip|over and over.fact: "Over and Over" was Hot Chip's breakthrough single, from their 2006 album The Warning. Joe Goddard built the track while trying to recreate the bassline from ESG's "Dance," and Alexis Taylor's lyrics riff on the band's love of hypnotic, repetitive music like Terry Riley's "A Rainbow in Curved Air" — NME later named it the best single of 2006.

joanna newsom|peach, plum, pear.fact: "Peach, Plum, Pear" comes from Joanna Newsom's 2004 debut album The Milk-Eyed Mender and is driven entirely by a harpsichord rather than her signature harp. The song has since been covered by Owen Pallett (performing as Final Fantasy) on his 2006 EP Young Canadian Mothers, as well as by the band Straylight Run.

wilco|quiet amplifier.fact: "Quiet Amplifier" is widely seen as the centerpiece of Wilco's 2019 album Ode to Joy, pairing unusually heavy, march-like percussion with a warm cloud of guitars and cymbal shimmer. Jeff Tweedy's lyrics turn the song toward a hopeful close, singing "Shy little stars will shine."

bon iver|rabi.fact: "RABi" closes Bon Iver's 2019 album i,i, built from an interplay of horns, synths, and layered group vocals. The album itself was rolled out unusually, with tracks released one by one, hour by hour, the day before its official August 9, 2019 release, and features guest contributions from James Blake, Aaron Dessner, Bruce Hornsby, Moses Sumney, and Channy Leaneagh.

future islands|ran.fact: "Ran" was the lead single from Future Islands' 2017 album The Far Field, produced by John Congleton. Its music video, directed by Albert Berney, takes the title literally — following frontman Samuel T. Herring on a run that starts in a Baltimore suburb in daylight and ends in the Maryland countryside after dark.

beth gibbons|reaching out.fact: "Reaching Out" is a single from Beth Gibbons' debut solo album, Lives Outgrown, released in 2024 via Domino Recording Company — her first-ever solo full-length after decades fronting Portishead. The album, produced by Gibbons, James Ford, and Lee Harris, took roughly ten years to record, and the song's video was an interactive piece made with visual artist Weirdcore.

mx lonely|return to sender.fact: "Return to Sender" is a single from Brooklyn alt-rock band MX LONELY, released in January 2026 ahead of their debut album All Monsters, out via Julia's War Recordings. The band is made up of vocalist Rae Haas, guitarist Jake Harms, and bassist Gabriel Garman, and the track features driving rhythms and distorted guitars typical of their sound.

black flag|rise above.fact: "Rise Above" opens Black Flag's 1981 debut album Damaged and became one of hardcore punk's defining anthems about refusing to be controlled by outside pressure. It's also tied to the band's lineup history: singer Henry Rollins joined Black Flag after being pulled onstage to sing at an impromptu New York show, impressing the band enough that they asked him to become their permanent vocalist.

islands|rough gem.fact: "Rough Gem" comes from Islands' 2006 debut album Return to the Sea. Islands was formed by Nicholas Thorburn and Jamie Thompson right after their previous band, The Unicorns, broke up in 2004, and the record — released on Rough Trade in Europe and Equator in North America — blended orchestral pop with playful horn-and-whistle hooks.

chromatics|running up that hill.fact: Chromatics recorded a synth-heavy cover of Kate Bush's 1985 classic "Running Up That Hill" for their 2007 album Night Drive. The cover later reached a much wider audience after being featured in Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 film Drive, helping cement Chromatics' reputation in the synthwave/neo-'80s revival scene.

devo|s.i.b. (swelling itching brain).fact: "S.I.B. (Swelling Itching Brain)" is track seven on DEVO's 1979 sophomore album Duty Now for the Future. It's one of several songs on the record where the band leaned further into blending synthesizers with guitar, a sonic shift that helped pave the way toward their more keyboard-driven, new-wave sound of the early 1980s.

alvvays|saved by a waif.fact: "Saved by a Waif" is track nine on Alvvays' 2017 album Antisocialites, written by Molly Rankin and Alec O'Hanley. The record was recorded across three studios — Kingsize Soundlabs in Los Angeles, Tarbox Road Studios in upstate New York, and Union Sound Studios in Toronto — with O'Hanley and John Congleton producing.

turnstile|seein' stars.fact: "SEEIN' STARS," from Turnstile's 2025 album Never Enough, is a softer, disco-tinged departure for the hardcore band, featuring guest vocals from Blood Orange's Dev Hynes and Paramore's Hayley Williams. Critics noted its guitar riff echoes The Police's "When the World Is Running Down, You Make the Best of What's Still Around."

the jesus and mary chain|sometimes alway.fact: "Sometimes Always" is a 1994 duet by The Jesus and Mary Chain's Jim Reid with Mazzy Star singer Hope Sandoval, released as the lead single from the album Stoned & Dethroned. In the song the two trade verses playing an ex-couple weighing whether to get back together, and it became a minor UK hit.

guided by voices|space gun.fact: "Space Gun" is the title track and opener of Guided by Voices' 26th studio album, released in 2018. The song famously kicks off with a found-sound recording of an airport restroom paper towel dispenser before launching into Robert Pollard's trademark power-pop guitar charge.

pulp|spike island.fact: "Spike Island," released in 2025 as Pulp's first new song in over a decade, is named after The Stone Roses' legendary 1990 outdoor concert in Widnes, Cheshire, that drew nearly 30,000 fans. Jarvis Cocker said he wasn't actually there, but wrote about the event's lasting cultural ripple through British music — and about a DJ who kept shouting "Spike Island, come alive!" over the PA.

hum|stars.fact: "Stars" was the second single from Hum's 1995 album You'd Prefer an Astronaut, peaking at No. 11 on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and helping the album sell over 250,000 copies. The song's video and track also got an unexpected pop-culture boost from an appearance on MTV's Beavis and Butt-Head.

the white stripes|the big three killed m.fact: "The Big Three Killed My Baby," from The White Stripes' self-titled 1999 debut album, takes aim at Detroit's "Big Three" automakers — Ford, GM, and Chrysler — criticizing the industry's practice of planned obsolescence and its resistance to innovations like electric engines. Jack White wrote the track, which was also released as a 7-inch single.

belle and sebastian|the blues are still.fact: "The Blues Are Still Blue" was the second single from Belle and Sebastian's 2006 album The Life Pursuit, produced by Tony Hoffer. It's an unusually straightforward, rollicking rock song for the famously twee Scottish band, and despite its energy the lyrics are, as critics have noted, nominally about something as mundane as doing laundry.

cheekface|the fringe.fact: "The Fringe" opens Cheekface's 2022 album It's Sorted with the band's signature deadpan, sing-speak style. The lyrics playfully reference musique concrete, avant-garde sculpture, and skeptical art critics, poking fun at the pursuit of being seen as artistically unconventional.

broadcast|the games you play.fact: "The Games You Play" surfaced on Broadcast's 2024 rarities collection Spell Blanket, released via Warp Records. It's actually a vocal version of an earlier instrumental called "DDL," which had previously appeared on the All Tomorrow's Parties 1.0 compilation and the band's 2006 odds-and-ends album The Future Crayon, with the newly unearthed recordings dating from 2006-2009.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|the riv.fact: "The River" opens King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's 2015 album Quarters!, clocking in at exactly 10 minutes and 10 seconds to match the record's concept of four equal-length tracks. Built in a non-standard 5/4 time signature inspired by Dave Brubeck's "Take Five," the song moves through a jazzy, improvisational structure, and its parts were pieced together in unusual locations, including harmonica recorded in a touring van and vocals cut in a rented London rehearsal room.

beck|thinking about you.fact: Beck released "Thinking About You" as a surprise single in 2024 with no advance warning, marking his first new material since a 2022 Neil Young cover. The mellow, acoustic track was recorded in the same studio where Beck made his 2003 album Sea Change, and he debuted it live on Jimmy Kimmel Live.

medicine|time baby iii.fact: "Time Baby III" is a special version of Medicine's song recorded for the 1994 film The Crow's soundtrack, featuring guest vocals from Cocteau Twins singer Elizabeth Fraser (a different version, "Time Baby II," appears in the film itself). The Los Angeles shoegaze band, led by guitarist Brad Laner, got its distinctive tone by running guitars through a Yamaha 4-track recorder.

the kills|u r a fever.fact: "U.R.A. Fever" opens The Kills' 2008 album Midnight Boom, built from clattering, scrapyard-style percussion and metallic clunks rather than conventional drums. The duo recorded the album in Benton Harbor, Michigan, working with producer Alex Epton to push their raw blues-rock sound into grittier, more rhythmic territory.

r.e.m.|we walk.fact: On "We Walk," from R.E.M.'s 1983 debut Murmur, the odd dull thud heard throughout the track is actually a slowed-down recording of drummer Bill Berry playing pool. It's one of several unconventional recording tricks producers Mitch Easter and Don Dixon used to give the album its distinctive, hazy atmosphere.

the smiths|well i wonder.fact: "Well I Wonder" was the first song written for The Smiths' 1985 album Meat Is Murder. Guitarist Johnny Marr deliberately moved back to Manchester during pre-production to capture the right rainy atmosphere for the band's more instrumental, textured songs, and the finished track closes with the actual sound of rain and one of Morrissey's rare falsetto vocal turns.

brittany howard|what now.fact: "What Now" is the title track and lead single from Brittany Howard's second solo album, released in 2023 as her label debut on Island Records following 2019's Jaime. Howard wrote and produced the song with longtime Alabama Shakes collaborator Shawn Everett, recording at two storied Nashville studios, Sound Emporium and historic RCA Studio B.

friko|where we've been.fact: "Where We've Been" opens Chicago band Friko's 2024 debut album Where We've Been, Where We Go From Here, and has become the group's de facto theme song. Songwriters Niko Kapetan and Bailey Minzenberger have said the track's live performances typically close their shows, but they deliberately moved it to the album's opening slot so first-time listeners would get the full scope of the band right away.

rilo kiley|with arms outstretched.fact: "With Arms Outstretched," from Rilo Kiley's 2002 album The Execution of All Things, features a makeshift boy choir made up of friends and bandmates, including singer-songwriter Conor Oberst. The song has had a long cultural afterlife, soundtracking the final scene of Showtime's Weeds (mirroring its use in the show's pilot) and later appearing in the Looking for Alaska miniseries.

new order|your silent face.fact: "Your Silent Face," from New Order's 1983 album Power, Corruption & Lies, was written by Bernard Sumner as a tribute to Kraftwerk, carrying a melody reminiscent of the German electronic pioneers' work. Its original working title was simply "KW1," short for "Kraftwerk One," before the band gave it a proper name for release.
